whyRecommended: Middle East policy analysts, diplomats, intelligence analysts, and international affairs specialists use regional comparison and power analysis to prepare country briefings, interpret alliances, and assess political developments.

title: Law and Religion
courseDescription: Examines the Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses of the First Amendment and the legal boundaries between government and religion. Students analyze constitutional disputes involving government support of religion, religious liberty, and laws that burden religious practices.
whyRecommended: Constitutional attorneys, religious liberty counsel, civil rights policy analysts, and legislative analysts use this knowledge to review proposed policies, construct constitutional arguments, and assess church-state legal risks.

title: Arabic IV
courseDescription: Continues Arabic III by strengthening fourth-semester speaking, listening, reading, and writing proficiency. Students complete structured language work inside and outside the classroom, while heritage speakers consult the instructor to determine appropriate placement.
whyRecommended: Foreign service officers, international development coordinators, Arabic-language program assistants, and community outreach coordinators use developing Arabic proficiency for basic professional interactions, community communication, and continued advanced language training.
prerequisites: AB 103 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Chinese IV
courseDescription: Reviews and reinforces the language skills developed throughout Chinese I, II, and III while helping students reach intermediate-low proficiency. Students strengthen practical Chinese speaking, listening, reading, and writing for continued study and increasingly independent communication.
whyRecommended: Foreign service officers, international business coordinators, China research assistants, and localization project coordinators use developing Chinese proficiency to support basic professional communication, regional research, and multilingual projects.
prerequisites: CI 103 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Intermediate Italian II
courseDescription: Reviews and reinforces the Italian skills developed in IT 101 through IT 103 while moving students toward intermediate proficiency in reading, writing, speaking, listening, and cultural knowledge. Students work with authentic readings, Italian discussions, film clips, and required language-laboratory activities.
whyRecommended: Italian travel operations coordinators, study-abroad assistants, cultural exchange staff, and localization assistants use intermediate Italian to communicate with partners, interpret routine materials, and support Italy-focused programs.
prerequisites: IT 103 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Comprehensive Beginning French
courseDescription: Compresses the content of FR 101 and FR 102 into one intensive semester covering French reading, listening, speaking, writing, grammar, and cultural knowledge. Students attend six class sessions each week, complete required laboratory study, and prepare to begin intermediate French.
whyRecommended: International program assistants, travel coordinators, cultural exchange staff, and community outreach assistants use the French foundation developed here when supporting French-speaking participants and preparing for intermediate language training.
prerequisites: Open to students beginning a second modern language or placed into FR 101 or FR 102
Closed to students who completed FR 101, FR 102, or equivalent

title: Comprehensive Beginning Spanish
courseDescription: Compresses the content of SN 101 and SN 102 into one intensive semester covering Spanish reading, listening, speaking, writing, grammar, and cultural knowledge. Students attend six class sessions each week, complete required laboratory study, and prepare to enter intermediate Spanish.
whyRecommended: International program assistants, travel coordinators, community outreach staff, and education assistants use the Spanish foundation developed here when supporting Spanish-speaking participants and preparing for intermediate language training.
prerequisites: Open to students beginning a second modern language or placed into SN 102
Closed to students who completed SN 101, SN 102, or equivalent

title: Business French: A Functional Approach
courseDescription: Develops functional French for business settings while introducing the economic and professional environment of the French-speaking world. Students learn technical vocabulary, business idioms, cultural expectations, and the rules used to write formal business correspondence.
whyRecommended: International sales coordinators, export account coordinators, global marketing specialists, and French-language client service professionals use these skills to write correspondence, communicate with clients, and navigate Francophone business practices.

title: Contemporary Spanish Civilization and Culture
courseDescription: Examines Spain's historical, political, and cultural development from Francisco Franco's death in 1975 to the present. Students use Spanish-language readings, films, and music to analyze the transition to democracy, the cultural expansion of the 1980s, regional politics, and Spain's cultural diversity.
whyRecommended: Spain program coordinators, foreign service officers, Iberian market researchers, and cultural affairs specialists use this knowledge to interpret Spanish political developments, regional identities, media, and cultural expectations.
prerequisites: SN 203 or SN 217 or written permission of the instructor

title: History of the Spanish Language
courseDescription: Traces Spanish from its origins in spoken Latin through its development into the modern language. Students examine how historical events produced language changes and how literature contributed to the standardization of Spanish.
whyRecommended: Linguists, Spanish teachers, translators, and localization specialists use historical language analysis to explain word origins, recognize structural changes, and make informed translation and language-use decisions.
prerequisites: SN 203 or SN 217 or written permission of the instructor

title: U.S. History Since Reconstruction
courseDescription: Examines United States history from the Civil War through the country's development as an industrial and international power. Students analyze Reconstruction, immigration, industrialization, democratic reform, the world wars, the Great Depression, the Cold War, postwar culture, and modern social movements.
whyRecommended: Public historians, policy research analysts, museum educators, and social studies teachers use this historical framework to explain modern institutions, connect policies to their origins, and interpret major changes in American society.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The Civil Rights Era
courseDescription: Examines the Black struggle for equality from disfranchisement in the 1890s through the civil rights conflicts of the 1960s and 1970s. Students analyze institutional and cultural barriers in the North and South and the organized strategies African Americans and their allies used to challenge them.
whyRecommended: Civil rights policy analysts, museum educators, public historians, and advocacy researchers use this knowledge to document discrimination, explain movement strategies, interpret legislation, and connect current policy debates to historical institutions.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Africa in the Age of Globalization
courseDescription: Examines African history since World War II through decolonization, the Cold War, independence, and the post-Cold War era of globalization. Students evaluate the development choices available to newly independent states and how colonial legacies constrained political, social, and economic progress.
whyRecommended: Africa policy analysts, international development specialists, country risk analysts, and NGO program officers use this historical context to assess development barriers, interpret government decisions, and design regionally informed programs.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Introduction to Modern Latin America
courseDescription: Surveys Latin American history from pre-Columbian societies to the present while examining political, social, and economic change across Central and South America. Students analyze the roles of Indigenous peoples, Africans, people of mixed ancestry, and women in forming regional identities, along with United States-Latin American relations and major regional trends.
whyRecommended: Latin America analysts, foreign service officers, international development specialists, and cultural affairs officers use this regional history to prepare country briefings, interpret U.S.-Latin American relations, and assess political and economic developments.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Law, Lawyers, and Litigants in European History
courseDescription: Traces European law and jurisprudence from Ancient Rome through the Enlightenment, including Roman legal compilations, canon law, the medieval ius commune, professional legal practice, and codification. Students examine how legal institutions interacted and how law both influenced and responded to social and cultural change.
whyRecommended: Legal researchers, law librarians, public historians, and attorneys use this historical foundation to trace legal doctrines, interpret institutional change, and explain how modern European legal systems developed.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: History of South Asia in the Twentieth Century
courseDescription: Examines twentieth-century South Asia with primary attention to India and additional coverage of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Burma. Students analyze colonial rule, nationalism, independence movements, Partition, religion, economic development, foreign policy, technological change, and regional cultural life.
whyRecommended: South Asia policy analysts, foreign service officers, international development specialists, and regional risk analysts use this history to prepare country briefings, interpret political divisions, and evaluate regional development and diplomatic issues.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The Golden Age of Athens
courseDescription: Examines the political and cultural forces that shaped fifth-century Athens, including Athenian democracy, the Persian Wars, Pericles, imperial expansion, and the Peloponnesian War. Students evaluate how democratic institutions, military power, philosophy, and political conflict contributed to Athens' rise and decline.
whyRecommended: Classical historians, museum curators, civic education specialists, and archaeology program coordinators use this material to interpret democratic institutions, explain classical conflicts, and develop historically accurate educational content.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Gender, Race, and Class in Modern Europe
courseDescription: Examines modern European history from the French Revolution to the present through the experiences of women, people of color, workers, and the poor. Students analyze how gender, race, and class were used to regulate people and how marginalized groups resisted through feminism, labor conflict, anti-imperialism, migration, and other movements.
whyRecommended: European affairs researchers, migration policy analysts, museum curators, and public historians use this analysis to explain inequality, interpret social movements, and develop historically grounded policy and educational materials.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Introduction to the Modern Middle East
courseDescription: Surveys the Arab world, Turkey, and Iran from World War I to the present. Students examine imperialism, nationalism, modern state formation, Islamism, oil politics, the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, the Gulf Wars, and the 2011 Arab uprisings.
whyRecommended: Middle East policy analysts, foreign service officers, energy policy analysts, and international business risk analysts use this history to interpret regional conflicts, assess political risk, and explain how oil, nationalism, and state formation affect current decisions.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The Black Death in Global Perspective
courseDescription: Examines the Black Death as a pandemic affecting Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East rather than as an exclusively European event. Students combine historical texts with evidence from paleobiology and archaeology to evaluate the plague's spread, regional responses, and political, religious, and social consequences.
whyRecommended: Public health historians, global health policy analysts, museum curators, and historical researchers use these skills to reconstruct disease outbreaks, compare societal responses, and communicate how pandemics reshape institutions.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The History of Modern China
courseDescription: Surveys major social, political, economic, and cultural developments in China from the early Qing dynasty through the People's Republic. Students use discussions, films, analytical papers, and a library project to connect historical transformations with modern Chinese society.
whyRecommended: China research analysts, foreign service officers, international business analysts, and cultural affairs specialists use this history to prepare country reports, evaluate market and political conditions, and interpret Chinese institutions and culture.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The First World War
courseDescription: Examines the origins, progression, and aftermath of the First World War across its European and global theaters. Students analyze soldiers' and civilians' experiences, colonial participation, home-front mobilization, gender, revolutions, border changes, international organizations, and the war's political and cultural memory.
whyRecommended: Military historians, foreign policy analysts, museum curators, and conflict researchers use this knowledge to explain the origins of international crises, interpret wartime evidence, and trace the borders and institutions created by global conflict.

title: Modern Iran Between Monarchy, Democracy, and Theocracy
courseDescription: Examines Iranian history from the Qajar dynasty through the Pahlavi monarchy, the 1979 Iranian Revolution, and the Islamic Republic. Students analyze modernization, European influence, oil politics, revolutionary change, Iran's relationship with the West, and its development as a regional power.
whyRecommended: Iran policy analysts, foreign service officers, energy policy analysts, and geopolitical risk analysts use this history to assess Iranian institutions, explain revolutionary politics, and evaluate regional and oil-related policy risks.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Psychology of Learning
courseDescription: Provides an in-depth examination of classical conditioning, instrumental learning, and cognitively based learning theories. Students apply these theories to human behavior and clinical situations involving behavior acquisition, reinforcement, and change.
whyRecommended: Behavior technicians, clinical research assistants, instructional designers, and learning and development specialists use these theories to design reinforcement plans, structure training, and evaluate how people acquire or change behaviors.

title: Sensation and Perception
courseDescription: This class follows sensory information from environmental stimulation through the sensory organs and into human perception. Students connect physiology to everyday experience by studying how emotion, learning, thought, and personal expectations can change what a person perceives.
whyRecommended: For UX researchers, human-factors specialists, occupational therapists, and perception researchers, the course builds the ability to separate what users physically sense from how attention and prior experience shape what they report.

title: Sleep, Circadian Rhythms, and Behavior
courseDescription: Students study how sleep and circadian rhythms are measured, regulated, and connected to cognition, performance, behavior, and physical and mental health. The course also applies sleep research to workplace scheduling, education, healthcare, public policy, and the treatment of sleep problems and disorders.
whyRecommended: Sleep technologists can apply the measurement concepts, while health psychologists, occupational-health specialists, and policy analysts use circadian evidence to address fatigue, scheduling, safety, and performance.

title: Life Span Development
courseDescription: This class tracks how people change from childhood through later adulthood from biological, behavioral, cognitive, and social perspectives. Students compare development across life stages and consider how changes in health, thinking, behavior, and relationships affect the support a person may need.
whyRecommended: A life-span perspective helps school counselors interpret age-appropriate behavior, human-services case managers plan support during major transitions, and gerontology professionals respond to changes in later adulthood.

title: Psychology of Personality
courseDescription: Students compare psychodynamic, trait, humanistic, and other major explanations of personality using research connected to each approach. They learn how personality develops, how different theories organize patterns of thought and behavior, and how to apply more than one framework when interpreting a person or case.
whyRecommended: Comparing personality frameworks gives counselors a disciplined foundation for case formulation and helps talent-development and market-research professionals interpret behavioral patterns without relying on stereotypes.

title: Introduction to Health Psychology
courseDescription: This course connects everyday behavior and environmental conditions to health and disease, with attention to diet, exercise, stress, smoking, weight, and pollutants. Students consider personal responsibility, behavior change, healthcare decisions, and nontraditional approaches to medicine without reducing health outcomes to individual choice alone.
whyRecommended: Public health educators can turn behavior-change evidence into prevention campaigns, while patient advocates and wellness coordinators use it to address stress, exercise, smoking, and adherence to health plans.

title: Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders
courseDescription: The course introduces major classes of psychoactive drugs, their effects, and the criteria used to identify substance-related and addictive disorders. Students compare treatment models and interventions, examine how addiction affects families, and consider the practical role of 12-step programs in recovery.
whyRecommended: Its practical diagnostic and intervention focus directly supports work in addiction counseling, behavioral-health intake, case management, and community recovery programs.

title: Multicultural Issues in Psychology
courseDescription: Students examine how culture and identity affect psychological research, professional practice, and the way behavior is interpreted. Through practice guidelines and structured self-reflection, they consider racial identity, sexual orientation, cultural assumptions, and the delivery of psychological services to diverse populations.
whyRecommended: Cultural self-reflection and practice guidelines prepare future counselors, school psychologists, inclusion specialists, and community-program staff to recognize bias and adapt services for diverse clients.

title: Psychology of Religion
courseDescription: This class approaches religion as a psychological experience that can be studied through learning, development, mental health, peak experiences, and social behavior. Students compare major psychological explanations of religious experience and evaluate research involving belief, prejudice, personal growth, and well-being.
whyRecommended: Chaplains and pastoral counselors gain language for recognizing the psychological dimensions of spiritual experience, while clinicians and researchers learn to study belief and well-being without treating religion as one uniform phenomenon.

title: Psychology of Gender
courseDescription: Students trace how gender develops through psychological processes, social expectations, media representation, parenting, relationships, sexuality, and ideas about masculinity. They also use feminism and intersectionality to evaluate research claims about sex differences and identify where study design or interpretation may introduce bias.
whyRecommended: In counseling, gender-equity advocacy, public relations, and user research, the course helps professionals evaluate gender claims and recognize when messages, services, or policies reinforce stereotypes.

title: Psychological Tests and Measurements
courseDescription: Students learn how individual and group psychological tests are designed, standardized, and validated before their scores can support real decisions. They apply measurement theory to intelligence, aptitude, and personality testing while examining what specific tests can diagnose and where their interpretations have limits.
whyRecommended: Assessment assistants, school psychologists, talent-selection specialists, and program evaluators rely on these measurement skills to choose instruments, interpret scores, and explain testing limitations responsibly.

title: Ethics in Psychology
courseDescription: Students work through professional and scientific ethics problems that arise in psychological research and practice. Using case studies, they apply ethical standards, identify competing responsibilities, compare possible responses, and defend decisions during seminar discussions.
whyRecommended: Clinical research coordinators, behavioral-health case managers, and future psychologists use this training to identify ethical risks, protect clients and participants, and document defensible professional decisions.

title: Theology and the Arts: A Global History
courseDescription: This course follows the changing relationship between Christian theology and the arts across two thousand years and multiple regions. Students interpret theological ideas in visual art, music, and architecture, consider how artists have challenged religious teachings, and apply their analysis during a museum visit.
whyRecommended: Museum educators, curators, arts writers, and sacred-space designers benefit from understanding how art and architecture communicate, reinterpret, or challenge theological ideas across cultures.

title: Women in the Christian Tradition
courseDescription: Students trace the contributions of women to Christianity through primary writings and historical research. Topics include women in the early church, medieval widows and abbesses, reformers, evangelical women, feminist critiques, and women's religious experiences in the United States.
whyRecommended: Archivists, museum educators, religious-studies researchers, and ministry leaders can use the course to recover overlooked sources and explain how women shaped Christian institutions and debates.

title: History and Storytelling in the Bible
courseDescription: This class compares the Bible's accounts of Israel, early Judaism, Jesus, and the early Christian church with evidence from other historical sources. Students learn to distinguish a text's historical claims from its rhetorical and theological purposes instead of treating every biblical narrative as modern historical reporting.
whyRecommended: Biblical researchers, editors, educators, and faith-based communicators need this source-comparison skill to explain where theological storytelling and historical evidence support, complicate, or challenge one another.

title: Christian Theology and World Religions
courseDescription: Students compare historical and contemporary Christian approaches to other religious traditions, with sustained attention to at least one non-Christian tradition. The course helps them identify genuine agreements and disagreements between traditions without reducing different religions to interchangeable beliefs.
whyRecommended: Interfaith coordinators, diplomats, religious-affairs analysts, and chaplains use comparative theological reasoning to discuss religious differences accurately and work across communities without relying on stereotypes.

title: Why Do We Suffer? Theological and Spiritual Perspectives on Suffering
courseDescription: Students compare Buddhist, Islamic, Jewish, Christian, philosophical, political, and musical responses to physical and emotional suffering. They evaluate whether particular beliefs and practices support healing, create additional harm, or fail to address what a suffering person actually needs.
whyRecommended: Chaplains, grief counselors, healthcare advocates, and trauma-informed ministry workers can draw on these perspectives when supporting people whose pain involves spiritual, cultural, and emotional questions.

title: Ethics: Immigration and Catholic Social Teaching
courseDescription: Students use Christian scripture, theological thinkers, and Catholic social teaching to evaluate the ethics of immigration. They apply those sources to public policy, economic interests, political responsibilities, and the treatment of migrants rather than discussing immigration only as an abstract moral issue.
whyRecommended: Immigration advocates, nonprofit policy staff, pastoral leaders, and public-interest lawyers gain a structured way to evaluate immigration policies, advocacy claims, and community responses through Catholic social ethics.

title: Worship, Culture, and Justice
courseDescription: Students study how worship practices interact with culture and how including or excluding cultural traditions affects religious communities. Using theology, liturgical texts, sociology of religion, and cultural anthropology, they evaluate worship among immigrants, racial minorities, people with disabilities, and communities in the United States and the majority world.
whyRecommended: Campus ministers, worship planners, community organizers, and inclusion specialists can use the course to evaluate who is represented, welcomed, or excluded when institutions design public religious practices.

title: Encounters between Christianity, Judaism, and Islam
courseDescription: Students compare medieval and contemporary encounters among Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, with particular attention to Jewish responses to Christian and Islamic claims of Abrahamic heritage. They analyze disagreements about God, creation, revelation, prophets, human nature, and the limits of religious language without treating the three traditions as interchangeable.
whyRecommended: Interfaith program coordinators, chaplains, religious-affairs analysts, and researchers use this kind of precise comparison to facilitate dialogue while accurately representing where religious communities agree and disagree.

title: War, Health, and Peacebuilding
courseDescription: Students study how armed conflict damages individual health, public-health systems, and access to medical care, then consider how healthcare work can contribute to peacebuilding. The course connects war ethics, global health, religious responses, and reconciliation so students can evaluate support for communities recovering from conflict.
whyRecommended: The course prepares humanitarian health officers, peacebuilding coordinators, and global-health analysts to connect damage to health systems with ethical recovery, reconciliation, and community-support strategies.

title: Bioethics and Social Justice
courseDescription: Students apply social-justice principles to decisions in biomedical research, healthcare policy, and medical practice. Using theological sources and cases ranging from Henrietta Lacks to the COVID-19 pandemic, they identify who receives medical benefits, who bears risks, and how institutions should respond to unequal outcomes.
whyRecommended: Clinical research coordinators, healthcare policy analysts, compliance professionals, and forensic scientists rely on these skills when reviewing medical practices for fairness, informed consent, institutional responsibility, and defensible ethical standards.

title: Religion, Poverty, and American Health Care
courseDescription: This course shows how religious institutions have shaped American healthcare and how poverty, social identity, and religious difference affect access to care. Students examine Catholic hospitals, nonprofit organizations, and partnerships between religious communities and medical agencies to determine whether limited resources are being used in culturally sensitive and sustainable ways.
whyRecommended: Hospital community-benefit staff, patient advocates, faith-based nonprofit managers, and public-health coordinators can apply this material when building programs for low-income and religiously diverse communities.

title: Character Ethics: Becoming Good
courseDescription: Students compare major Christian approaches to ethics while focusing on how habits and character shape moral choices. Case studies ranging from war to social media require them to explain why an action is good, what kind of person it encourages someone to become, and how repeated choices build character.
whyRecommended: Whether setting workplace standards, advising students, leading a ministry, or designing leadership training, professionals use character-based reasoning to translate broad values into expectations for everyday conduct.

title: The Ethics of War and Peace
courseDescription: Students compare holy-war traditions, just-war reasoning, and pacifism across Jewish, Christian, and Islamic history. They then evaluate twentieth-century Catholic peace efforts and contemporary initiatives to determine how religious ideas are translated into decisions about violence, restraint, reconciliation, and peace.
whyRecommended: Peacebuilding specialists, humanitarian policy analysts, military-ethics researchers, and interfaith mediators apply these frameworks when assessing whether force is justified and what responsible reconciliation requires afterward.

title: The Holocaust and Jewish Law
courseDescription: Students study how Jewish communities interpreted and continued observing Jewish law under genocidal persecution during the Holocaust. The course first explains how Jewish law develops and functions, then uses historical debates to show how people made religious and ethical decisions under conditions designed to destroy communal life.
whyRecommended: Holocaust museum educators, religious archivists, genocide researchers, and Jewish studies coordinators need this historical and legal grounding to explain responses to persecution without flattening the experiences or decisions of affected communities.

title: Intermediate Accounting I
courseDescription: Focuses on the development of financial information for investors and others external to the organization. Topics include review of the accounting cycle, cash, receivables, inventories, preparation of financial statements, and revenue recognition. Students learn to prepare, understand, and interpret financial statements.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate accounting i and strengthens skills used in accounting work.

title: Intermediate Accounting II
courseDescription: Students learn to develop and analyze the information reported in financial statements. Topics include operational assets, intangible assets, short-term and long-term investments, short-term and long-term liabilities, leases, and financial analysis. Pronouncements of the AICPA, FASB, IFRS, and SEC are an integral part of the course.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate accounting ii and strengthens skills used in accounting work.

title: Intermediate Accounting III
courseDescription: Students learn to develop and analyze information reported in financial statements. Topics include stockholder's equity, dilutive securities and earnings per share, pensions, income taxes, statement of cash flows, accounting changes, and financial analysis. Pronouncements of the AICPA, FASB, IFRS, and SEC are an integral part of the course.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate accounting iii and strengthens skills used in accounting work.

title: International Travel Course: Comparative Business
courseDescription: The operation of business today requires that firms take an international perspective to remain competitive and profitable. Students are familiarized with key aspects of the international political, economic, and institutional environment in which firms operate. Topics covered include: how and why the world's cultures, countries, and regions differ; the economics and politics of international trade and investment; international challenges related to ethics, corporate social responsibility, and sustainability; the functions and forms of the global monetary system including exchange rates; and the strategies and structures of international businesses.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in international travel course: comparative business and strengthens skills used in accounting / finance work.
prerequisites: AC 315: A cumulative 2.500 GPA or higher; Written or electronic permission of the instructor
FI 315: A cumulative GPA of 2.500 or higher; Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Global Business Study Tour
courseDescription: Designed to expose students to different international cultures. The course encompasses ethics, the basic concepts of international accounting standards and their comparison with U.S. GAAP, sustainability, and cultural practices.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in global business study tour and strengthens skills used in accounting work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomore, juniors, or seniors

title: Advanced Accounting
courseDescription: Focuses on specialized financial accounting topics including business combinations and consolidated financial statements; financial reporting for multinational corporations, including foreign currency translation and transactions; and hedge accounting, with a primary emphasis on foreign exchange risk. Students develop a thorough understanding of these topics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced accounting and strengthens skills used in accounting work.

title: Individual Income Tax
courseDescription: Studies the federal tax law for preparation of individual income tax returns. A consideration of the ethical obligations of tax preparers is also included.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in individual income tax and strengthens skills used in accounting work.

title: Forensic Accounting Seminar
courseDescription: A synthesis of prior forensic accounting knowledge, the course combines real-world case studies, faculty experiences, and guest lectures to enhance and showcase the ability to identify and analyze forensic accounting issues and reach well-founded conclusions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic accounting seminar and strengthens skills used in accounting work.

title: Forensic Accounting
courseDescription: Focuses on fraud principles that relate to the psychology of fraud, basic fraud schemes including asset misappropriations, corruption, and fraudulent financial statements. An emphasis is placed on the examination and review of major fraud schemes, investigative strategies, and controls utilized to detect and prevent the impact fraud has on an organization. Fraud principles that relate to the psychology of fraud, basic fraud schemes including asset misappropriations, corruption, and fraudulent financial statements are also studied.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic accounting and strengthens skills used in accounting work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, or seniors

title: Basic Volunteer Income Tax Assistance
courseDescription: Students gain practical experience in preparing federal and state individual income tax returns. Students complete a training program and must pass an IRS basic-level certification exam as part the course. Students communicate and interact in-person with clients, while receiving training on the use of professional income tax preparation software.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in basic volunteer income tax assistance and strengthens skills used in accounting work.

title: Advanced Volunteer Tax Assistance
courseDescription: Students gain practical experience in preparing federal and state individual income tax returns. Students complete a training program and must pass an IRS basic-level certification exam as part the course. Students communicate and interact in-person with clients, receive training on the use of professional income tax preparation software, and complete a reflection paper on the experience at the end of the tax season.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced volunteer tax assistance and strengthens skills used in accounting work.

title: Arabic I
courseDescription: Introduces the four language skills: reading, understanding, speaking, and writing, as well as the structure of Modern Standard Arabic and the cultures of Arabic-speaking countries. For students with no previous knowledge of the language. Heritage speakers should discuss placement with the instructor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in arabic i and strengthens skills used in arabic work.

title: Arabic II
courseDescription: A continuation of AB 101. Laboratory study outside the classroom is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in arabic ii and strengthens skills used in arabic work.
prerequisites: AB 101 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Arabic III
courseDescription: A continuation of AB 102. Further development of speaking, understanding, and writing skills of Modern Standard Arabic, as well as the cultures of Arabic-speaking countries. Heritage speakers should discuss placement with the instructor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in arabic iii and strengthens skills used in arabic work.
prerequisites: AB 102 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Arabic Composition and Conversation
courseDescription: Increases students' oral and written proficiency through assimilation of advanced structural patterns, stylistic analysis, and discussion of contemporary topics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in arabic composition and conversation and strengthens skills used in arabic work.

title: Global Art
courseDescription: A survey of the history of art addressing one or more artistic traditions beyond Europe. Topic varies by instructor. Fulfills fine arts core requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in global art and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: Western Art: Paleolithic to Gothic
courseDescription: A broad overview of the art of the West from the Paleolithic age to the Gothic era, focusing on Egyptian, Greek, Roman, early Christian, and Medieval art and architecture. Fulfills fine arts core requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in western art: paleolithic to gothic and strengthens skills used in art history / classics work.

title: Medical Humanities: Intersections of Visual Art and Health Science
courseDescription: Explores the compelling dialogue between art and health science with a series of historical case studies and projects. Through this exploration, students discover ways to sharpen observational skills, nurture empathetic understanding, develop creative problem-solving skills, and link self-expression to research. Participants also practice reflecting critically upon methods of gaining knowledge, the limits of those methods, and ways that different domains of knowledge are valued in society.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in medical humanities: intersections of visual art and health science and strengthens skills used in art history / biology work.

title: Arts Management
courseDescription: Explores how to manage visual and performing arts organizations with a focus on nonprofits. Topics include creating and sustaining an institutional mission, fundraising, budgeting, marketing, grant writing, and artistic programming. The course includes opportunities for experiential learning with local arts organizations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in arts management and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: Discovering Difference: Art in the Age of Encounter
courseDescription: The centuries following Columbus's "discovery" of the New World in 1492 were marked by an unprecedented degree of interchange between formerly unconnected cultures. In Europe, Asia, and the Americas this contact had wide-ranging effects in terms of politics, economics, religion, culture, and art. Using art and visual culture as points of entry, this course examines the historical, cultural, and aesthetic implications of this interchange.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in discovering difference: art in the age of encounter and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: The Renaissance in Italy
courseDescription: Investigates art's reflection of the rise of humanism, the rebirth of interest in antiquity, and a new concentration on the earthly world in thirteenth- to sixteenth-century Italy. Studies art and patronage in Republican Florence, Papal Rome, and the ducal courts of Northern Italy, from the time of Giotto to the High Renaissance of Leonardo and Michelangelo, and on to Mannerism and the Counter-Reformation.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the renaissance in italy and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: Renaissance Art in Northern Europe
courseDescription: Studies the developing humanism of the fifteenth century in Flanders where the manuscript tradition of painting developed into the naturalistic and symbolic painting of the late Gothic period, as well as the increasing influence of Italian art on Northern Europe in the sixteenth century.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in renaissance art in northern europe and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: African American Art: Race and Racism in the American Imagination
courseDescription: Surveys the work of African American artists from the colonial period through the present. The artworks studied illuminate how race and racism have shaped the lives of African Americans and demonstrate the centrality of African American experiences in American history.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in african american art: race and racism in the american imagination and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: Realism and Impressionism
courseDescription: Throughout the second half of the nineteenth century, artists such as Courbet, Manet, and Monet struggled to free themselves from older art forms in an effort to become "modern," to capture the life and spirit of their own times. Investigates the artistic transformation that occurred in an era of rapid social change as artists struggled with new avenues for marketing their works (through dealers and galleries), mined new urban spaces and newly created suburbs, and combed the diminishing countryside for their images.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in realism and impressionism and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: History of Photography
courseDescription: An examination of the major technical and aesthetic movements in the history of photography since its invention. Covers the works of major artists working in this medium as well as the major styles. Students in this class will not be expected to produce photographs.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in history of photography and strengthens skills used in art history / photography work.

title: Michelangelo
courseDescription: Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475-1564) was arguably the most important artistic figure of the sixteenth century. Active as a painter, sculptor, architect, draftsman, and poet, Michelangelo greatly influenced the development of art in Italy (and Europe) both during and after his life. Works such as David and the Sistine Chapel ceiling are examined in the context of the political, religious, artistic, and philosophical concerns of the time.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in michelangelo and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: Gothic Art and Architecture
courseDescription: Beginning around Paris in the mid-twelfth century, this course investigates the emergence and development of Gothic-a style of art and architecture that dominated Western Europe for centuries and offered new ways of envisioning the world and the divine. Gothic is studied in its social contexts across a range of media, from towering churches to manuscripts in local collections.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in gothic art and architecture and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: The Crusades in Medieval Visual Culture
courseDescription: Explores the crusades as a catalyst for artistic encounter between western European, Byzantine, and Islamicate cultures in the Holy Land and the Mediterranean from the eleventh through the fourteenth centuries. The investigation of the richly varied art and architecture of this period-which includes intricately carved ivory boxes, scintillating mosaics, and imposing castles-provides critical insights into the complex historical processes of cultural conflict and convergence. Fulfills Art History non-Western requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the crusades in medieval visual culture and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: Islamic Art
courseDescription: A survey of the rich and diverse artistic heritage from the seventh century to the present. A wide range of media is covered, including architecture, calligraphy, ceramics, textiles, and manuscript illumination. Religious and secular art is examined within its historical context in Spain, North Africa, the Middle East, and central and south Asia.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in islamic art and strengthens skills used in art history work.

title: Visual Thinking
courseDescription: Focuses on methods of interdisciplinary study essential to scholar and artist. This course combines elements of studio art, photography, and art history in a hybrid, seminar/ studio format investigating the history, theory, and material practices of the visual arts. The course offers a versatile, topics-based curriculum bringing the techniques of the artist and the labor of the scholar together in one class.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in visual thinking and strengthens skills used in art history / photography / studio art work.
prerequisites: AH 350: AH 109 or AH 110 or AH 111 or PT 270 or SA 224 or SA 227; Restricted to visual arts majors and art history, interArts, photography, and studio art minors
PT 350: PT 270 or AH 109 or AH 110 or AH 111 or SA 224 or SA 227; Restricted to visual arts majors and art history, interArts, photography, and studio arts minors
SA 350: SA 224 or SA 227 or AH 109 or AH 110 or AH 111 or PT 270; Restricted to Visual Arts majors and art history, interArts, photography, and studio art minors

title: Posters! A History of Art and Persuasion
courseDescription: Introduces the cultural and visual history of posters. Drawing on Baltimore’s rich poster resources, students examine the poster as a key participant in both modern life and modern art. Beginning with the prehistory of the poster in the Reformation broadsheet and moving on to the posters of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, students investigate how the poster and its visual language has participated in and shaped art, history, politics, culture, and commerce.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in posters! a history of art and persuasion and strengthens skills used in art history / communication and media work.

title: Prints and Printmaking: A History of Printmaking in the West
courseDescription: Examines the history of European and American prints from the early fifteenth century up to the present day. Prints are viewed in their historical, artistic, material, and cultural contexts, and numerous meetings are held in the print room of the Baltimore Museum of Art. The course uses critical theory and features practical demonstrations of printmaking techniques.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in prints and printmaking: a history of printmaking in the west and strengthens skills used in art history work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Museum Studies: History, Politics, and Practices
courseDescription: Offers a critical introduction to museums, one of the most influential types of cultural institutions. Far more than repositories of objects, museums today are vital crucibles of discussion and debate about public values, memory, and identity. Participants survey the historical development of museums from the Renaissance to the present and consider challenges that currently confront museums.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in museum studies: history, politics, and practices and strengthens skills used in art history work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Albrecht Dürer
courseDescription: Best known as a maker of innovative engravings and woodcuts, the German artist Albrecht Dürer (1471-1528) was also a painter and artistic theorist who, in his work and writings, brought together Northern European and Italian elements. He revolutionized the print medium, influenced artists throughout Europe, and was influenced by the Protestant Reformation. This course holds approximately half of its meetings in the print room of the Baltimore Museum of Art.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in albrecht dürer and strengthens skills used in art history work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: STiNTS-Pro for Biology
courseDescription: Successful Transition into Natural and Technology Science Programs (STiNTS-Pro) for Biology is designed to assist students in the transition to college-level work in the sciences and to enhance the academic community experience. STiNTS-Pro Bio functions as a supportive community of students and faculty. STiNTS-Pro Bio engages students in previewing and reviewing course materials and assists them in the development of effective learning strategies to understand the most difficult course material.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in stints-pro for biology and strengthens skills used in biology work.
prerequisites: BL 118, BL 119 ; or BL 150, BL 151 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Insects in Our World
courseDescription: Touches on the practical aspects of the effects of insects on man, animals, agriculture, and the environment. Topics include a brief overview of general entomology, medical entomology, forensics, methods of insect control, beneficial insects, pesticide use, IPM, and transgenic technologies. Fulfills the natural science core requirement for nonscience majors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in insects in our world and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Microbes and Man: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly
courseDescription: Microorganisms shape the world that we live in in countless ways. This course provides a framework for understanding microorganisms like viruses, bacteria, and protozoans while focusing on their influence on day-to-day life. Topics range from the beneficial uses of microorganisms to diseases caused by them, as well as our efforts to control them.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in microbes and man: the good, the bad, and the ugly and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Twisted Planet: Global Issues in Biology
courseDescription: An examination of biological issues of significance in our global society, which is increasingly marked by an understanding of environmental consequences; worldwide markets and technology; competition for resources; civil/ethnic wars; changing traditional boundaries to disease; and the increasing disparity between developed and developing countries and regions. Major topics include biological considerations of race, population dynamics, the consequences of war, forest and biodiversity loss, global climate change, global water distribution, and the threats of emerging diseases. Fulfills the natural science core requirement for nonscience majors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in twisted planet: global issues in biology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Introduction to Anatomy and Physiology
courseDescription: A lecture/laboratory course designed for psychology majors that introduces basic anatomy and physiology of the human body, from a single cell to the coordinated whole. Topics include the function of each organ system, development, and interactions with the central nervous system. The laboratory component emphasizes physiological experiments.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to anatomy and physiology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Life on the Edge
courseDescription: Biology is the study of life. Perhaps the most fascinating examples of adaptations for life occur in extreme environments such as salt marshes, deep ocean vents, hot springs, and arctic tundra. Students examine a wide diversity of organisms "living on the edge" in extreme environments to investigate the pivotal relationship between structure and function.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in life on the edge and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Modern Marvels of Biotechnology
courseDescription: Biotechnology is an exploding, ever-changing field. This course explores current techniques in biotechnology, the impact of this technology on human life, and the ethics of this new science. Topics may include recombinant DNA; medical forensic science; genetic engineering; and medical research for the advancement of understanding of human disease and conditions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in modern marvels of biotechnology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Human Biology
courseDescription: A general introduction to biology focusing on humans. Topics include cell biology, genetics, molecular biology, form and function of organ systems, and the interaction between humans and their environment. Intended for nonscience majors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in human biology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Food: Environmental and Human Impacts
courseDescription: The development of agriculture was one of the great innovations in human history, allowing our species to expand to the current population size of over six billion. However, this change in diet has had broad implications for human health and the health of the Earth. This course investigates the science and issues involved in food production.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in food: environmental and human impacts and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Foundations of Biology II
courseDescription: Introduces organismal structure and function, including how and why cells are organized into tissues, organs, and organ systems, transmission and expression of genetic information, the role of positive and negative feedback in maintaining homeostasis, and how organisms use different strategies to solve problems such as reproduction, repair and regeneration, response to the environment, transport of materials, and control via cellular communication. Required for biology, biochemistry, and forensic studies majors. Fulfills the natural science core requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in foundations of biology ii and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Foundations of Biology II Lab
courseDescription: A continued introduction to laboratory work at the organismal level, in which students demonstrate proper dissection techniques, express and interpret data in graphs and tables, perform scientific calculations and statistics, design, conduct, and adapt experiments and protocols, and work in diverse teams. Required for biology, biochemistry, and forensic studies majors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in foundations of biology ii lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Foundations of Biology III
courseDescription: Introduces ecology, evolution, and population biology including the relationships among organisms, responses to stress, the mechanisms of genetic change and maintenance of diversity, mechanisms of evolution and speciation, biogeography, energy flow through ecosystems and resource allocation, food webs and ecosystem services, and biogeochemical cycles. Required for biology majors. Fulfills the natural science core requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in foundations of biology iii and strengthens skills used in biology work.
prerequisites: BL 118 or BL 150, BL 119 or BL 151, BL 121 or BL 152, BL 126 or BL 153

title: Foundations of Biology III Lab
courseDescription: An intermediate lab course in which students conduct a long-term research project that requires: responsible use of living materials, revision and adaptation, expression and interpretation of data in graphs and tables, the completion of scientific calculations and statistics, and communication of results. Students also engage in computational analysis, modeling, and simulation of complex processes, discuss current topics in biology using evidence-based arguments, and explore sub-fields and career options in biology. Required for biology majors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in foundations of biology iii lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.
prerequisites: BL 118 or BL 150, BL 119 or BL 151, BL 121 or BL 152, BL 126 or BL 153

title: Professional Development in Biology
courseDescription: Students gain the opportunity to explore various biology career paths and their requirements. It examines a diverse array of professions and offers guidance on preparatory steps, including the development of application materials such as resumes and CVs. Additionally, guest speakers provide insight into their unique career experiences.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in professional development in biology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology Lab I
courseDescription: A laboratory course designed to provide exercises and other activities that supplement and reinforce topics covered in BL 206.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in human anatomy and physiology lab i and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology Lab II
courseDescription: A laboratory course designed to provide exercises and other activities that supplement and reinforce topics covered in BL 208.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in human anatomy and physiology lab ii and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Introduction to Human Nutrition
courseDescription: Introduces nutrition principles including the digestive system; the six nutrients and their roles in the body; food sources with an emphasis on the anatomy, physiology, and biochemical processes; nutrient recommendations; nutritional needs during the life cycle; nutritional factors in food selection and preparation of foods with an emphasis on the nutritional and chemical properties of foods; nutrition in health and disease: weight control, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, dental health, cancer and nutrition; conducting a diet history; development of healthful recipes and menus; and evaluation of nutrition information for the public.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to human nutrition and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Avian Biology with Lab
courseDescription: Introduces the study of birds, their evolutionary origins, diversity, special adaptations, life histories, social behavior, and ecology. The laboratory includes bird watching, identification, dissections, and behavior. Two or three weekend day trips are included.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in avian biology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Invertebrate Zoology
courseDescription: An integrated lecture/lab course looking at the amazing world of animals without backbones. The course focuses on the structure, physiology, ecology, and behavior of some invertebrate groups found in marine, freshwater, and terrestrial ecosystems. The role of invertebrates in natural environments and human society is also considered.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in invertebrate zoology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Invertebrate Zoology with Lab
courseDescription: Introduces the exciting and amazing world of animals without backbones. The course focuses on the life histories, behavior, structure, physiology, and ecology of common invertebrate groups. Consideration is given to adaptations for interacting with plants and animals.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in invertebrate zoology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Introduction to Biomedical Research
courseDescription: A stand-alone laboratory course aimed at developing essential, practical skills utilized in various areas of basic biomedical research. The course introduces students to commonly used laboratory techniques such as pipetting, mammalian cell culture and sterile technique, isolation of DNA/RNA/protein, PCR, western blotting, gel electrophoresis, DNA/RNA/protein quantification, and generation of standard curves. Additionally, students learn basic laboratory math skills, the process of experimental design, laboratory record keeping, key concepts in scientific ethics, troubleshooting experimental challenges, and scientific research communication.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to biomedical research and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Human Health and the Environment
courseDescription: What does Lyme disease have to do with climate change? Why did children lose millions of IQ points to leaded gasoline and paint? Why do so many children in Baltimore have asthma?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in human health and the environment and strengthens skills used in biology / sociology work.
prerequisites: BL 276: BL 111 or BL 154 or BL 201 or CH 114; or written permission of the environmental and sustainability studies minor director; One SC 100-level course; or written permission of the environmental and sustainability studies minor director (may be taken concurrently)
SC 276: BL 111 or BL 201 or CH 114, or written permission of the environmental and sustainability studies minor director

title: Insect Biology
courseDescription: Provides an introduction to the spectacular diversity of insects and their behavior, ecology, morphology, and physiology. The course emphasizes major innovations in insect evolution as well as emerging research on current threats to insect diversity such as climate change. The impact of insects on humans, including disease, pollination services, and more are also examined.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in insect biology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Vertebrate Anatomy with Lab
courseDescription: Vertebrate Anatomy uses an integrated approach to understand the gross anatomy of the major organ systems in vertebrates, with special attention to humans. To provide better understanding, it examines each system within the context of its evolutionary origin as well as its embryological development. The lab focuses on the microscopic examination of early embryonic development, followed by dissection of major organ systems in the cat.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in vertebrate anatomy with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Ecology of the Burren
courseDescription: Explores the special geoecology of the Burren, with special emphasis on the anthropogenic factors that threaten the very existence of the unique ecosystem. Students use field-based methods that integrate the geology and ecology of the landscape, and explore environmental issues that impact the sustainability of the habitat and lifestyles that coexist in the Burren. Field trips and independent research projects are an essential aspect of the hands-on learning that occurs in this immersive course.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ecology of the burren and strengthens skills used in biology work.
prerequisites: BL 111 or BL 154 or BL 201 or CH 114

title: Natural and Cultural History of Burren
courseDescription: Explores the natural history of the Burren, and how it intersects with the human story in the area. Students are expected to do short readings, view videos, and attend field trips and events such as a visit with Farmer/Poet Patrick McCormack, and the Irish folklorist Eddie Lenihan, with a chance to analyze these in writing, through the lens of ecology. Offered in Ireland only.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in natural and cultural history of burren and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Biology Research: Plant Science
courseDescription: A laboratory only course where students gain hands-on understanding of the importance of plants to humans by exploring interactions within agricultural, urban, and natural ecosystems. The course emphasizes skills that integrate practical knowledge of plant science techniques and more universally applicable scientific skills. Laboratory topics include plant identification, plant propagation (including tissue culture), agricultural and urban ecology, and plant secondary compound production (including interactions with bacteria, fungi, animals, and humans).
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biology research: plant science and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Biology Research: Molecular Microbial Ecology
courseDescription: Provides students the experience of performing semester long in-depth research on microbial communities based around ecological principles. Students use molecular tools to study the interactions and diversity of microorganisms (who is there and what are they doing) in natural and man-made environments. Students cultivate microorganisms and analyze nucleic acids and genes using microbiology, microscopy, DNA extraction, PCR, gel electrophoresis, sequencing, data analysis, and bioinformatics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biology research: molecular microbial ecology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Bench to Bedside: Translating Science to Patient Care
courseDescription: How do bioinnovations advance patient care and improve our ability to diagnose and treat disease in the clinical setting? Any new medical device or molecular diagnostic on the market today started originally as an idea in a scientific laboratory. This seminar course follows this exciting “Bench to Bedside” path from idea creation to impacting patient care.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in bench to bedside: translating science to patient care and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Comparative Physiology
courseDescription: A comprehensive introduction to the similarities and differences in the functional processes of animals at selected levels in phylogeny. Emphasis is placed on the adaptive significance of life processes that have evolved as a consequence of an ever-changing environment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in comparative physiology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Synthetic Biology
courseDescription: Introduces the field of synthetic biology, focusing on the design and engineering of biological devices and synthetic genomes. Topics include genome structure and organization in prokaryotes and eukaryotes; gene synthesis technology; methods for the synthesis of whole genomes; design of genetic circuits; and the practical applications of synthetic biology in the creation of biofuels, production of pharmaceuticals, and development of vaccines. Closed to students who have taken BL 322.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in synthetic biology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Synthetic Biology with Lab
courseDescription: Examines the emerging field of synthetic biology, focusing on the design of biological devices and organisms. Topics include gene structure and regulation; genome organization; synthesis of whole genomes; genetic circuits; and the practical applications of synthetic biology in the creation of biofuels, production of pharmaceuticals, and development of vaccines. The laboratory employs bioinformatic tools to analyze DNA sequences and design genes, as well as bioengineering techniques to construct a portion of a genome.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in synthetic biology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: The Biology of Sleep
courseDescription: We spend one-third of our lives sleeping, and scientists still don't know why. This class examines some of the leading theories for why we sleep and observes what happens when organisms (including ourselves) do not sleep enough. It also examines the cognitive and clinical consequences of lack of sleep.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the biology of sleep and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Microbiology
courseDescription: Introduces the fascinating world of microorganisms. Topics for discussion include the structure and function of microbes; microbial metabolism, nutrition, and growth; the control of microorganisms in the environment and in the body; the classification of microorganisms and viruses; infection and immunity; and applied microbiology. An overview of microbial diseases by body system is also provided.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in microbiology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Molecular Genetics with Lab
courseDescription: Students are introduced to the basic principles of molecular genetics and how studies in molecular genetics have advanced fields such as genetic engineering, archaeology, and medicine. Topics include structure and function of nucleic acids and proteins; gene expression and regulation in prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms; and mutations and DNA repair. Examines some of the genetic tools used to analyze genes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in molecular genetics with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Plant-Animal Interactions
courseDescription: Interactions between plants and animals may strongly influence their evolution and ecology. These interactions are arguably the most important forces structuring ecological communities. Students explore the predominant interactions between plants and animals (e.g., pollination, herbivory, seed dispersal) using evolutionary and ecological approaches.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in plant-animal interactions and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Plant-Animal Interactions Seminar
courseDescription: Students explore the expansive plant-animal interactions literature, with human impacts on the dynamics of plant-animal interactions as the main theme of the seminar. The class is conducted in the style of a journal club, where individual students take the responsibility for leading discussions on current articles from the literature. Students learn to critically analyze experimental designs, ecological and evolutionary theory, and key conclusions of the articles, while working toward research proposals to study the potential effects of continued anthropogenic influences.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in plant-animal interactions seminar and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Biology of Mammals
courseDescription: Examines the diversity found within the class Mammalia to gain an understanding of the evolution, physiology, and ecology of these animals. An examination of the conservation problems of this group is included.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biology of mammals and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Biology of Mammals with Lab
courseDescription: The diversity found within the class Mammalia is examined to gain an understanding of the evolution, physiology, and ecology of these animals. An examination of the conservation problems of this group is included. Students examine the distinctive characteristics of mammals, both in the lab and through field study of natural populations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biology of mammals with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Plant Physiology with Lab
courseDescription: Studies the basic processes of plant life including photophysiology, nutrition, water relations, transport phenomena, growth and development, and stress physiology. The laboratory portion examines techniques and instruments physiologists use to study plant function. Activities include comparative photosynthesis, nutrient analysis using atomic absorption spectroscopy, and tissue culture.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in plant physiology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Pathophysiology
courseDescription: Introduces the most common acute and chronic disease conditions as well as injuries across the human life span from cellular and systemic perspective, with attention to etiology, pathogenesis, manifestation, physiological adaptation, and principles of treatment. The role of genetics and psycho-social mechanisms, such as stress and lifestyle, are addressed as factors that may impact the development of disease and recovery from it. Case studies that clarify topics such as signs and symptoms of illness or injury as well as risk potential of further adverse conditions associated with existing morbidity are reviewed.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in pathophysiology and strengthens skills used in biology work.
prerequisites: BL 121, BL 126; or BL 152, BL 153, NUR 205; or BL 154, BL 155

title: Insect Biology with Lab
courseDescription: Provides an introduction to the spectacular diversity of insects and their behavior, ecology, morphology, and physiology. The course emphasizes major innovations in insect evolution as well as emerging research on current threats to insect diversity such as climate change. The impact of insects on humans, including disease, pollination services, and more are also examined.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in insect biology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Pharmacology
courseDescription: Introduces the study of how drugs affect the human body (pharmacodynamics) and how the human body alters drugs (pharmacokinetics). Students examine the fundamental concepts and terminology required to understand the differences among drug effects, as well as the mechanisms of action of various drug classes used to treat common diseases in society. Topics of discussion include: drug-receptor theory, drug metabolism, common drug side effects, treatments for diabetes, and treatments for depression.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in pharmacology and strengthens skills used in biology work.
prerequisites: BL 121, BL 126; or BL 154, BL 155; or BL 152, BL 153, NUR 205

title: Evolutionary and Ecological Genomics
courseDescription: Introduces the basic principles and applications of molecular genomics and how these approaches and related insights are being used across a wide range of basic and applied applications. Students explore eco-evolutionary data sets from an evolutionary perspective, including the impact of disease and changing biotic and abiotic conditions on past and future genetic and phenotypic patterns in a broad range of species and ecosystems. Topics include molecular genomic technologies and analytic tools, with students analyzing, presenting, and discussing data sets and papers of current genomic applications.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in evolutionary and ecological genomics and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Conservation Biology
courseDescription: A comprehensive survey of the theoretical background and current practices in conservation biology. Students examine local and global threats to biological diversity; the measure and value of biological diversity; conservation strategies including the design and management of protected areas, captive breeding, reintroduction programs, and associated legislation; and ethical and moral responsibilities of our society as it interacts with nature and other nations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in conservation biology and strengthens skills used in biology work.
prerequisites: BL 392 or BL 393 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Conservation Biology Seminar
courseDescription: Faculty, small groups of students, and guest speakers present seminars on selected topics in conservation biology. The course supports lecture concepts through primary literature summary and synthesis in oral and written form. Presentation, discussion and writing skills emphasized.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in conservation biology seminar and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Cancer Biology
courseDescription: Examines the current biological and clinical aspects of cancer. Through lectures, in-class activities, assignments, and primary journal articles, students explore a wide range of topics that include normal cells versus cancer cells; disease progression; diagnosing, detecting, and treating cancer; and the bioethical aspects of oncology (the clinical field of cancer). Closed to students who have taken BL 424.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in cancer biology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Endocrinology
courseDescription: An examination of the mammalian endocrine system with emphasis on humans. General aspects of endocrinology are covered, including pertinent anatomy, receptor dynamics, techniques used to study endocrinology, and how the system is regulated. An in-depth exploration of multiple endocrinological examples follows.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in endocrinology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Neurobiology with Lab
