courseDescription: An integrated examination of the mammalian nervous system with emphasis on the human brain. A review of basic neuroanatomy and neurophysiology. Students conduct in-depth explorations of specific topics such as neuropathologies, neuropharmacology, neuroanatomical sex differences, aging, and the molecular and cellular bases of memory and learning.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in neurobiology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Neurobiology
courseDescription: A review of basic neuroanatomy and neurophysiology. Students conduct in-depth explorations of specific topics such as neuropathologies, neuropharmacology, neuroanatomical sex differences, aging, and the molecular and cellular bases of memory and learning. Closed to students who have taken BL 403.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in neurobiology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Endocrinology with Lab
courseDescription: Students gain a greater understanding of vertebrate endocrinology with a focus on the molecular, developmental, and network mechanisms of endocrine function. General aspects of endocrinology covered include pertinent anatomy, receptor dynamics, mechanisms of action and regulation, and technical methods used in endocrinology. Students review primary literature and case studies in order to explore more in-depth endocrinological processes within medical and research-based contexts.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in endocrinology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Developmental Biology with Lab
courseDescription: Examines the patterns of development from fertilization through organ formation, utilizing several model organisms. The course covers topics including gamete formation and fertilization, mechanisms of cellular differentiation, complexities of gene expression programs, essential cell signaling pathways, as well as key events in development including gastrulation and organogenesis. Throughout the course students are exposed to examples of alteration or failure of the precise steps in the developmental program and relating these examples to mammalian developmental disorders.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in developmental biology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Developmental Biology
courseDescription: Examines the patterns of development from fertilization through organ formation. Utilizing several model organisms, this course covers topics including gamete formation and fertilization, mechanisms of cellular differentiation, complexities of gene expression programs, essential cell signaling pathways, as well as key events in development including gastrulation and organogenesis. Additionally, throughout the course students are exposed to examples of alteration or failure of the precise steps in the developmental program and relating these examples to mammalian developmental disorders.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in developmental biology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Cancer Biology with Lab
courseDescription: Examines the biological and clinical aspects of cancer. Topics include normal cells versus cancer cells; cancer disease progression; studying clinical outcomes, and diagnosing, detecting, and treating cancer. Laboratory work focuses on current techniques used in cancer biology research, with emphasis on cell culturing.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in cancer biology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Bioterrorism
courseDescription: A survey of the history and biology of bioterrorism and biowarfare agents. The course focuses on the cellular and molecular biology of organisms identified by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as bioweapons. Emphasis is placed on scientific communication (student-led lectures) and reading/understanding of relevant scientific literature.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in bioterrorism and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Biochemistry I
courseDescription: General principles of biochemistry including studies of the macromolecules (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids), enzyme kinetics and reaction mechanisms, and intermediary metabolism.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biochemistry i and strengthens skills used in biology / chemistry and biochemistry work.
prerequisites: BL 431: BL 121 or BL 152, BL 126 or BL 153, CH 302, CH 308; BL 433 (must be taken concurrently)
CH 431: CH 302, CH 308; CH 433 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Biochemistry II
courseDescription: An examination of select topics in biochemistry, focusing on how life processes are regulated by the interactions between molecules. Topics vary and may include energy metabolism (oxidative phosphorylation, photosynthesis, and glycogen metabolism); signal transduction cascades; amino acid and lipid metabolism; enzyme reaction mechanisms; and protein synthesis. Students lead discussions and/or make oral presentations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biochemistry ii and strengthens skills used in biology / chemistry and biochemistry work.
prerequisites: BL 432: BL 431, BL 433; BL 434 (must be taken concurrently)
CH 432: CH 431; CH 434 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Biochemistry Lab I
courseDescription: Designed to supplement and reinforce concepts covered in the lecture course and introduce students to the techniques of the modern biochemistry laboratory. Experiments include computer visualization of biomolecules, enzyme kinetics, chromatography, and electrophoresis.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biochemistry lab i and strengthens skills used in biology / chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Biochemistry Lab II
courseDescription: Modern experimental biochemistry focusing on techniques for the purification, characterization, and analysis of proteins.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biochemistry lab ii and strengthens skills used in biology / chemistry and biochemistry work.
prerequisites: BL 434: BL 431, BL 433; BL 432 (must be taken concurrently)
CH 434: CH 431, CH 433; CH 432 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Evolution
courseDescription: An examination of the evidence of Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection. Students study the details of the process of evolution from several perspectives including population genetics, evolutionary ecology, and macroevolution. Topics include genome evolution, adaptation, speciation, and extinction.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in evolution and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Exploring the Human Genome
courseDescription: Introduces the human genome, including the structure, function, and evolution of the genome. Students explore techniques of genome-wide analysis, applications of genomics findings to questions of human health, and ethical issues surrounding the acquisition and sharing of human genome sequences. Topics include similarities and differences in genetic sequences among individuals; identification of genes that cause inherited human diseases and cancer; use of genome sequences to track human ancestry; and use of genomic sequencing to identify microbes that live on and in the human body in healthy and diseased states.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in exploring the human genome and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Laboratory Techniques in Stem Cell Biology
courseDescription: Laboratory only course that allows students to explore the key properties and potential of stem cells through the use of common laboratory techniques. Students examine various mammalian stem cell types including embryonic, adult, induced pluripotent, and cancer stem cells. Molecular and cellular techniques such as sterile cell culturing, PCR, western blotting, cell growth, differentiation assays, and microscopy are used, among others.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in laboratory techniques in stem cell biology and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Stem Cell Biology with Lab
courseDescription: Examines the key concepts, and techniques used in mammalian stem cell biology. This integrated lecture and laboratory course focuses on stem cell topics including categorization of the various mammalian stem cell types, ethics of stem cell development and use, pluripotency, culture methods, stem cell characterization, and monitoring tools. Additionally, the course utilizes primary scientific literature to explore the expanding applications of various human stem cell types for medical treatment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in stem cell biology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Conservation and the Tree of Life
courseDescription: The field of conservation biology is changing rapidly, with evolutionary principles of growing importance in the preservation of biodiversity. Students explore the greatest threats to biodiversity and examine the biology of threatened and endangered species. The Tree of Life is examined along with the processes that have shaped the last 4.5 billion years of life on Earth.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in conservation and the tree of life and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: General and Human Physiology with Lab
courseDescription: Students are exposed to the general physiological principles of mammals, particularly humans, at the organismal, tissue, cellular, and molecular levels. This integrated lecture laboratory course covers key physiological concepts such as homeostasis, feedback mechanisms, cellular metabolism, signaling pathways, and both normal and pathological states of the major human organ systems. The laboratory component provides hands on experience measuring specific physiological parameters, dissecting various mammalian organs to observe structure/function relationships, generating and investigating independent scientific questions in physiology, as well as practicing scientific analysis and communication skills.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in general and human physiology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Animal Behavior
courseDescription: A comprehensive introduction to the field of animal behavior. Topics include the hormonal and neural mechanisms that control behavior; development and evolution of behavior; and diverse topics in behavioral ecology, animal communication, and sociobiology.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in animal behavior and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Animal Behavior Lab
courseDescription: Students develop observational skills and the ability to quantify behavior and design behavioral experiments through laboratory exercises, field trips, and an independent group research project.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in animal behavior lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Immunology with Lab
courseDescription: Provides a detailed examination of the human immune system. The function, properties, and interactions of the cells, tissues, and organs comprising the immune system are covered. Additional topics center on medical immunology and include autoimmunity, vaccination, and cancer immunotherapies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in immunology with lab and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Biology Research I
courseDescription: Requires a preliminary paper outlining the nature and scope of the problem, the experimental procedures, and associated literature. Also requires progress reports and a final research paper. Students should secure a faculty sponsor the semester prior to enrollment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biology research i and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Biology Research II
courseDescription: A continuation of BL 481. Written or electronic permission of a sponsoring faculty member. Does not count towards fulfillment of major requirements for the Biology or Biology interdisciplinary program.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biology research ii and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Biology Research III
courseDescription: A continuation of BL 482 . Written or electronic permission of a sponsoring faculty member.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biology research iii and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Honors Biology Research I
courseDescription: Requires the student to create a faculty committee of at least three members, including the sponsoring biology faculty member and at least one other biology faculty member. Prior to registration, students must write, submit and have an honors thesis proposal approved by the committee. Additional requirements include the submission and defense of a final paper to the committee in a format decided by the sponsoring faculty member, and presentation of research in a departmental seminar.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in honors biology research i and strengthens skills used in biology work.
prerequisites: Two upper-level biology courses (BL 222 or higher)
Restricted to students with a cumulative GPA of 3.000 or higher
Written or electronic permission of the department chair

title: Honors Biology Research II
courseDescription: A continuation of BL 491. Students must apply for this course and receive written or electronic permission of a sponsoring faculty member. Does not count towards fulfillment of major requirements for the Biology or Biology interdisciplinary program.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in honors biology research ii and strengthens skills used in biology work.

title: Environmental Studies Experience
department: Biology / Chemistry and Biochemistry / Communication and Media / Economics / Philosophy / Sociology / Writing
courseDescription: A capstone experience in the environmental and sustainability studies minor, in which a student arranges an internship, independent study, or research experience with a faculty sponsor to engage in an in-depth exploration of a topic associated with environmental or sustainability issues. Written or electronic permission of a sponsoring faculty member and the environmental studies director. Generally completed during the senior year.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in environmental studies experience and strengthens skills used in biology / chemistry and biochemistry / communication and media / economics / philosophy / sociology / writing work.
prerequisites: SC 496: SC 100; Restricted to environmental studies minors

title: Forensic Science Experience
courseDescription: A capstone experience in forensic science in which a student may arrange an internship, independent study, or research experience with a faculty sponsor to engage in an in-depth exploration of a topic associated with forensic or criminal investigation. Written or electronic permission of a sponsoring faculty member or department chair (for internships). ; students should secure a faculty sponsor and obtain the approval of the forensic science director early in the term before registration.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic science experience and strengthens skills used in biology / sociology work.
prerequisites: SC 498: SC 100; SC 260 or SC 332; Restricted to junior and senior forensic science majors

title: Business Essentials: A Hands-on Approach for Nonprofit and For-profit Organizations
courseDescription: An exploration of contemporary business, this course enables students to contribute more effectively to non-profit organizations or business and provide an understanding of the structure and moving parts of providing both goods and services. Designed for students majoring in the sciences, humanities, or social sciences, topics covered include basic accounting, budgeting, human resource management, marketing, IT applications, management theory and how laws impact business. Students build their knowledge by participating in a simulation that lets them experience how business actually works.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in business essentials: a hands-on approach for nonprofit and for-profit organizations and strengthens skills used in business administration work.
prerequisites: Restricted to bachelor of arts and bachelor of science majors, excluding the bachelor of science in finance
Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors (Fall only)

title: Creative Mindset
courseDescription: Provides accessible and engaging content to encourage learning about innovation and entrepreneurship as a discipline and practice that can be applied to a variety of academic or professional career paths. The course highlights the thinking, creating, and acting processes needed for a creative mindset. Through a collection of self-discovery activities, case studies, texts, articles, and interactions with entrepreneurs and innovators, students are provided with tools that can be applied to entrepreneurial thinking in their studies,career, and life.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in creative mindset and strengthens skills used in business administration work.

title: Design Thinking and Innovative Solutions
courseDescription: Innovation and human-centered design are the driving force behind the collaborative mindsets that employers and communities are looking for to create socially focused solutions. By adopting this human-centered approach, successful entrepreneurs not only create new social or commercial ventures, but also reinvent companies to remain competitive in an ever-changing market. Students apply the tools, methods, and self-reflection techniques necessary to thrive in a fast-paced environment that puts a premium on empathy and the exchange of diverse ideas to bring innovative solutions to reality.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in design thinking and innovative solutions and strengthens skills used in business administration work.
prerequisites: Restricted to innovation and entrepreneurship minors or written permission of the instructor

title: Entrepreneurial Finance
courseDescription: Examines how to fund and maintain a financially healthy entrepreneurial venture. Specific emphasis is placed on learning how to research, plan, and forecast financial requirements of the venture. Unlike traditional business finance, which assumes ongoing cash flows and public data, this course introduces students to the uncertainties, information asymmetries, and forecasting aspects unique to start-ups.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in entrepreneurial finance and strengthens skills used in business administration work.

title: New Venture Creation
courseDescription: Students are expected to work on launching a start-up in either independent or organizational (intrapreneurship) settings. Working in teams, students experiment with different business models, validate a market need, and build all facets of a start-up. Students are expected to achieve milestones and identify key risks on which the enterprise’s success depends.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in new venture creation and strengthens skills used in business administration work.

title: Investing in Black and Women Entrepreneurs
courseDescription: Examines how anti-Black practices of the twentieth century have resulted in disparate access to capital and wealth creation for Black and women entrepreneurs. Students use historical and sociological readings, as well as the context and lived experiences of Black entrepreneurs and their families, to develop empathy and the tools to become equitable and inclusive investors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in investing in black and women entrepreneurs and strengthens skills used in business administration work.

title: Applied Angel Investing
courseDescription: Startup organizations often require "angel" investors, individuals or groups who are willing to accept the unique financial risks occurring during the early stages of a business, to help them launch and establish their business plans. Angel investing is evolving in relation to economic forces and demands for innovation, as well as ensuring that this practice does not continue to exclude historically marginalized communities. This course provides students with hands-on experience as angel investors and an opportunity to make an impact on early-stage Maryland companies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in applied angel investing and strengthens skills used in business administration work.

title: Introduction to Chemistry
courseDescription: Introduces college-level chemistry with an emphasis on developing problem solving skills. Topics covered include the fundamental concepts of chemistry such as essential chemical calculations and working with scientific notations and units, atomic theory, chemical bonding, and naming compounds along with the mathematics required for quantitative problem solving. This course is designed for students that have not recently taken high school chemistry or with a limited mathematics background.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to chemistry and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: General Chemistry II
courseDescription: A continuation of CH 101.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in general chemistry ii and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: General Chemistry Lab I
courseDescription: Introduces the laboratory study of the physical and chemical properties of matter; the principles and applications of gravimetric, volumetric chemical, and qualitative analysis.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in general chemistry lab i and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: General Chemistry Lab II
courseDescription: A continuation of CH 105.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in general chemistry lab ii and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Chemistry and Society
courseDescription: Why does science matter and how does it work? How is chemistry useful to explain the world we live in? Though specific topics covered may vary by instructor, students are introduced to basic principles of chemistry and a consideration of the benefits and problems arising from applications of chemistry.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chemistry and society and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Quantitative Analysis
courseDescription: An investigation into techniques used to determine chemical composition. Includes application of statistical analysis to chemical systems and emphasizes chemical equilibrium. Provides a foundation for advanced level courses in physical chemistry, instrumental analysis, and laboratory techniques.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in quantitative analysis and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in CH 102

title: Organic Chemistry II
courseDescription: A continuation of CH 301, with an expanded discussion of reaction mechanisms and synthesis. Topics include the use of spectroscopy in structure determination, the reactions of aromatic compounds and carbonyl compounds, heterocyclic chemistry, and medicinal chemistry.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in organic chemistry ii and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Organic Chemistry Lab II
courseDescription: A continuation of CH 307.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in organic chemistry lab ii and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Medicinal Chemistry
courseDescription: An examination of drug action and drug discovery at the molecular level. Chemical aspects of drug structures, biological targets, drug-target interactions, pharmacology, and drug development are studied in detail. Specific classes of drugs vary and may include antibacterial, antiviral, anticancer, and cardiovascular drugs.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in medicinal chemistry and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Physical Chemistry I
courseDescription: A detailed examination and analysis of kinetics and the laws of classical thermodynamics with applications to the properties of gases, liquids, and solids, as well as to solutions, phase, and chemical equilibria.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in physical chemistry i and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Physical Chemistry II
courseDescription: Introduces quantum chemistry and spectroscopy. The theory of quantum mechanics is presented at a fundamental level and applied to the electronic structure of atoms and molecules, atomic and molecular spectroscopy, and statistical mechanics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in physical chemistry ii and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.
prerequisites: CH 102 (C or better); MA 251 or MA 252

title: Physical Chemistry Lab I
courseDescription: Principles of experimental physical chemistry and introduction of techniques and instruments used in modern chemical research. Emphasis is placed on interpreting results, critical thinking, and writing formal reports.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in physical chemistry lab i and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Physical Chemistry Lab II
courseDescription: Principles of experimental physical chemistry are applied to the acquisition and interpretation of basic data on atomic and molecular structure using spectroscopic instrumentation and computational chemistry techniques. Emphasis is placed on interpreting results, critical thinking, and writing formal reports.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in physical chemistry lab ii and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Quantitative Chemical Analysis Lab
courseDescription: Introduces the application of analytical chemistry techniques with an emphasis on understanding chemical systems and equilibrium and a focus on data and error analysis. Students conduct various wet chemical analyses such as gravimetric, volumetric, and potentiometric analysis. Provides a foundation for advanced level courses in physical chemistry, instrumental analysis, and laboratory techniques.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in quantitative chemical analysis lab and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Organic Synthesis
courseDescription: A detailed survey of methods used to make molecules using organic chemical synthesis. Students become well-versed in drawing organic reaction mechanisms and in designing and evaluating synthetic strategies and tactics. Syntheses of medicinally important molecules (antibiotics, antivirals, and other drugs) will be used to introduce new reactions and reinforce understanding of mechanism and strategy.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in organic synthesis and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.
prerequisites: CH 302, CH 308. At least a C or better in CH 302

title: Instrumental Methods
courseDescription: Principles and applications of analytical instrumentation. An introduction to spectroscopic, chromatographic, and electrochemical techniques.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in instrumental methods and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.
prerequisites: CH 201, CH 311, CH 315. At least a C or better in CH 311

title: Instrumental Methods Lab
courseDescription: Covers principles and applications of some spectroscopic and chromatographic techniques. Applications of chemometrics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in instrumental methods lab and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Inorganic Chemistry with Lab
courseDescription: The application of thermodynamic, kinetic, and structural principles to the synthesis and characterization of the chemical elements and main group, transition metal, and organometallic compounds. Lecture/Laboratory.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in inorganic chemistry with lab and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Inorganic Chemistry
courseDescription: Explores the application of thermodynamic, kinetic, and structural principles to the synthesis and characterization of the chemical elements and main group, transition metal, and organometallic compounds.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in inorganic chemistry and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Chemistry Research
courseDescription: Official credit range: 1-3 credits. Supervised faculty/student research projects. May be repeated for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chemistry research and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the department chair

title: Research Methods in Organic Chemistry
courseDescription: Develops the skills and independence necessary for modern research in organic chemistry. Building on techniques introduced in the introductory organic chemistry lab sequence, the course emphasizes hands-on experience with contemporary methods in reaction design, execution, and analysis. Students learn advanced techniques in reaction setup and monitoring, product purification (including chromatography and recrystallization), and compound characterization using spectroscopic tools such as NMR, IR, and GC-MS.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in research methods in organic chemistry and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Social Justice Chemistry Seminar
courseDescription: Chemistry has a direct impact on some of the issues that influence historically disadvantaged populations. This course considers chemistry-based solutions to these issues that impact daily life, with a focus on the poor and marginalized populations of Baltimore. Taking into consideration the impacts of chemistry and how it can be changed in the future, students begin to answer the question of "what can a chemist do, that no one else can?".
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in social justice chemistry seminar and strengthens skills used in chemistry and biochemistry work.

title: Chinese I
courseDescription: Builds a solid foundation of the four language skills: reading, understanding, speaking, and writing in Mandarin Chinese, introducing the structure of the language and the different aspects of Chinese culture. For students with no previous knowledge of the language. Laboratory study outside the classroom is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chinese i and strengthens skills used in chinese work.

title: Chinese II
courseDescription: A continuation of CI 101 for students who have learned the basics of Chinese pronunciation, grammar patterns, and a limited amount of Chinese characters. Laboratory study outside the classroom is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chinese ii and strengthens skills used in chinese work.
prerequisites: CI 101 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Chinese III
courseDescription: A continuation of CI 102. Designed for advanced introductory students of Chinese. Introduces more complex patterns of Chinese using essential vocabulary.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chinese iii and strengthens skills used in chinese work.
prerequisites: CI 102 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Chinese in Context I
courseDescription: Chinese language study with intensive oral practice and review of elementary language structures. Includes contemporary culture in Beijing and comprehensive strategies for five-skills abilities.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chinese in context i and strengthens skills used in chinese work.
prerequisites: Restricted to students studying in Beijing

title: Chinese in Context II
courseDescription: A continuation of CI 150.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chinese in context ii and strengthens skills used in chinese work.
prerequisites: Restricted to students studying in Beijing

title: Chinese Composition and Conversation
courseDescription: Increases students' oral and written proficiency through assimilation of advanced structural patterns and stylistic analysis through communicative exercises and activities.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chinese composition and conversation and strengthens skills used in chinese work.

title: Advanced Chinese Composition and Conversation
courseDescription: A continuation of CI 201. Students acquire more fluent conversational skills and more efficient writing skills, as well as a broader perspective on Chinese culture with active discussions of contemporary and thought-provoking topics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced chinese composition and conversation and strengthens skills used in chinese work.

title: Chinese in Context III
courseDescription: A continuation of CI 151.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chinese in context iii and strengthens skills used in chinese work.
prerequisites: Restricted to students studying in Beijing

title: Chinese in Context IV
courseDescription: A continuation of CI 250.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chinese in context iv and strengthens skills used in chinese work.
prerequisites: Restricted to students studying in Beijing

title: Selected Readings in Modern Chinese
courseDescription: Readings in modern Chinese at the advanced level. Texts include literary selections, newspaper articles, and scholarly essays.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in selected readings in modern chinese and strengthens skills used in chinese work.

title: Introduction to Formal Written Chinese
courseDescription: Strengthens student intuition for formal written Chinese, as well as reading and writing skills. Texts include longer selections in various genres covering topics in politics, economics, education, philosophy, etc.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to formal written chinese and strengthens skills used in chinese work.

title: The Construction of Male and Female in Greece and Rome
courseDescription: Studies the idea of gender in ancient Greece and Rome in art, literature, and philosophy. Readings include selections from Sappho, Plato’s Symposium and Republic, Hesiod’s Theogony, Aeschylus’s Oresteia, and Catullus’s love poetry among others.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the construction of male and female in greece and rome and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: Gladiators and Olympians
courseDescription: Examines sport and athletics in the ancient Greek and Roman worlds including the Greek Olympics, the culture of the great gymnasia, and the gladiators and animal fighters who thrilled and appalled immense crowds in the Roman Colosseum. Students learn the nuts and bolts of the actual sports but also how the sports reflected and affected the broader society, to which they mattered significantly. For ancient athletes, the stakes were high, and the competitions often violent.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in gladiators and olympians and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: Medical Terminology
courseDescription: Studies the most common Greek and Latin roots in medical terms as well as the basic elements in a medical word (prefix, suffix, root word, and combining vowel) which allow students to understand any medical term as a whole entity.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in medical terminology and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: Classical Mythology
courseDescription: Studies the traditional stories of the Greeks and Romans as expressed in their literature and art with an emphasis on the literature's background, value, and influence. Usually offered fall semester. Art elective for elementary education majors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in classical mythology and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: The Classical Epics
courseDescription: Studies the epic poetry of Homer and Virgil in translation, with an emphasis on the poetry's background, value, and influence. The course may include a short survey of other epics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the classical epics and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: Greek Drama
courseDescription: Studies selected plays in English translation by Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, and others, with an emphasis on the literature's background, value, and influence. Specific readings vary with the instructor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in greek drama and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: The Ancient Novel
courseDescription: Studies the ancient novel in English translation, with particular emphasis on Apuleius and Petronius-master stylists and literary innovators who chronicled life in the Roman Empire at its most diverse, complex, and decadent.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the ancient novel and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: The Golden Age of Rome
courseDescription: Studies selected works in translation by some of Rome's greatest writers, with special emphasis on Vergil, Ovid, and Livy. The course may be organized chronologically or thematically. Specific readings vary with the instructor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the golden age of rome and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: Commenting on Scripture from Philo to Facebook
courseDescription: What happens when an artist like Taylor Swift releases portions of their journal that comment on their own songs? Does that change how you hear the song? Can you listen to that song "just as well" without knowing her commentary?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in commenting on scripture from philo to facebook and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Peace and War in Ancient Rome
courseDescription: The Romans are famous for their success in war, building an empire stretching from Damascus to London and Gibraltar to Iraq. Defeats taught them self-sacrifice and the adoption of tactics and weapons from their foes. Constant warfare, both foreign and civil, deeply affected their politics, society, economy, and culture.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in peace and war in ancient rome and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.

title: Images of God in Scripture
courseDescription: Examines the various images/titles given to God in the Old and New Testaments from an historical theological perspective. Some images/titles discussed are God the Father, God the Mother, the Divine Warrior, the Good Shepherd, the Storm God, Christ the King, the Lamb of God, and God the Judge. Since our understanding of God is largely shaped by the image we have of Him, this course explores the influences these images/titles have had and continue to have on our approach to worship, on our concept of Church, and on our self understanding in relation to God.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in images of god in scripture and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Food, Hunger, and the Bible
courseDescription: Investigates issues related to food and hunger in the Hebrew Bible and New Testament texts, the ways in which these biblical concepts inform a Christian theology and spirituality of food, and how these biblical concepts relate to modern ethical and social justice issues including: poverty, hunger, and food access; food production; ethical labor practices in agricultural and food industries; sustainability; ethical treatment of animals; and community and hospitality. Students investigate biblical principles and apply them to current issues—both local and global.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in food, hunger, and the bible and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Who is Jesus?
courseDescription: Explores the identity of Jesus Christ, as expressed in Scripture, the doctrine and tradition of the Church, as well as in art and literature. Emphasizes the historical context of Jesus’ life, the variety of ways in which the significance of that life has been articulated over the centuries, and the ways in which one might discern faithful from unfaithful articulations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in who is jesus? and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Death of the Roman Republic
courseDescription: Studies the final century of the Roman Republic when Rome suffered under the struggles for personal power of men like Sulla, Mark Antony, and Julius Caesar. Focuses on primary sources with a particular emphasis on the writings of Cicero who documented the final years of the Republic in public speeches as well as private, biting personal letters.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in death of the roman republic and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: History of Christmas
courseDescription: Is Christmas the commemoration of Jesus' birth? Or is it a pagan winter festival hiding behind a thin but deceptive veil of Christian images and ideas? Students discover the holiday is both of these things and a good deal more.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in history of christmas and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Gladiators and Roman Spectacles
courseDescription: An examination of ancient Rome's spectacles, including gladiatorial combat, chariot racing, animal fights and exhibitions, and mock battles. The course explores the intersection of power, violence, entertainment, class, and sex in Roman spectacles.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in gladiators and roman spectacles and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Volcanoes, Fire, and Flood: Disasters of Ancient Rome
courseDescription: An examination of ancient Rome's greatest disasters: the destruction of Pompeii, the Great Fire of Rome, floods, and plagues. Students investigate the causes of these events; the Romans' efforts to navigate and make sense of them; and the transformations they brought to the ancients' environment, behavior, and thought.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in volcanoes, fire, and flood: disasters of ancient rome and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Gender and Sexuality in Greece and Rome
courseDescription: An examination of the lives of and attitudes toward women in ancient Greece and Rome. Classic texts of ancient literature are read, masterpieces of art are viewed, and the sociology of ancient women is probed. Topics include the family; prostitution; women of the imperial family; Cleopatra; health, child bearing, and birth control; the source and psychology of Greek misogyny; jet-setters and women's liberation under the early Roman Empire; women and work; women in myth; women in early Christianity; the legacy of classical civilization for modern women.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in gender and sexuality in greece and rome and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Roman Private Life
courseDescription: Studies family and social life in Ancient Rome which focuses on how environment and custom determine one another. Topics include women, crime, racism, pollution, class structure, private religion and magic, Christianity, blood sports, medicine, travel, theater, and death.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in roman private life and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The Multicultural Roman Empire
courseDescription: In conquering and attempting to unify lands as diverse as Egypt, Iran, Britain, and Algeria, the Romans undertook one of the greatest social and political experiments in the history of the world. They assimilated some of the peoples they conquered, but the vanquished, in turn, assimilated their Roman conquerors-it is no accident that one third century emperor was named Philip the Arab. This course examines the strategies by which the Romans attempted to hold together their vast, multicultural empire, and the strategies by which many of their subjects preserved and even promulgated their cultures.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the multicultural roman empire and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Greece and Rome on Film
courseDescription: Sex, violence, insanity, and monsters are the main ingredients in Hollywood's recipe for movies about ancient Greece and Rome. By watching films like Gladiator, 300, Troy, Ben-Hur, and others, students discover the truth behind the extravagant images and see some very good (and very bad) films along the way.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in greece and rome on film and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: History of Ancient Greece
courseDescription: Studies Greece from the Bronze Age to Alexander the Great, with special attention to the development of the Greek polis or city-state and the various constitutional, social, economic, and religious forms which this took.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in history of ancient greece and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: The Gladiator
courseDescription: A first-year Messina seminar that uses ancient and modern texts (e.g., The Colosseum, The Roman Games: A Sourcebook) and films (e.g., Gladiator, Spartacus, The Hunger Games) to illuminate the intersection of cruelty, ideology, and entertainment in the ancient arena.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the gladiator and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: Race, Conquest, and Identity in Ancient North Africa
courseDescription: A first-year Messina seminar that examines questions of race, imperialism, and cultural/ethnic identity in ancient North Africa, both before and after the Roman conquest. Students are exposed to global diversity and issues of justice, especially with reference to conquered populations, and to questions of assimilation and resistance.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in race, conquest, and identity in ancient north africa and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: Ethics: Ancient, Modern, and Christian Approaches to Ethics
courseDescription: Studies the ways in which Christians of the first six centuries answered the question: How should one live? Pays particular attention to the themes which emerge in their answers to this question; e.g., the imitation of Christ, holiness, and the virtues. While some New Testament texts are included in the reading, the primary focus is on the writings of the Church Fathers.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethics: ancient, modern, and christian approaches to ethics and strengthens skills used in classics work.

title: Parthenon to Pantheon: Greek and Roman Art
courseDescription: An overview of ancient Greek and Roman masterpieces approached in thematic units focusing on four case studies: the Parthenon, the Prima Porta Augustus, the Aphrodite of Knidos, and the Pantheon. Fulfills the Fine Arts core requirement for Honors students.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in parthenon to pantheon: greek and roman art and strengthens skills used in classics / honors work.

title: Seminar: The Persecution of the Christians in the Roman World
courseDescription: An exploration of the causes, nature, and extent of early Christian persecutions until Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire in the fourth century. Topics include the Jewish-Greek- Roman environment of early Christianity; Rome's policies toward foreign cults; Christians' reputation for extreme promiscuity and cultic atrocities; comparison with competing cults; the danger of open profession of the new faith; and Christian acceptance of the ancient world. Given the muddled understanding of the early Christian persecutions, the course examines and dispels the myths and brings some order to the chaos.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: the persecution of the christians in the roman world and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.
prerequisites: One HS 100-level course, one HS 200-level course or HS 300-level course
Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: An Introduction to the Theology of Saint Augustine
courseDescription: Studies the life and writings of the great fifth-century bishop and theologian, Augustine of Hippo. Topics include grace, free will, scripture, and the role of civil authority.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in an introduction to the theology of saint augustine and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Biblical Hebrew I
courseDescription: An enriched beginning course emphasizing grammar, syntax, and vocabulary. Intended for students with no previous knowledge of the language.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biblical hebrew i and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Biblical Hebrew II
courseDescription: A continuation of CL 340.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biblical hebrew ii and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Biblical Hebrew III
courseDescription: A continuation of CL 341 .
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biblical hebrew iii and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Biblical Hebrew IV
courseDescription: A continuation of CL 342 .
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biblical hebrew iv and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Jesus and the Gospels
courseDescription: Students examine a variety of issues surrounding the portrayal of Jesus in the Gospels of the New Testament and in other early Christian writings.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in jesus and the gospels and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Prophets and Peacemakers
courseDescription: The Old Testament (Hebrew Bible) contains stories about prophets as well as texts attributed to these prophets. This course examines both. In addition, students study prophetic activity from a sociological/cross-cultural perspective, examine New Testament reinterpretations of prophetic texts, and explore the possibility of modern prophets and modern applications of ancient prophetic texts.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in prophets and peacemakers and strengthens skills used in classics / theology work.

title: Studies in Plato
courseDescription: An inquiry into the epistemological, moral, and metaphysical writings of Plato's middle and later periods, with special reference to the relation of anamnesis, participation and the theory of forms in the middle dialogues to koinonia and the theory of the greatest kinds in the later dialogues.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in studies in plato and strengthens skills used in classics / philosophy work.
prerequisites: CL 366: PL 201 and one additional PL200-level course

title: Platonic Political Philosophy
courseDescription: Socrates and the founding of political philosophy; Thucydides and the crisis of the polis; the critique of Aristophanes; Plato's Apology, Crito, Gorgias, Republic, Theaetetus; Plato's modern enemies: Machiavelli and Mill.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in platonic political philosophy and strengthens skills used in classics / political science work.

title: Aristotelian Political Philosophy
courseDescription: An investigation of the founding of political science by Aristotle devoted to a reading of Nicomachean Ethics and Politics, as well as selections from Aristotle's scientific and logical treatises. Subsequent contributions to the tradition are also considered, including those of Marsilius of Padua and Saint Thomas Aquinas. Aristotle's modern enemies: Hobbes and Marx.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in aristotelian political philosophy and strengthens skills used in classics / political science work.

title: Socratic Political Philosophy
courseDescription: Socrates, the first political philosopher, wrote nothing. His unique life and thought are known only through the writings of others-both friends and enemies. By reading works by Aristophanes, Plato, Xenophon, and Nietzsche, students seek to understand the Socratic way of life.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in socratic political philosophy and strengthens skills used in classics / political science work.

title: The Political Challenge of Socrates
courseDescription: Draws on the striking stance of Socrates in the Athenian crisis of the fifth century to illuminate a perennial tension now evident in our age of political hyper-partisanship. How are we to balance the need for political concord and patriotism against the need for critical independence and moral self-examination? Did Socrates deserve his hemlock for sowing disunity in a time of trouble, or was he the tragically unheeded voice of reasoned rehabilitation?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the political challenge of socrates and strengthens skills used in classics / philosophy / political science work.

title: Magic in Ancient Greece and Rome
courseDescription: Explores the many kinds of magic regularly used by ancient Greeks, Romans, and the peoples they conquered and encountered. Students study why and how such practices developed and what it meant to those who used them. Literary stories of witches, sorcerers, werewolves, and magic potions are compared to primary materials including curse tablets and charms for health and good luck.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in magic in ancient greece and rome and strengthens skills used in classics / history work.

title: Popular Culture in America
courseDescription: An upper-level introduction to the issues surrounding popular culture and ways to study it. The American arts and entertainment industry is an economic and cultural powerhouse that influences how we live our everyday lives as well as our beliefs and values. Students learn how to use different tools for analyzing songs, movies, TV shows and social media to go much deeper than just saying "I love" or "hate" a song or movie, including using interdisciplinary, cross-cultural comparisons to better understand the cultural work done by media texts.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in popular culture in america and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Hearing the Movies
courseDescription: Surveying representative works in a wide range of genres - from silent film, to film musicals, to contemporary epics - this course explores the technical relationships between soundtracks and image tracks, and investigates how the sonic dimension of film can influence narrative interpretation and audience responses.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in hearing the movies and strengthens skills used in communication and media / music work.

title: Web I
courseDescription: Offers students the conceptual understandings—such as design principles, Web usability, and search engine optimization—associated with website design and development. Students also learn essential skills with applications such as HTML, CSS, Content Management systems and other related programs needed to build effective websites.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in web i and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Communication for Environmental and Social Justice
courseDescription: Explores how to use communication skills to promote environmental and social justice. Inspired by examples of communication advocacy and nonviolent activism from around the world, and particularly within the Catholic, Jesuit tradition, the course teaches different dimensions of communication advocacy and how students can apply what they learn to their work on campus, in our Baltimore community, and beyond.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in communication for environmental and social justice and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: History of Graphic Design
courseDescription: Examines graphic communication from the earliest forms of writing to modern day digital technology. In addition to readings from Meggs' History of Graphic Design, students are required to apply what they have learned to projects that bring history into perspective.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in history of graphic design and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Data Visualization and Storytelling
courseDescription: Presenting data clearly and meaningfully is a storytelling skill in communication, journalism, and relevant professional fields. It is also a visual communication skill. The course considers data not only as a multimedia storytelling component but also as a narrative – both visual and textual.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in data visualization and storytelling and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Video Art
department: Communication and Media / Photography / Studio Art
courseDescription: An examination of the aesthetics and history of video art, as well as a study of the techniques of video production. Students produce numerous short and long video works., SA 386.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in video art and strengthens skills used in communication and media / photography / studio art work.
prerequisites: CM 327: CM 308 or PT 270 or PT 300 or PT 301 or SA 224 or SA 227
PT 386: PT 270 or PT 300 or PT 301 or CM 308 or SA 224 or SA 227
SA 386: SA 224 or SA 227 or CM 308 or PT 270 or PT 300 or PT 301

title: Backpack Video Production
courseDescription: Explores professional field production techniques. Students are equipped with the skills required for creating a variety of visual multimedia content. Topics include aerial videography, photography, VR video, motion graphics, and cloud-based production workflows.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in backpack video production and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Philosophy of Information and Media
courseDescription: Today we are living through one of human history’s great media shifts, on par with the invention of the written language and the printing press. A shift of this magnitude invites philosophical reflection: both historical and phenomenological reflections on the nature of reading, writing, and thinking as well as a general examination of the way media affects consciousness. In this course, students trace the history of media shifts and their impact by looking at thinkers as diverse as Plato and Marshall McLuhan.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of information and media and strengthens skills used in communication and media / philosophy work.

title: Global Trends in Social Marketing
courseDescription: Focuses on the trends and tactics global marketers, media companies, and transnational media agencies are using to get messages out around the world.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in global trends in social marketing and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Collage, Assemblage, and the Found Object
courseDescription: Using found and altered materials, students are led from varied technical approaches for creating collages on/of paper through a range of conceptual approaches to design and content. Includes the altering and constructing of relief and three-dimensional, preexisting materials into works of art (assemblages and found object sculpture). Digital visual construction of collage and assemblage included in projects.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in collage, assemblage, and the found object and strengthens skills used in communication and media / studio art work.

title: The Documentary Tradition
courseDescription: A close study of the documentary tradition-including ethnography, propaganda, cinema verité, and postmodernism-that testifies to the tremendous vitality of the form, assesses its current state, and projects the future. Screenings celebrate human dignity and diversity in its many variations of race, gender, ethnicity, national origin, culture, religion, and sexual orientation. Students view, discuss, and write about majors works and apply insights to their own documentary projects.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the documentary tradition and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Book Arts and Artists' Books
department: Communication and Media / Photography / Studio Art
courseDescription: Students are introduced to the materials, techniques, concepts, and equipment used in the craft of making traditional and nontraditional books. They learn folding, stitching, enclosing, and binding methods while creating three-dimensional works that literally or metaphorically reference the structure of books, address contemporary ideas about visual content, and exist as three-dimensional works of art./SA 353.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in book arts and artists' books and strengthens skills used in communication and media / photography / studio art work.
prerequisites: CM 349: SA 224 or written permission of the instructor
PT 353: SA 224 or SA 227 or written permission of the instructor
SA 353: SA 224 or SA 227 or written permission of the instructor

title: Introduction to Radio and Digital Audio
courseDescription: Introduces audio storytelling and techniques for sound production. The course explores creative exercises for students to become better communicators through the art of sound, with an emphasis on engaging an audience. Students participate in workshops to write and perform for the ear, craft conversations, and produce compelling stories for listeners.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to radio and digital audio and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Digital Mixed Media
department: Communication and Media / Photography / Studio Art
courseDescription: A combination studio and digital photography course in which the computer is used as a tool and an integral part of the creative process, but work is achieved through mixed media studio methods. Two- and three-dimensional projects may include installation and/or virtual works that exist only on the Internet. Some prior computer experience is recommended. and SA 360 .
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in digital mixed media and strengthens skills used in communication and media / photography / studio art work.
prerequisites: CM 360: SA 224 or SA 226 or written permission of the instructor
PT 360: SA 224 or SA 226 or SA 227
SA 360: SA 224 or SA 226 or SA 227

title: Contemporary Digital Art
department: Communication and Media / Photography / Studio Art
courseDescription: Students taking this course gain an understanding of contemporary artists focusing on new media, while developing their own digital art practice. Video, animation, sound, web-based artwork, 3-D, interactivity, and other media practices are addressed. Classes consist of research, discussion, studio projects, critiques, and written work. / SA 364.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in contemporary digital art and strengthens skills used in communication and media / photography / studio art work.
prerequisites: CM 364: SA 224 or SA 226 or written permission of the instructor
PT 364: SA 224 or SA 226 or SA 227
SA 364: SA 224 or SA 227 or written permission of the instructor

title: Voice and Speech
courseDescription: Students explore oral communication with an emphasis on harnessing the communicative power of the spoken word. We speak all the time - how can we do it with more confidence and effectiveness? This course addresses the many contexts in which we use the spoken word and how we can adapt to these contexts for maximum impact.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in voice and speech and strengthens skills used in communication and media / theatre work.

title: Entertainment, Media, and Politics
courseDescription: Students explore how a range of entertainment media (comedy, melodrama, the sitcom, film, etc.) reflects the intersection of politics and culture. The course reviews political themes in entertainment content and the rise of politics as spectacle and entertainment. While the course has a contemporary focus it also looks at the history behind the mixing of entertainment and politics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in entertainment, media, and politics and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Digital Image
department: Communication and Media / Photography / Studio Art
courseDescription: Examines the ways in which the computer and various software programs can be used to modify and enhance an image as a visual statement for artistic and photojournalistic use. Students are expected to supply a digital SLR camera (with full manual controls). and SA 361.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in digital image and strengthens skills used in communication and media / photography / studio art work.
prerequisites: PT 361: PT 270 or PT 300 or PT 301
SA 361: PT 270 or PT 300 or PT 301

title: Public Art
courseDescription: An examination of the field of public art. Students also meet with community partners in the city of Baltimore and collaboratively determine the details of a public art project.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in public art and strengthens skills used in communication and media / studio art work.
prerequisites: CM 370: SA 224 or SA 226 or written permission of the instructor
SA 367: SA 224 or SA 226 or SA 227

title: Web II
courseDescription: Students extend their knowledge of website design, publishing, aesthetics and concepts through community-focused projects.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in web ii and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Studio Television Production
courseDescription: Students crew live-to-tape studio productions for telecast and streaming on the campus television station. Leadership, teamwork, technological innovations, ethics, and social responsibility are explored.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in studio television production and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Mixed Media: Color
courseDescription: Building upon the drawing and painting base formed by foundation courses and personal experience, this course introduces many mixed media techniques and processes that can be used to expand one’s ideas and expressions. Projects incorporate contemporary aesthetics, abstraction, and perceptual work. Digital projects and hands-on techniques include, but are not be limited to, the use of transparency and layering, transfers of various kinds, and the creating of surfaces upon which to build content.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in mixed media: color and strengthens skills used in communication and media / studio art work.

title: Media Training
courseDescription: Teaches professional skills for effective self-presentation in any communication medium. Students learn how to develop and deliver clear messages; represent organizations during media interviews; pitch and build relationships with TV, audio, and print media professionals; and recognize their personal strengths as spokespeople. A significant portion of the course requires students to act as and train spokespeople in various scenario-based exercises.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in media training and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Studio Lighting
courseDescription: Aims at expanding students’ visual awareness and their ability to create fine art imagery through the controlled use of studio lighting. Students work in film or digital as they explore a variety of light sources from natural light, to hot lights, to professional strobe lights in a studio environment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in studio lighting and strengthens skills used in communication and media / photography work.

title: Advanced Study in Communication
courseDescription: An upper-level, hands-on project class in professional media, guided by the sponsoring faculty member. Written permission of the sponsoring faculty member. May be repeated with instructor permission.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced study in communication and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Photojournalism
courseDescription: Engages students in photography as a storytelling medium and narrative vehicle, specifically in news and documentaries. Students learn how to communicate compelling stories via single images and photo essays, and are introduced to the various types and outlets of news and journalistic image-making. In addition to producing images, students analyze published materials and are introduced to professional ethics in the field.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in photojournalism and strengthens skills used in communication and media / photography work.

PT 381: PT 270 or PT 300 or PT 301 or CM 308

title: Book Marketing and Promotion
courseDescription: Students learn to position books in the marketplace by direct sales and by wholesale distribution to chain and independent bookstores; write news releases; pitch review media; conduct print and electronic publicity campaigns; and plan author events. Projects support books published by Apprentice House.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in book marketing and promotion and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Book Publishing: Manuscript Evaluation and Development
courseDescription: Students solicit and evaluate manuscripts submitted to Apprentice House for publication and work with authors to edit manuscripts and prepare them for publication.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in book publishing: manuscript evaluation and development and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Media Presence and Performance
courseDescription: Students learn the techniques used by broadcast journalists in presenting stories on the air. Topics include how to frame stories for field reporting, how to shape voice and body language for studio-based performance, how to conduct both short and long interviews on camera, and how to develop personal on-air presence. Recommended for students interested in careers in broadcast news both in front of and behind the camera.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in media presence and performance and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Greyhound News
courseDescription: Students work as reporters and/or editors for the Greyhound student online newspaper. Students engage in collaborative team meetings, cover stories on campus and in the community on deadline, and peer review each other’s copy among other duties involved in publishing an online newspaper. May be repeated twice for degree credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in greyhound news and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Research Experience
courseDescription: Following the apprenticeship model, students work with professors on on-going qualitative or quantitative research projects. Research activities might include library database searches, development of questionnaires, interviews in the field, online surveys, collection and analysis of data, and research report writing. The course is ideally suited to seniors who can handle a significant amount of independent work.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in research experience and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.

title: Senior Capstone in Multimedia Journalism
courseDescription: Students work in teams to develop a magazine with multimedia components. Each team prepares a project prospectus outlining content and a business plan, and creates a prototype magazine for one or more media platforms, including print, video, or online. The finished magazine prototype may be submitted to a national contest.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior capstone in multimedia journalism and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.
prerequisites: CM 203; CM 308; CM 301 or CM 324 or CM 333

title: Senior Capstone in Digital Media
courseDescription: Project based class where students work in teams to create either small websites, promotional print materials, and/or videos for community clients. Students demonstrate their proficiency and creativity in a variety of digital media.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior capstone in digital media and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.
prerequisites: CM 203; CM 308; CM 312 or CM 322 or CM 324; one additional 300-level digital media specialization course

title: Senior Capstone in Advertising
courseDescription: A capstone course for the advertising specialization. Students work in a simulated advertising agency environment in order to develop a comprehensive advertising plan and ad campaign on behalf of a client. Students demonstrate their ability to conduct appropriate research, develop advertising strategy, design a media plan, and develop a sales promotion program in service of a comprehensive plan.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior capstone in advertising and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.
prerequisites: CM 203, CM 307, one additional 300-level advertising/public relations specialization course

title: Senior Capstone in Public Relations
courseDescription: A capstone course for the public relations specialization integrating all facets of the public relations mix. Students demonstrate their ability to conduct research, develop a public relations program, and execute the plan. Generally, students work in teams to develop a campaign on behalf of a client.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior capstone in public relations and strengthens skills used in communication and media work.
prerequisites: CM 203, CM 307, CM 354, one additional 300-level advertising/public relations specialization course

title: Making Sense of Data with Database Management Systems
courseDescription: The world is flooded with data, but data by itself is useless. It needs to be gathered, processed, analyzed, visualized, and finally interpreted. This course examines real world data and the tools needed to make sense of it.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in making sense of data with database management systems and strengthens skills used in computer science work.

courseDescription: The world is flooded with data, but data by itself is useless. It needs to be gathered, processed, analyzed, visualized, and finally interpreted. This course examines real world data and the tools needed to make sense of it.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in making sense of data with spss and strengthens skills used in computer science work.

courseDescription: The world is flooded with data, but data by itself is useless. It needs to be gathered, processed, analyzed, visualized, and finally interpreted. This course examines real world data and the tools needed to make sense of it.
