courseDescription: The world is flooded with data, but data by itself is useless. It needs to be gathered, processed, analyzed, visualized, and finally interpreted. This course examines real world data and the tools needed to make sense of it.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in making sense of data with academic research and strengthens skills used in computer science work.

title: Opportunities in STEM
courseDescription: The colloquium focuses on internships, research, and career options available to students in Computer Science, Physics, Mathematics, and Statistics (CPaMS) through speaker talks, career center workshops, and field trips to research and industry partners. This course is intended for natural and applied science majors. Required for all CPaMS Scholars in their second year., PH 200, ST 200.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in opportunities in stem and strengthens skills used in computer science / mathematics / physics / statistics work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Computational Thinking: Exploring Computing through Robotics
courseDescription: Introduces the great ideas of computing through hands-on experiments with robotics. The course explores the nature and limits of computers; engages with the philosophical and social implications of intelligent machines; and asks what the science of computing can tell us about creativity, reasoning, and the human mind. Students gain experience developing logical thinking using a programming language to control small robots; conducting field studies to obtain data; storing and accessing data from a database using queries; and performing data analysis with spreadsheet formulas.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in computational thinking: exploring computing through robotics and strengthens skills used in computer science work.

title: Computer Engineering I
courseDescription: Introduces circuit design and computer organization. Topics include Boolean algebra, combinatorial and sequential circuit design, and modern computer design fundamentals. Students explore how hardware design decisions influence programming language design and provide optimization opportunities in high-level code.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in computer engineering i and strengthens skills used in computer science work.
prerequisites: CS 295 or MA 295 or MA 395 (may be taken concurrently)

title: Computer Science Research
courseDescription: Official credit range: 1-4 credits. Supervised research projects may be taken for credit by qualified students. Requires a preliminary paper outlining the scope of the problem and the associated literature. Requires progress reports and a final research paper.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in computer science research and strengthens skills used in computer science work.

title: Electronic Digital Circuits
courseDescription: Design and testing of complex sequential state machines including machine controllers, modulator/demodulator circuits and CPUs using HDL. Design and testing of several 8-bit multipliers, binary to decimal converters, a CISC CPU, several RISC CPUs, a microcontroller with microprogramming as a controller for a RISC CPU and a CISC CPU, methods to implement hardware for parallel processing, and a wide variety of CPU interrupt structures. Also included are introductions to FPGAs, machine-to-machine communications, using the OSI model.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in electronic digital circuits and strengthens skills used in computer science work.

title: Introduction to Quantum Computing
courseDescription: Students gain an understanding of the transformative impact of this new technology through simulation of a quantum computer and studying the mathematical principles that underlie quantum computation. Topics include quantum logic gates, quantum circuits, quantum entanglement, the measurement problem, and the quantum Fourier transformation. Python programming is used to reinforce student understanding.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to quantum computing and strengthens skills used in computer science / engineering / physics work.
prerequisites: CS 488: CS 212; Written or electronic permission of the instructor
EG 488: EG 140 or CS 151, MA 251; Written or electronic permission of the instructor
PH 488: CS 151 or EG 140, MA 251; Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Technical Innovation and Entrepreneurship
courseDescription: A survey of innovation and entrepreneurship. Introduces theoretical frameworks and examples of issues, skills, and challenges of innovating in the fields of science and engineering. Establishes multidisciplinary skill sets for creating and managing technology-based entrepreneurship.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in technical innovation and entrepreneurship and strengthens skills used in computer science / engineering work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Quantum Computing II
courseDescription: Studies advanced topics and applications in quantum computing. Topics include quantum Fourier transformation, eigenvalue estimation, and their applications such as Shor's algorithm and the HHL algorithm. Other topics may include an introduction to quantum machine learning using quantum kernels and quantum variational methods, quantum computing as applied to quantum chemistry, and quantum error correction.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in quantum computing ii and strengthens skills used in computer science / engineering / physics work.
prerequisites: CS 492: CS 488; Written or electronic permission of the instructor
EG 492: EG 488 or PH 488; Written or electronic permission of the instructor
PH 492: EG 488, PH 488; Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Computer Science Project Planning
courseDescription: Introduces formal writing in the field of computer science. The course addresses topics in support of the senior project including how to find and define a capstone project, the structure of research papers, usability of Git software, and advanced Git usage in support of project management.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in computer science project planning and strengthens skills used in computer science work.

title: Computer Science Project I
courseDescription: Students work with an external client on a substantial research or software development project. Students gather project requirements through consultation with their clients and document them in a proposal approved by the client and the course instructor. Classroom discussions focus on social and ethical issues in computer science, as well as reading, critiquing, and presenting technical literature.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in computer science project i and strengthens skills used in computer science work.

title: Construction Management: Studio I
department: Construction Management and Real Estate Development
courseDescription: Introduces sustainable construction and real estate development drawing, modeling, and project life cycles and management.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in construction management: studio i and strengthens skills used in construction management and real estate development work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomore construction management, construction engineering concentration majors

title: Construction Management: Studio II
department: Construction Management and Real Estate Development
courseDescription: Examines sustainable construction and real estate development, including materials and methods of the built environment, drawing, and modeling. Introduces safety, legal, and contractual issues in the construction industry. The legal framework includes topics such as employment and labor law, workplace discrimination, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and the National Labor Relations Act.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in construction management: studio ii and strengthens skills used in construction management and real estate development work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomore construction management, construction engineering concentration majors

title: Construction Management: Studio III
department: Construction Management and Real Estate Development
courseDescription: Examines sustainable construction and real estate development, built environment materials and methods, drawing and details, safety, contractual issues, and the legal environment of the industry. Introduces project management, project control, soil and foundations, contract negotiation, and dispute resolution.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in construction management: studio iii and strengthens skills used in construction management and real estate development work.
prerequisites: Restricted to junior construction management, construction engineering concentration majors

title: Sustainability in the Built Environment
department: Construction Management and Real Estate Development
courseDescription: This course applies the three E's—environment, economics, and social equity—to construction and real estate development practice. Students explore sustainability from the perspective of the built environment, including the history of construction and development, and the ways buildings interact with natural systems. The course examines human impacts on natural systems through the built environment and introduces the variety of disciplines working to create a more sustainable future.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sustainability in the built environment and strengthens skills used in construction management and real estate development work.
prerequisites: Construction management, construction engineering concentration major

title: Accessible Housing Environment
department: Construction Management and Real Estate Development / Real Estate
courseDescription: Explores physical, social, and service contexts related to housing and environments for people across the age and ability spectrums. Ecological perspectives and social theories on aging are examined and applied. Students examine evidence regarding how older adults use, perceive, and are affected by their homes and environments.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in accessible housing environment and strengthens skills used in construction management and real estate development / real estate work.
prerequisites: CMR 311: CMR 202; Restricted to construction management, real estate development concentration majors

title: Structural Building Systems
department: Construction Management and Real Estate Development
courseDescription: Introduces the general principles of loads on buildings and the design and analysis of conventional structural building systems in steel, concrete, wood, and masonry. It also addresses the construction of different building systems.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in structural building systems and strengthens skills used in construction management and real estate development work.
prerequisites: Restricted to construction management, real estate development concentration majors

title: Construction Management Studio Capstone
department: Construction Management and Real Estate Development
courseDescription: Examines sustainable construction and real estate development, built environment materials and methods, drawing and details, safety, contractual issues, and the legal environment of the industry. Introduces project management, project control, soil and foundations, contract negotiation, and dispute resolution.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in construction management studio capstone and strengthens skills used in construction management and real estate development work.
prerequisites: Construction management, construction engineering concentration major

title: Ethical Data Science Capstone
courseDescription: Students work with an external client on a substantial data science project. Students gather project requirements through consultation with their clients and document them in a proposal approved by the client and the course instructor. Classroom discussions focus on social and ethical issues in data science.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethical data science capstone and strengthens skills used in data science work.

title: Survey of International Economics
courseDescription: Utilizes the tools of economic principle to analyze the global economy that is increasingly open to trade and capital flows across borders. Major topics are international trade in goods and services, and the workings of international finance, particularly the foreign exchange market. Additional topics include a comparison of economic trade systems, regional trade arrangements, and the role of institutions such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund on the global economy.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in survey of international economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.
prerequisites: EC 102, EC 103, or written permission of the instructor

title: Urban Economics
courseDescription: Develops an understanding of the economic approach to the role of cities in today's economy and historically. The course utilizes the economist's toolkit to study major contemporary issues confronting urban areas and explores economic solutions to problems of housing, transportation, education, poverty, crime, growth, employment, taxes, and redevelopment. Emphasis is placed on urban policies in the developed and developing worlds.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in urban economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: Development Economics
courseDescription: Examines the theory and practice of the economic development of nations. The first segment focuses on the meaning of development. The second segment considers the internal and external forces that encourage or discourage economic development.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in development economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: Community Development
courseDescription: Studies community development, with a focus on topics related to the formation of physical and social capital. These topics include the role played by community development banks, social capital, entrepreneurship, and cooperatives. Students learn to assess development through standard measures of poverty, inequality, and human development in general.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in community development and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: Environmental Economics
courseDescription: Examines contemporary issues of environmental quality, natural resource allocation, and conservation from the economic perspective. Students develop an understanding of the history of the environmental movement and learn to analyze environmental issues using economic tools. Topics include benefit-cost analysis, property rights, incentive-based pollution control policies, and a review of government regulatory performance.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in environmental economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: Sports Economics
courseDescription: Applies the tools of price theory to professional and amateur sports. Students develop analytic tools useful in the management of sports (and other) enterprises and the evaluation of strategy in the contests themselves. Topics include market demand analysis; performance measurement and compensation of athletes; economic impact analysis and stadium subsidies; labor market discrimination; and collegiate sports.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sports economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.
prerequisites: EC 220 or ST 210 (may be taken concurrently)

title: Monetary Economics
courseDescription: Examines micro- and macroeconomic monetary issues, problems, and theory. Students learn to predict the effect of monetary events on financial markets and the real economy. Topics include functions and measures of money; interest rates, present value, and yield; capital asset pricing model; diversification; risk and term structure of interest rates; financial intermediaries; creation and determination of the money supply; the Federal Reserve System; tools, goals, and targets of monetary policy; demand for money; money and real GDP; transmissions mechanisms.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in monetary economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: International Financial Economics
courseDescription: Examines the financial side of international economic activity. Topics include balance of payments; foreign exchange; spot markets and forward markets; covered and uncovered interest parity conditions; monetary and portfolio balance models of exchange rate determination; macroeconomic policy in an open economy; under fixed and flexible exchange rates; optimum currency areas; and issues surrounding the European Monetary Union. Students delve deeper into a specific area by conducting original research and writing a paper on a topic they develop in conjunction with the professor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in international financial economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: International Trade
courseDescription: Investigates the theory and practice of international trade. The course begins with an analysis of the basis and gains from trade and considers trade policy and obstructions to trade. It reaches focus on special topics such as the relationship between trade and the environment and the development of other economies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in international trade and strengthens skills used in economics work.
prerequisites: EC 102, EC 103, EC 302, or written permission of the instructor

title: Managerial Economics
courseDescription: Combines theory, case studies and classroom discussions to help students learn and master the economic theories that are relevant to management decision making. Topics include transaction costs economics, risk and uncertainty, economic coordination, disruption theories, entrepreneurship, and innovation. The course also explores solutions to problems managers face including outsourcing, insurance, diversification, automation, and adaptive enterprises.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in managerial economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: Business and Government
courseDescription: Examines the nature of business behavior in competitive and noncompetitive markets and the nature and consequences of government regulation of this behavior. Students acquire tools useful in the development of competitive strategies and develop a sophisticated understanding of regulatory institutions and behavior. Topics include collusion; mergers and acquisitions; predatory behavior and monopolization; and emerging deregulation of telecommunication, transportation, and financial institutions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in business and government and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: Behavioral and Experimental Economics
courseDescription: Applies insights from psychology to understand how economic decisions are influenced by factors outside of rational self-interest. A field of growing importance within economics, behavioral economics is used in a wide range of contexts from marketing to management to economic development. Also studied is the design, implementation, and analysis of economic experiments that are used to evaluate behavioral economic effects.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in behavioral and experimental economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: Labor Economics
courseDescription: Individuals make decisions on how much to work, where to work, and how to utilize the earnings from their labor. Firms develop compensation systems and make hiring decisions to efficiently extract the most from their workers, and governments make decisions on what policies are required to regulate the labor market. At a micro level, these decisions determine a family's financial resources, whether college is a good investment, and whether women face wage discrimination.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in labor economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: Health Economics
courseDescription: Examines the basic concepts and models of health economics. Students learn to understand and critique the health care industry and proposed policies. Topics include the institutional and economic structure of the health care industry; the incentives provided by the market, government, and insurance; the private and public demand; production; and the political economy of health care.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in health economics and strengthens skills used in economics work.

title: Introduction to Urban Education
courseDescription: Seeks to provide an overview of the complex issues that impact the development and maintenance of urban schools in the United States. More specifically, the course introduces students to a variety of frameworks through which they learn to examine the nature of urban schools, their historical development, their link to the social and political contexts, and perspectives of the people whose narratives define not only urban schools but also urban communities. Students analyze the formation, development, and current conditions of urban education from a number of different perspectives.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to urban education and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: First Generation Student Success: Revealing the Hidden Curriculum
courseDescription: Reinforces the understanding of the unique challenges and qualities that first-generation students bring to college campuses across the U.S. Students learn through readings, group discussion, and reflection how first-generation students are changing the landscape of higher education, both nationally and at Loyola University Maryland. In addition to exploring how a Jesuit education inherently facilitates first-generation student success, first-generation student experiences, best practices for supporting first-generation students, and research on student retention are critically examined.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in first generation student success: revealing the hidden curriculum and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: Foundations in Early Childhood Education
courseDescription: Students gain a comprehensive understanding of early childhood development, focusing on current theories and practices grounded in relevant research. Students examine the foundational theories of childhood development, analyzing the role of brain development, executive functions, and self-regulation in the child's cognitive and emotional growth. The course explores the interconnectedness of developmental domains and helping students understand how physical, cognitive, social, and emotional domains impact growth and development.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in foundations in early childhood education and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: Wilderness First Responder Course
courseDescription: Designed to provide outdoor leaders and/or current EMS or healthcare professionals with the knowledge and skills necessary to deal with medical and traumatic emergencies in remote settings. Topics include patient assessment, difficult extraction and patient movement, basic search and rescue, emergency childbirth, allergies (includes anaphylaxis certification), toxins, burns, wounds, fractures, dislocations, shock, spinal assessment and management, brain/head injuries, respiratory distress, heat and cold injuries, BLS CPR, legal issues, and treatment of common backcountry ailments such as lost fillings, fish hook removal, fever, etc. Most importantly, the course helps students improve their critical thinking skills in medicine.

Foundational content like Kolb's Experiential Learning Process and William Glasser's Choice Theory compliment topics such as how to give/receive professional feedback, the tenants of an effective lesson, conflict management, facilitating debriefs, and decision-making processes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in outdoor leadership foundations and strengthens skills used in education work.

whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in computational thinking in pk-8 schools and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: Literature and Climate Change
courseDescription: Investigates the various ways in which humans have used literature to understand instances of climate change, past and present. Students read a range of fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in literature and climate change and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Growing Up Modern
courseDescription: Childhood and adolescence are modern inventions. Building upon this fact, students explore how the literature of the past two centuries has depicted childhood, adolescence, and early adulthood. Among the questions asked in the course are: What trials do children and adolescents endure on their way to adulthood?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in growing up modern and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Introduction to Film
courseDescription: Introduces cinematic techniques and critical methods. The course may be organized around themes, genres, or periods; writing assignments range from screenplay treatments to a research paper.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to film and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Race, Law, and American Literature
courseDescription: Explores questions of race and justice in America through a careful study of law and literature. Students read a range of American fiction, poetry, and drama as well as legal texts, such as statutes and court decisions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in race, law, and american literature and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Great Traditions
courseDescription: A survey of some of the most important preromantic authors in English literature in their historical context, thus offering students a coherent overview, as well as an introduction to individual writers and texts. Required for English majors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in great traditions and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Chaucer
courseDescription: An intensive study of The Canterbury Tales and Troilus and Criseyde. Also includes selected readings from Chaucer's other works.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chaucer and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Shakespeare: Histories and Tragedies
courseDescription: The achievement of Shakespeare, primarily the histories and tragedies, set against the background of his time and the works of his contemporaries.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in shakespeare: histories and tragedies and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Shakespeare: Comedies and Romances
courseDescription: The achievement of Shakespeare, primarily the comedies and romances, set against the background of his time and the works of his contemporaries.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in shakespeare: comedies and romances and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Renaissance Literature
courseDescription: Studies Renaissance poetry, drama, and prose, with primary emphasis on English literature but possible consideration of influential continental traditions and masterworks. Readings may include Dante, Petrarch, Erasmus, Castiglione, Machiavelli, Rabelais, Montaigne, More, Marlowe, Sidney, Spenser, Shakespeare, Jonson, and Milton.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in renaissance literature and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Milton
courseDescription: Through epic and tragedy, Milton reigns supreme in English. After a brief excursion through his lyrics, this course focuses on his major works-Paradise Lost, Paradise Regained, and Samson Agonistes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in milton and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Book, Edition, Archive
courseDescription: How does literature become literature? This course examines the production of literature from editorial, material, and digital perspectives, considering how editorial decisions and practices help give form—and meaning—to literary texts. Students take on an editorial project that enables them to apply course concepts and gain experience in editing and preparing texts for production and dissemination.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in book, edition, archive and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Literary Criticism and Theory
courseDescription: An examination of major schools, movements, and trends in modern literary criticism. Emphasis is placed on the competing practical claims made by literary and critical theory.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in literary criticism and theory and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: The Romantic Movement
courseDescription: Studies British literature written during the revolutionary era, 1780-1830, with special attention paid to the poetry and poetic theory of the age. Major figures include Blake, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Percy Bysshe Shelley, and Keats.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the romantic movement and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Jane Austen
courseDescription: An intensive study of the iconic author’s novels within the context of literary and cultural history.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in jane austen and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Philosophy and Literature
courseDescription: Literature gives concrete expression to our sense of reality and in its history “re-presents” the status of man and human events as each age presupposes it. Herein resides the intimate relationship which has always existed between literature and philosophy. The history of this relationship explains both the continuity and the discontinuity which is present in Western literature.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy and literature and strengthens skills used in english / philosophy work.

title: The Nineteenth-Century English Novel
courseDescription: Covers the evolution of the novel from Jane Austen through the Age of Reform. Authors studied may include Dickens, Thackeray, Trollope, the Brontes, Hardy, and Eliot. Some reading of applied theory.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the nineteenth-century english novel and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: American Literature to the First World War
courseDescription: A survey of primarily nineteenth-century American literature, with special emphasis on the writers of the American Renaissance and the rise of American realism. Students who take EN 203 may not count EN 366 toward their English major.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in american literature to the first world war and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Modern Fiction
courseDescription: The development of British, American, Commonwealth, and/or transatlantic fiction from 1900 to 1950, with an emphasis on the evolution of an aesthetic that values poetic composition and experimentation with narrative methods above traditional concepts of narrative structure. Authors studied may include Conrad, Dos Passos, Faulkner, Hemingway, Joyce, Lawrence, and Woolf. May be repeated once for degree credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in modern fiction and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Modern Poetry
courseDescription: An intensive study of a revolution in modern poetry from 1900 to 1950 that challenged almost every aspect of the genre's style, theme, attitude, and structure. Extensive attention to major authors such as Yeats, Pound, Eliot, and Williams within the context of a broader modernist movement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in modern poetry and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: African American Literature
courseDescription: Studies African American literature, with special attention to placing literary expression in the context of slavery, segregation, civil rights, and the black diaspora. The course may survey the development of a black literary tradition, or it may focus on an important era, movement, writer, or issue in that tradition.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in african american literature and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Modern Drama
courseDescription: Examines significant playwrights, themes, and developments in twentieth-century and contemporary theater.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in modern drama and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Postcolonial Literature
courseDescription: Introduces writing about the colonized world, from the perspectives of colonized peoples, in order to locate the sources and discuss the conditions of postcolonial thought.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in postcolonial literature and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Neurodiversity: Mental Disability in Literature and Film
courseDescription: The neurodiversity movement proposes that people with cognitive disabilities add something unique and valuable to the human spectrum. This course proceeds from that idea, using Disability Studies to investigate how writers and filmmakers have depicted neurological and intellectual differences.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in neurodiversity: mental disability in literature and film and strengthens skills used in english work.

title: Literature of the U.S.-Mexico Border
courseDescription: An exploration of the literature and culture of the borderlands, from 1848 to present day. Selections may include poems, novels, short stories, films, and important texts in border theory.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in literature of the u.s.-mexico border and strengthens skills used in english work.

courseDescription: A close and intensive study of a theme, issue, problem, or author in American literature. Recent topic: "The Book in America." Topic announced each time the course is offered. May be repeated once for credit with different topic.

title: Capstone Project in American Studies
courseDescription: As the capstone experience for the American Studies minor, each student develops an independent research project, internship, or service-based project, to be advised by two professors from different departments and presented at an end-of-year American Studies Symposium. The project constitutes the culmination of the student's work in American Studies and provides an opportunity for the student to bring together the perspectives of two different disciplines on a research area of particular interest. A project proposal must be submitted to and approved by the American Studies committee prior to registration for either the fall or spring semesters of senior year.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in capstone project in american studies and strengthens skills used in english / history / political science work.

HS 408: HS 100-level course, HS 200-level or HS 300-level course; Written or electronic permission of the instructor
