title: Introduction to Environment, Society, and Policy
courseDescription: Guided by the Universal Apostolic Preference, 'Caring for Our Common Home', students explore the interactions between human society and the natural world while surveying current environmental policies. Concepts such as environmental history, racism, and justice are introduced. Students gain a foundation in environmental economic theory, including markets, externalities, non-renewable resources, and the commons, while also learning basic environmental accounting.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to environment, society, and policy and strengthens skills used in environmental science and studies work.

title: From Evolution to Communities
courseDescription: Spans the realms of ecology, evolution, population biology, and community ecology, providing students with a comprehensive framework for understanding of the mechanisms shaping Earth's biodiversity. The course is constructed to study the fundamental principles of ecology, exploring the interactions between organisms and their environments. Students gain insights into how species adapt and evolve over time, shaping the biodiversity observed in different environments, while also exploring the factors that shape the size and distribution of populations through the introduction of models and real-world examples.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in from evolution to communities and strengthens skills used in environmental science and studies work.

title: From Evolution to Communities Lab
courseDescription: Laboratory work that supports and enhances the lecture. Focuses on the fundamental principles of ecology, exploring the interactions between organisms and their environments, how species adapt and evolve over time using urban, Chesapeake Bay, and other mid-Atlantic biomes. Students engage in both field and laboratory observations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in from evolution to communities lab and strengthens skills used in environmental science and studies work.

title: Environmental Science and Sustainability Lab
courseDescription: Laboratory work that supports and enhances material from the lecture. A hands-on learning experience that takes place in laboratory and outdoor settings. Students collect and analyze environmental samples and are introduced to methods of statistical, graphical, and modeling analyses.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in environmental science and sustainability lab and strengthens skills used in environmental science and studies work.
prerequisites: ENV 114; MA 151 or MA 251 or ST 210

title: Integral Ecology Capstone
courseDescription: Provides students the opportunity to integrate and apply what they have learned in other courses to assess challenges, develop strategies, and to communicate effectively for healing Earth. Students learn from their peers and engage with communities beyond the classroom.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in integral ecology capstone and strengthens skills used in environmental science and studies work.
prerequisites: ENV 491 or ENV 492 or ENV 495 or ENV 496 (may be taken concurrently)
Restricted to environmental science and environmental studies majors or minors

title: Environmental Science Research
courseDescription: Official credit range: 1-3 credits. To augment classroom learning, students engage in independent scientific research on an environmental science topic under the supervision of a faculty member. Students meet regularly with the supervising faculty member to discuss their research progress and keep accurate records of their progress. Students work with their supervising faculty member to develop a paper or final product detailing their research results.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in environmental science research and strengthens skills used in environmental science and studies work.

title: Environmental Studies Research
courseDescription: Official credit range: 1-3 credits. To augment classroom learning, students engage in independent academic research on a topic related to the environment or sustainability under the supervision of a faculty member. Students meet regularly with the supervising faculty member to discuss their research progress and keep accurate records of their progress. Students work with their supervising faculty member to develop a paper or final product detailing their research results.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in environmental studies research and strengthens skills used in environmental science and studies work.
prerequisites: Restricted to environmental science and environmental studies majors or minors

title: Personal Financial Management
courseDescription: Designed to allow students to develop a framework for planning and implementing a lifetime finance program. Investigates alternative personal financial decisions with a view toward optimizing personal wealth and creating more informed consumers. Students develop a personal financial plan.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in personal financial management and strengthens skills used in finance work.

title: Fundamentals of Financial Risk Management
department: Finance / Financial Risk Management and Insurance
courseDescription: Explores the basics of financial risk management with a focus on risk management in a corporate setting. Students learn how to define, identify, measure, and monitor various types of risks in business environments. The course provides an overview of key risk management topics including enterprise risk, human capital risk, financial risk, cybersecurity risk, and emerging risks.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in fundamentals of financial risk management and strengthens skills used in finance / financial risk management and insurance work.
prerequisites: FI 230 or BH 230 or FI 320 or BH 320; EC 220 or ST 210

title: Fundamentals of Insurance
department: Finance / Financial Risk Management and Insurance
courseDescription: Introduces the insurance industry, covering key concepts such as health, liability, life, property, workers' compensation, and environmental insurance. The course explores the insurance industry from the perspective of individuals, corporations, and insurance companies. Students gain an understanding of insurance pricing, underwriting and claims processes, and reinsurance practices.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in fundamentals of insurance and strengthens skills used in finance / financial risk management and insurance work.
prerequisites: FI 230 or BH 230 or FI 320 or BH 320; EC 220 or ST 210

title: Investments
courseDescription: Students gain an introduction to the organization and functionality of securities markets with an emphasis on fundamental analysis. Topics include bonds, equities, risk definition and measurement, return analysis, and models of valuation. Students are also introduced to the primary types of derivative securities such as options and futures.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in investments and strengthens skills used in finance work.

title: Real Estate Law and Regulation
courseDescription: Examines the fundamentals of real estate finance and development from both legal and managerial perspectives, with a focus on residential and commercial transactions. Topics include land acquisition, deeds, tax consequences, property titling, zoning and restrictive covenants, environmental compliance, sustainability, foreclosure, disposition of property, and recent legal developments.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in real estate law and regulation and strengthens skills used in finance / real estate work.

title: Global Financial Management
courseDescription: Students gain a fundamental understanding of the international dimensions of corporate finance function. Students apply the concepts, approaches, and technology to support financial management in a multinational business environment. Topics include a detailed examination of foreign exchange markets, foreign exchange risk and its management, and international financial markets.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in global financial management and strengthens skills used in finance work.

title: Fixed Income Securities: Valuation and Markets
courseDescription: Students gain a fundamental understanding of the pricing of bonds and operation of the bond market. Emphasis is placed on the various types of bonds and their characteristics and the risks associated with bonds. The mathematics of bond pricing and duration are also explored.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in fixed income securities: valuation and markets and strengthens skills used in finance work.

title: Financial Services Firms and Their Environments
courseDescription: Surveys financial services firms including commercial banks, savings banks, credit unions, insurance companies, mutual funds, securities firms, investment banks, and finance companies. Addresses operational issues within the financial services environment. Develops a framework for analyzing and measuring the risks faced by financial institutions by considering the environment in which these firms operate.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in financial services firms and their environments and strengthens skills used in finance work.

title: Derivative Securities and Markets
courseDescription: Designed for students' understanding of derivative-related financial instruments such as forwards, futures, and options and the use of derivatives in investment and corporate financial management. An introduction to derivative security markets, the valuation of derivatives, derivative trading strategies, and the management of corporate risk with derivatives are covered.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in derivative securities and markets and strengthens skills used in finance work.

title: Portfolio Management
courseDescription: Introduces portfolio theory and management in the practical world that integrates students' knowledge of equity and fixed income valuation. Topics include portfolio strategies, futures and options, commodities, the Internet, and portfolio management under live market conditions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in portfolio management and strengthens skills used in finance work.

title: Financial Analysis and Valuation
courseDescription: The assessment of business financial performance and valuation from the point of view of equity and credit analysts. Students learn to analyze a firm's profitability and risk by applying both financial and strategic analysis, prepare pro forma financial statements, ascertain the intrinsic value of a business, and apply spreadsheet models for financial decision making.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in financial analysis and valuation and strengthens skills used in finance work.

title: Advanced Corporate Finance
courseDescription: A capstone experience for finance majors. The implementation of financial decisions and policies by using actual case situations. Students learn to apply the concepts and decision-making tools employed in effective financial decision making and increase their knowledge and understanding of the underlying theories of financial management.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced corporate finance and strengthens skills used in finance work.

title: Climate Risk Management and Insurance
courseDescription: Equips students with the knowledge and tools to assess, manage, and mitigate the growing climate risks facing organizations. Students explore both physical risks, such as extreme weather events, sea-level rise, and resource scarcity, and transitional risks that result from regulatory and market shifts. Through scenario modeling and stress testing, they learn to quantify climate risk and examine how financial markets contribute to risk management.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in climate risk management and insurance and strengthens skills used in financial risk management and insurance work.
prerequisites: FRI 300 or FI 300; FRI 305 or FI 305

title: Quantitative Financial Risk Management
courseDescription: Explores quantitative financial risk management with the goal of preparing students for the first portion of the Financial Risk Manager (FRM) Certification Exam. Throughout the course, students learn advanced financial risk management concepts such as portfolio optimization, value-at-risk (VaR), expected shortfall analysis, Monte Carlo simulations, scenario analysis, decision trees, and stress testing. Students combine these quantitative risk management techniques with time- series econometrics, including ARIMA and GARCH models.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in quantitative financial risk management and strengthens skills used in financial risk management and insurance work.
prerequisites: FRI 300 or FI 300; FRI 305 or FI 305

title: Practical Applications of Financial Risk Management and Insurance
courseDescription: Offers a hands-on experience that integrates and applies the concepts and skills acquired throughout the Financial Risk Management and Insurance major. Students engage in in-depth analysis of various risk management and insurance issues, addressing both traditional and emerging risks across multiple sectors. They learn to identify complex risks, assess their underlying causes, and develop innovative solutions by employing a combination of risk management and insurance strategies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in practical applications of financial risk management and insurance and strengthens skills used in financial risk management and insurance work.
prerequisites: FRI 300 or FI 300; FRI 305 or FI 305

title: How to Get Away with Murder (Or Not)
courseDescription: Is it possible to design the 'perfect' crime and get away with it? Students develop an opinion to this question by exploring crime, especially homicides, through multiple lenses to understand modern approaches to criminal investigation, applications of forensic analyses, criminal psychology, and victimology. The impacts of criminal investigations and homicides on issues and perceptions surrounding communities such as wrongful convictions, profiling, corruption, and trust in policing, forensic science, and law enforcement are also examined.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in how to get away with murder (or not) and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Scientific Basis of Forensic Investigation
courseDescription: Students gain an in-depth introduction to the scientific method and its application to forensic disciplines founded on the natural sciences and emerging areas of forensic investigation. Through case studies, laboratory/field work, and reading of the primary literature, students practice observation, critical analysis of data sets, and communication of research findings using symbolic data representation, and apply statistical analysis of forensic data through the lens of appropriate ethical and moral standards. Does not fulfill natural science core requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in scientific basis of forensic investigation and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: Restricted to forensic science majors or minors

title: Introduction to Criminalistics
courseDescription: Introduces the problems and techniques of scientific examination of forensic physical evidence with emphasis on documentation and interpretation of physical patterns. Emphasis is placed on the theoretical bases of methods of comparison and their influence on scientific interpretation of evidence. Topics include scientific photography, imprints, impressions, tool marks, gunshot residue, cordage and textile examinations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to criminalistics and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Forensic Chemistry
courseDescription: Examines the fundamental issues, concepts, and methodologies associated with forensic chemical analysis of physical and trace evidence. Topics include drug analysis, toxicology, explosives analysis, arson, firearms and tool marks, and latent prints.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic chemistry and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Crime Scene Investigation
courseDescription: Introduces the basic procedures and practices used in crime scene investigation including documentation and processing, methods for recovery and processing of physical and trace evidence, and procedures for establishing chain of custody and continuity of evidence. Legal and ethical requirements associated with crime scene processing are also examined. Some field trips may be required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in crime scene investigation and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Introduction to Fingerprints
courseDescription: Introduction to the discovery and historical use of fingerprints, biology of the skin and formation of fingerprints, and fundamentals of how and why fingerprints are used. Students learn how latent fingerprints are recovered from items of evidence, the chemical and physical techniques associated with processing different surfaces, as well as learn to recognize various pattern types and the levels of detail and anatomical features of fingerprints and palm prints.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to fingerprints and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Supporting Twenty-First Century Policing with Forensic Evidence
courseDescription: Examines the importance of valid and reliable forensic evidence in twenty-first century policing. Starting with historical perspectives of law enforcement in the U.S., students learn how policing has changed, the challenges facing police organizations today, and the role sound forensic evidence plays in strengthening public trust and improving the legitimacy of policing.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in supporting twenty-first century policing with forensic evidence and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Forensic Serology of Animal and Human Body Fluids
courseDescription: Introduces the basic concepts of forensic serology as it applies to the collection, preservation, and testing of biological evidence in the form of body fluids. Lectures and laboratories examine concepts and techniques related to the collection and analysis from humans as well as in veterinary and wildlife forensic investigations. Closed to students who have taken FO 322, FO 356, BL 355, or BL 356.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic serology of animal and human body fluids and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: FO 101; BL 118 or BL 150; BL 119 or BL 151; BL 121 or BL 152; BL 126 or BL 153
Restricted to forensic science majors or minors

title: Forensic Ecological Evidence
courseDescription: Introduces biological and ecological evidence associated with crime scenes, especially evidence associated with violent crimes and death investigations. Lectures and laboratories examine concepts and techniques used for the collection and analysis of anthropological, biological, botanical, entomological, and microbial physical and trace evidence commonly discovered during crime scene investigations. Closed to students who have taken FO 320, FO 356, BL 355, or BL 356.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic ecological evidence and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: FO 101; BL 118 or BL 150; BL 119 or BL 151; BL 121 or BL 152; BL 126 or BL 153
Restricted to forensic science majors or minors

title: DNA Analysis in Forensic Investigations
courseDescription: Examines the biological basis for using genetic information in legal investigations. The course places an emphasis on the scientific principles behind DNA analysis techniques, including DNA extraction, quantification, STR amplification, interpretation of STR data including mixtures, interpretation of Y STR data, and statistical analysis of both types of DNA profiles. The course also studies advanced topics such as the application of CODIS, DNA profiling and phenotyping, and Investigative Genetic Genealogy to criminal investigations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in dna analysis in forensic investigations and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Biological and Forensic Science Quality Assurance
courseDescription: Introduction to theory and practice of quality assurance to include quality control/assurance, management, and application of statics, as applied in bioscience industry and forensic laboratory environments. Standards associated with ALCOA, ASCLD-LAB and ISO accreditation and professional certification procedures are emphasized.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biological and forensic science quality assurance and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Forensic Toxicology
courseDescription: Examines the practical and theoretical aspects of forensic toxicology, with an emphasis on the analysis of biological samples to detect and quantify drugs, chemicals, poisons, and other substances. The evaluation and interpretation of the potential toxicity on an individual are discussed. Topics covered include postmortem, DUI/DUID, workplace, human performance, and other forensic toxicology areas of focus.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic toxicology and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: Restricted to forensic science majors or minors

title: Trace Evidence and Questioned Documents
courseDescription: Introduces the basic procedures and practices used for the analysis of trace evidence and forensic document evidence (questioned documents) casework. The course covers general microscopy, fire debris and arson, physical match, tool mark, hair, fibers, and paint examinations. Forensic document examinations topics include handwriting and forgeries; altered, obliterated, and indented writing; and printer examinations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in trace evidence and questioned documents and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: Restricted to forensic science majors or minors

title: Foundations of Comparative Sciences
courseDescription: Explores the principles, methodologies, and applications of comparative analysis in forensic science, as well as the use of laboratory equipment including stereo microscopes and calipers. Topics include the documentation, collection, and analysis of fingerprints, firearms, toolmarks, footwear, and tire track evidence, as well as an introduction to the ACE-V examination method and database search tools including Ballistics IQ.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in foundations of comparative sciences and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Forensic Entomology with Lab
courseDescription: Forensic entomology is the application of insect science to legal issues. Lectures explore the use of insects and other terrestrial arthropods in death investigations; cases of neglect and abuse; use of insects in toxicological analyses; contamination of food products and other marketable goods; and subsequent litigation. Laboratories focus on techniques associated with death scene investigation, particularly in the collection and identification of arthropods found on a corpse.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic entomology with lab and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Introduction to Investigative Genetic Genealogy
courseDescription: Introduces the use of genetic genealogy in ancestry investigations as well as applications to criminal investigations of violent crimes and unidentified human remains.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to investigative genetic genealogy and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Digital and Forensic Imaging
courseDescription: Explores forensic imaging through discussions and laboratory and field work associated with 2D imaging and enhancement, 360 imaging done at crime scenes, 3D imaging and printing, visual evidence enhancement, witness reproduction, and medical imaging. The course includes discussions of application of forensic imaging as well as the regulation and ethical consideration of the associated methodology.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in digital and forensic imaging and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Death Investigation
courseDescription: Introduces the basic procedures and practices used in death investigation including documentation of the body, injury, scenes, photography, and determining possible methods for cause and manner of death. Legal and ethical requirements associated with working side by side with detectives and crime scene investigators are also examined. Some field trips may be required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in death investigation and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Introduction to Firearms and Toolmarks Analysis
courseDescription: A foundational course for the forensic examination of firearms and toolmark evidence. Firearm and ammunition development are explored, along with class and individual characteristics and identification criteria. Instrumentation, serial number restoration, and other manufacturer-related markings are also addressed.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to firearms and toolmarks analysis and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Crime Scene and Evidence Photography
courseDescription: Explores the concepts and techniques used across various forensic disciplines. Students engage in a range of practical exercises while reviewing the fundamentals of proper lighting and composition. These exercises are reinforced through crime scene and evidentiary photography examples, including footwear impressions, chemically processed latent fingerprints, and bloodstain patterns.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in crime scene and evidence photography and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Victimology and Applications to Violent Crimes
courseDescription: Examines the issues related to victims of violent crimes, including measurement of victimization, the impact on victims, discussions of typology of victims, and analysis of the victim-offender relationship. The course also explores the role of victimology in investigations of violent crimes, specifically within the context of forensic victimology and investigative profiling that require an in-depth, holistic understanding of the victim's life.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in victimology and applications to violent crimes and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Investigations of Violent Crimes
courseDescription: Examination of the concepts, techniques, and methodologies used to investigate violent crimes, including sexual assault, aggravated assault, and homicides. Topics include identification and analysis of physical and trace evidence, interviewing witnesses and suspects, and understanding of victimology and suspectology in the context of violent crimes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in investigations of violent crimes and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: Restricted to forensic science majors or minors

title: Animal Law
courseDescription: Examines the legal aspects of animal cruelty investigations, animal law, and the basic concepts of crime scene documentation and forensic evidence processing. Topics include the types of animal crimes and their legal definitions; the roles and responsibilities of investigators, crime scene analysts, veterinarians and prosecutors; forensic techniques and methodologies for processing a crime scene and evidence; and legal procedures that are required to seize animals. An emphasis is placed on Maryland animal welfare laws pertaining to domesticated and agricultural animals.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in animal law and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: Restricted to forensic science majors or minors

title: Forensic Anthropology
courseDescription: Introduces the basic knowledge of human anatomy and osteology, including human remains recovery and laboratory processes that are required of a forensic anthropologist, especially for person’s identification.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic anthropology and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: Restricted to forensic science majors or minors

title: Bloodstain Pattern Analysis and Crime Scene Reconstruction
courseDescription: Teaches the correct identification, classification, and application of bloodstain pattern analysis (BPA) as it contributes to crime scene reconstruction (CSR). In addition, the history and evolution of current CSR procedures and applications to present day crime are discussed. Students investigate how CSR relates to event analysis and the scientific method.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in bloodstain pattern analysis and crime scene reconstruction and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: FO 101, FO 102; FO 300 with a B or higher
Restricted to forensic science majors or minors

title: Forensic Cognitive Psychology
courseDescription: Introduction to the application of cognitive psychology to the improvement of forensic science policy and practice. Students examine current challenges for the forensic science community, including the contribution of forensic science errors to wrongful convictions and the increasing demand for forensic examinations to produce probative results in criminal trials.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic cognitive psychology and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: Restricted to forensic studies science majors or minors

title: Forensic Science Errors and Wrongful Convictions
courseDescription: Performs reviews of cases associated with wrongful convictions and elucidates causative factors related to scientific validity, testimony standards, laboratory management, professional development, system issues, and legal professionals and frameworks. Students learn to analyze common factors across forensic disciplines and jurisdictions, perform root cause analyses, and develop systemic reforms.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic science errors and wrongful convictions and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Cold Case Investigations
courseDescription: A capstone experience focused on investigations of cold homicide cases. The class examines some high-profile cold cases as means to learn the methodologies and techniques used during investigations. Each student spends the term on a real cold case for investigation, culminating in an investigative and a victimology report.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in cold case investigations and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Advanced Cold Case Investigation
courseDescription: Focuses on advanced techniques and concepts in investigations of cold homicide cases. The class works as a team to investigate a real cold case lead by cold case investigators. Students are taught how to examine case files including how to organize the information, to initiate a cold case investigation, and to search for old and new leads.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced cold case investigation and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the department chair

title: Forensic Techniques
courseDescription: Introduces advanced techniques and technologies used in forensic laboratories and at crime scenes. Each semester has a unique focus or theme, such as drone use in crime scene investigation, techniques for evaluation of fingerprints, recovery techniques of interred remains, and advanced photographic and digital imaging techniques in forensic investigations. May be repeated once for credit with a different topic.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic techniques and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.

title: Forensic Science Research I
courseDescription: A hands-on capstone experience in forensic science in which a student may engage in an in-depth exploration of a topic associated with forensic or criminal investigation, criminal justice/criminology, law, or forensic psychology through research with a sponsor/mentor (on or off campus). A preliminary paper outlining the nature and scope of the problem, experimental procedures, and associated literature and a final research paper are required. Generally complete during senior year.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic science research i and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the department chair

title: Forensic Science Research II
courseDescription: A hands-on capstone experience in forensic science in which a student may engage in an in-depth exploration of a topic associated with forensic or criminal investigation, criminal justice/criminology, law, or forensic psychology through research with a sponsor/mentor (on or off campus). The research is usually a continuation of a project started during FO 494. Generally complete during senior year.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forensic science research ii and strengthens skills used in forensic science work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the department chair

title: Introductory French I
courseDescription: A thorough grounding in the four language skills: reading, listening comprehension, speaking, and writing, as well as an introduction to Francophone cultures and literatures. For students with no previous knowledge of the language. Not recommended for students who have taken three years of high school French.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory french i and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: Introductory French II
courseDescription: A continuation of FR 101. Laboratory study outside the classroom is required. Summer sections
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory french ii and strengthens skills used in french work.
prerequisites: FR 101 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Intermediate French I
courseDescription: A systematic consolidation and expansion of the four basic skills: reading, listening comprehension, speaking, and writing. To increase students' proficiency in the language and broaden their understanding of Francophone cultures and literatures. Laboratory study outside the classroom is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate french i and strengthens skills used in french work.
prerequisites: FR 102 or FR 161 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Comprehensive Intermediate French
courseDescription: The material covered is essentially the same as for the FR 103-FR 104 sequence, except that it is covered in one semester instead of two. It consists of a systematic consolidation and expansion of the four basic skills: reading, understanding, speaking, and writing. To increase and perfect students' acquired abilities/proficiencies in the language and broaden their understanding of Francophone cultures and literatures, the second half is a capstone reviewing and reinforcing language skills to help students attain intermediate level as defined by ACTFL guidelines in the five skills: reading, writing, speaking, comprehension, and culture.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in comprehensive intermediate french and strengthens skills used in french work.
prerequisites: Open to students who have completed FR 102 or FR 161 or placed into FR 103

title: French Composition and Conversation I
courseDescription: Develops writing and speaking ability in French through models of style, related grammar, and composition exercises. Comprehension and speaking are built from authentic documents and other developing technologies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in french composition and conversation i and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: The Living Language
courseDescription: A transition between language study on the lower-division level, where grammar and oral practice are stressed, to more advanced upper-division courses in which the language becomes the primary means of expression and communication. Special emphasis is put on the study of Italian immigration into the United States, considering different aspects with the help of Italian literature, history, movies, and personal narratives.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the living language and strengthens skills used in french / italian work.
prerequisites: IT 202: IT 104 or IT 162 or IT 201

title: Living and Working in the French Caribbean Today
courseDescription: A volunteer and language immersion course offered in Baltimore and Guadeloupe, France. Students spend three weeks living with local families on the island of Marie Galante, part of the French overseas department of Guadeloupe, to organize and run volunteer activities in one of the island's small underprivileged communities. Participants apply their knowledge of French and other academic disciplines to real life situations as they live with and help a Creole French community.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in living and working in the french caribbean today and strengthens skills used in french work.
prerequisites: FR 205: FR 104 or FR 162; Restricted to students studying in Guadeloupe
FR 305: FR 201 or FR 216 or one FR 300-level course; Restricted to students studying in Guadeloupe

title: Highlights in French and Francophone Studies
courseDescription: Students are prepared to take advanced literature and culture classes. By reading and analyzing plays, poems, and short novels, students improve their ability to read and comprehend literary texts in French. To better understand context, the course introduces students to French and Francophone history.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in highlights in french and francophone studies and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: France Today
courseDescription: Studies the evolution of France since 1980 with emphasis on political, social, intellectual, and artistic issues. Includes various analyses of the role of France on the international scene and particularly as a member of the European Union. Students study articles drawn from the French press, recent films, and current French television news.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in france today and strengthens skills used in french work.
prerequisites: FR 201 or FR 216 or one FR 300-level course

title: The Reel Thing: French New Wave Cinema
courseDescription: Focuses on the works of French filmmakers Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rivette, and Resnais who rebelled against the conventionality of their predecessors. This new generation of filmmakers sought to establish the notion of director as author. Students study the esthetic, thematic, and theoretical aspects of their works from 1958 to 1964.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the reel thing: french new wave cinema and strengthens skills used in french work.
prerequisites: FR 201 or FR 216 or one FR 300-level course

title: French for Health Professions and Humanitarian Aid
courseDescription: Equips students with the necessary language skills, cultural understanding, and knowledge to effectively communicate and work in French-speaking medical environments and humanitarian aid contexts. Upon completion of the course, students may take the test given by the Paris Chamber of Commerce and Industry to obtain the Diplôme de français de la Santé (DFP).
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in french for health professions and humanitarian aid and strengthens skills used in french work.
prerequisites: FR 201 or FR 216 or one FR 300-level course

title: French for International Relations
courseDescription: Examine a variety of international themes such as diplomacy, education, health, culture, security, and more, to prepare for a career in international relations. Students practice presenting arguments to convince others and to defend their own point of view. Students gain tools to communicate effectively in different situations, how to write summaries and official statements, summarize and comment on a country’s status in a certain field, and to respectfully intervene during a meeting.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in french for international relations and strengthens skills used in french work.
prerequisites: FR 201 or FR 216 or one FR 300-level course

title: Speak Up
courseDescription: Designed to help students learn to express themselves more fluently and confidently in French. Students learn the French phonetic system in order to improve their pronunciation and eloquence. The course concentrates on speaking practice using music, film, television, radio, poetry, oral presentations, and public speaking exercises to explore contemporary French and Francophone culture while analyzing and practicing pronunciation and speaking skills.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in speak up and strengthens skills used in french work.
prerequisites: FR 201 or FR 216 or one FR 300-level course

title: Savoring Francophone Literature
courseDescription: Through the lens of gastronomy, students are introduced to the literature and cultures of several Francophone countries or regions, including Algeria, Cameroun, Guadeloupe, Reunion Island, and Senegal. The course explores how food is used in novels as a vehicle to discuss topics such as childhood, relationships, politics, history, and social issues. Taught in French.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in savoring francophone literature and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: Trauma and Testimony
courseDescription: Examines representations of the 1994 genocide of the Tutsis in Rwanda in a variety of literary genres (autobiographical testimony, novels, short stories, poetry, essays, and graphic novels), as well as the visual media (film, interviews, and photos). Students examine how the particularities of each genre allow authors to testify of trauma in different ways. Taught in French.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in trauma and testimony and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: Caribbean Identities in Movement
courseDescription: Examines dynamic shifts in Francophone Caribbean literature, culture, and identity throughout the twentieth century. This course analyses the particularities of the Indigénisme, Négritude, Créolité. and Antillanité movements. Moreover, it explores how major themes in Francophone Caribbean literature—including colonization, slavery, abolition, racism, commemoration, cultural belonging, linguistic tensions, Creole resistance, and ecology—inform Caribbean identity today.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in caribbean identities in movement and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: French Film in Context
courseDescription: Analyzes the history of French film in relationship to the evolution of France since 1895. From the works of Méliès and the Lumière brothers to the contemporary performances of actor Fabrice Luchini, the evolution of French film helps characterize key turning points in French society and history. Students analyze how important French films and directors represented and addressed issues of their time while benefiting from new technologies and narrative structures.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in french film in context and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: The Algerian War (1954-1962)
courseDescription: Examines the Algerian War of Independence in its historical, political, and international contexts. Topics studied include: colonization, the influence of World War II, the FLN (Front de libération nationale), the OAS (Organisation de l’armée secrète), military tactics used, the role of women, the use of torture, the Paris massacre of 1961, Évian Accords, the fall of the Fourth Republic of France, the exodus of pieds-noirs from Algeria, and the effect of the Algerian War on decolonization in Francophone Africa. Course conducted in French.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the algerian war (1954-1962) and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: The Text and the Screen
courseDescription: Analyzes the relationship between text, film, sound, and images by studying masterpieces of French cinema, as well as masterpieces of French literature and their screen adaptations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the text and the screen and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: The Holocaust in French Film
courseDescription: Discusses how the Holocaust and the persecution of the Jews were represented in French film from 1939 to the present. Students analyze how, at different times of their evolution, French cinema and French society have answered the questions: What happened? Who is responsible?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the holocaust in french film and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: Censored
courseDescription: Explores the social, historical, political, and poetic contexts of censorship in nineteenth-century France. By studying the forbidden best-sellers of the nineteenth century together with their popular and legal reception, students discover the ways in which ethics and politics play(ed) an integral role in the book trade. Once considered subversive for questioning marriage, virtue, religion, sexuality, gender, and imperialism, these banned books are now deemed classics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in censored and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: Les Misérables
courseDescription: Through a close reading of Les Misérables and an exploration of its ongoing cultural afterlives—from stage adaptations to modern retellings—students gain a deeper understanding of the text and its historical and contemporary significance. The course also examines the social questions confronting France in 1862, including poverty, revolution, and systemic injustice. Whether seasoned admirers of Victor Hugo's work or newcomers to the story, students engage critically with a masterpiece that has shaped international literature for more than a century.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in les misérables and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: Women's Voices in the Francophone World
courseDescription: Students read and discuss texts from contemporary women authors who write in French but whose links with French culture take on many forms. The authors studied hail from many parts of the world: not only from the French-speaking countries of Europe, but from different parts of Africa, Asia, Canada, the Near East, and the United States. For some, French was their native tongue; but for a great many, French was their language of adoption, the language they considered most suited to express the complex ties between their own personal story and the social, political, and cultural context in which that story has unfolded.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in women's voices in the francophone world and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: Crime Fiction in French
courseDescription: Introduces the roman policier or crime fiction in French. Tracing the genre from the nineteenth century to the present day, students examine how the popular polar responds to historical, societal, and spiritual concerns. Authors studied include: Émile Gaboriau, Edgar Allan Poe, Eugène Sue, Gaston Leroux, Georges Simenon, Georges Perec, and Fred Vargas.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in crime fiction in french and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: French Society through Comics
courseDescription: Examines the origins, evolution, and importance of comics in French and Belgian cultures and literatures. Students analyze the specific challenges of representing a culture at a specific time in history through voices of so called "high" or "low" cultures. Students also analyze how the histories of fine arts, literature, the press, cinema, and technology influenced the evolution of comics as they continued to reflect the politics and some key beliefs of two French speaking cultures.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in french society through comics and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: Strangers in a Strange Land
courseDescription: Examines how various francophone writers characterized their own cultures and sense of home. Students analyze how these writers from different cultures represented the challenges of creating a home in a foreign land, living in exile, or rebuilding a home after a loss. These literary texts enable students to characterize the importance of the concept of home in different cultures and literatures from North Africa, Japan, the United Stated, and France.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in strangers in a strange land and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: Advanced French Grammar
courseDescription: The systematic study of grammar at an advanced level. Strongly recommended for students prior to study abroad.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced french grammar and strengthens skills used in french work.

title: German Composition and Conversation
courseDescription: Increases students' oral and writing ability through the assimilation of advanced structural patterns, stylistic analysis of literature, discussion of current events.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in german composition and conversation and strengthens skills used in german studies work.

title: German for Oral Proficiency
courseDescription: Intensive oral practice in the classroom and with audio-visual media to develop facility in oral expression and aural comprehension.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in german for oral proficiency and strengthens skills used in german studies work.

title: Advanced German Composition
courseDescription: An in-depth study of styles of written communication: advanced grammatical concepts applied to personal, business, and narrative/creative writing.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced german composition and strengthens skills used in german studies work.

title: Venturing into the Text
courseDescription: This course prepares students to take advanced literature classes. By reading and analyzing poems, short stories, short novels and materials from the Internet, students improve their ability to read literary texts and analyze them. The course also introduces students to literary theory to help them to better understand the context in which literary texts were written.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in venturing into the text and strengthens skills used in german studies work.

title: German Culture and Civilization I
courseDescription: Studies the development of German culture from its origins to the present. The first semester covers the periods up to the eighteenth century with special emphasis on the history, politics, art and architecture of the period. The second semester continues examination of the contemporary social context and its historical background.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in german culture and civilization i and strengthens skills used in german studies work.

title: German Culture and Civilization II
courseDescription: A continuation of GR 301.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in german culture and civilization ii and strengthens skills used in german studies work.

title: Germany Today
courseDescription: For students who wish to become acquainted with major aspects of contemporary German culture, as well as social and political developments in Germany, and their influence on current literature and journalism. Focuses on developments after 1970.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in germany today and strengthens skills used in german studies work.

title: The Classic German Cinema
courseDescription: The course focuses on the function of film in the years between 1895 and 1945. Students discuss the role of filmmakers in the Weimar era and the use of film in the Third Reich. Special emphasis is placed on analyzing the films in relation to the artistic, societal, and historical currents at the time.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the classic german cinema and strengthens skills used in german studies work.

title: Contemporary German Cinema
courseDescription: The course offers a brief overview of classic German cinema and its contribution to the art of filmmaking, with its main focus being the development of German cinema from 1960 to the present. Students view and discuss works by von Trotta, Fassbinder, Herzog, Petersen, Tykwer, Becker, Tim, and Akin, and they investigate the films' relation to the societal, historical, and political developments in contemporary Germany and Europe. No German necessary.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in contemporary german cinema and strengthens skills used in german studies / modern languages work.

title: Berlin: The Crucible of Europe
courseDescription: Examines the intellectual currents that shaped Berlin in the early twentieth century. Students focus on the contributions made by prominent German-Jewish authors, discuss the foment of the Weimar years, and Berlin's contributions to a developing Europe.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in berlin: the crucible of europe and strengthens skills used in german studies work.

title: Enchanting the Listeners: The Art of Storytelling
courseDescription: Historical development of the novella in German from its beginnings in the eighteenth century to its modern exponents such as Thomas Mann and Franz Kafka. Special emphasis on the many problems in defining the form and function of a novelle.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in enchanting the listeners: the art of storytelling and strengthens skills used in german studies work.

title: Introduction to Global Studies
courseDescription: We live in an era of ever-increasing global interdependence, but what does this really mean? This course provides a multidisciplinary introduction to the topical components of global studies, focusing on themes such as globalization, development, sustainability, conflict, human rights, identity, and power. Course also provides an introduction to social science research design and methodology.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to global studies and strengthens skills used in global studies work.

title: Senior Seminar in Global Studies
courseDescription: An opportunity for integrating the student's experience of the global studies program. It consists of a senior project, guest lectures, and other integrative work selected by the instructor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior seminar in global studies and strengthens skills used in global studies work.

title: Introductory Greek I
courseDescription: An enriched beginning course, intended for students with no previous knowledge of the language, which emphasizes grammar, syntax, and vocabulary through extensive reading of easy passages from Greek authors. An introduction to the literature and culture of Athens.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory greek i and strengthens skills used in greek work.

title: Introductory Greek II
courseDescription: A continuation of GK 101.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory greek ii and strengthens skills used in greek work.

title: Intermediate Greek
courseDescription: Consolidation of the fundamentals of grammar and syntax. Transition to reading extended passages of real Greek.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate greek and strengthens skills used in greek work.

title: Greek Literature
courseDescription: Students complete their study of Greek grammar and syntax and move on to the reading of longer-form original Greek texts.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in greek literature and strengthens skills used in greek work.

title: Advanced Greek I
courseDescription: Readings in Greek at the advanced level. When possible choice of authors is based on student preference. May be repeated once for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced greek i and strengthens skills used in greek work.

title: Advanced Greek II
courseDescription: Readings in Greek at the advanced level. When possible, choice of author or genre is based on student preference. May be repeated once for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced greek ii and strengthens skills used in greek work.

title: Selected Readings in Greek I
courseDescription: Readings in Greek at the advanced level. Topics vary according to student interest. May be repeated once for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in selected readings in greek i and strengthens skills used in greek work.

title: Selected Readings in Greek III
courseDescription: Readings in Greek at the advanced level. Topics vary according to student interest. May be repeated once for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in selected readings in greek iii and strengthens skills used in greek work.

title: Greek Tragedy: Sophocles
courseDescription: A survey of Sophocles' tragedies, read partly in the original and partly in translation. Emphasis on style, characters, language, and themes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in greek tragedy: sophocles and strengthens skills used in greek work.

title: Perspectives on Global History

courseDescription: Traditional medical history has emphasized the march of science and the ideas of the "great doctors" that were assumed to have led to the improvement in medical care and the "conquering" of disease. This course looks beyond just medical care to the social, cultural, environmental, and economic factors that have shaped the development of the priorities, institutions, and personnel in the health-care system in the Americas.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in health and illness in latin america and strengthens skills used in history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: History of Afghanistan
courseDescription: Studies the history of Afghanistan from its emergence as a distinct political entity in 1747 to the return to power of the Taliban in August 2021. In the first part of the course, the impact of major power rivalry on state formation, modernization in the twentieth century, democratization in the 1960s, and the fall of the Old Regime in 1978 are studied. The second part of the course examines over four decades of war which witnessed varying regimes in power including Communists, Islamists, Taliban, and a U.S. backed government during the Global War on Terror after 9/11.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in history of afghanistan and strengthens skills used in history work.

title: World War II in America
courseDescription: The roots of contemporary American society took hold during the turbulent years of World War II. Examines the images of America and its enemies in popular culture, issues of race at home and abroad, changing experiences for workers and women, and the transformation of the economy, government, and foreign policy of the United States.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in world war ii in america and strengthens skills used in history work.

title: African American History as Public History
courseDescription: Whether it is 1920s congressional efforts to erect a national statue to the black women who nurtured young white children during slavery, twenty-first-century efforts to create memorials for the victims of lynchings, or Twitter conversations about Erik Killmonger, African American history has long been a matter of public debate and representation. The course considers the ways in which museums, historic sites, films, children’s books, public school lesson plans, and the broader public have interpreted African American history since the late nineteenth century.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in african american history as public history and strengthens skills used in history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Racial Justice and Truth Telling in Baltimore and Beyond
courseDescription: Explores racial (in)justice from sociological and historical perspectives and methods. In addition to studying slavery and its legacies at Loyola, students learn about lynching in Maryland through collaboration with the Maryland Lynching Truth and Reconciliation Commission (MLTRC). Students conduct oral history interviews with commissioners and develop ways to disseminate the findings and recommendations of the MLTRC.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in racial justice and truth telling in baltimore and beyond and strengthens skills used in history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond
Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: War Memory
courseDescription: Explores the formation of war memory, paying special attention to the ways in which individuals and communities mobilized representations of the past to achieve their contemporary goals. Working from a combination of text-based and visual primary and secondary sources, students navigate topics such as nationalism, imperialism, history textbook controversies, the Cold War, and the atomic bombs in an effort to understand the importance of historical memory in recent decades. Although the focus is on Japanese memories of the Asia-Pacific War (1937-1945), considerable time is also devoted to examining problems resulting from "memory wars" in places such as China, South Korea, the United States, and Germany.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in war memory and strengthens skills used in history work.
prerequisites: Open to student with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: African American Women’s History
courseDescription: How does our understanding of American history change when we center on Black women? From Harriet Tubman to the blueswomen of the early twentieth century; queer Black feminists of the 1970s to Anita Hill, this course explores how Black women have engaged with and shaped American culture, politics, and society from the antebellum period through the twentieth century. Students explore how race, color, gender, class, and sexuality have shaped ideas about and experiences of Black womanhood in America and learn how to use creative and rigorous historical methods to locate Black women’s experiences, which often have been placed on the periphery of American history.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in african american women’s history and strengthens skills used in history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022 - 2023 or beyond

title: The Palestinian-Israeli Conflict
courseDescription: Offers an in-depth exploration of the history of the Palestinian-Israeli conflict from the late Ottoman era to contemporary developments. The course examines key historical events that include the British Mandate in Palestine, the establishment of the State of Israel in 1948, the 1967 war, the Palestinian uprisings of 1987 and 2000, the Oslo peace process, and the 2023 Gaza war. The themes of nationalism, identity, colonialism, occupation, and international politics are also analyzed.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the palestinian-israeli conflict and strengthens skills used in history work.

title: The Vietnam War through Film and Literature
courseDescription: Documentary and feature film, autobiography, oral history, documents, and works of literature are used to probe the following themes: the origins, course, and historical meaning of the war; the antiwar movement and the home front; the clash of cultural values between East Asia and the West; and ethical and psychological issues raised by the experience of war.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the vietnam war through film and literature and strengthens skills used in history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Contesting Empire: Nationalism and Decolonization in the Afro-Atlantic World
courseDescription: Examines the various ways Black and African thinkers and activists imagined their futures at the end of World War II, and what they did to realize these visions. Students consider the influence of several intellectual and cultural movements, as well as the key events that sparked a broad, collective call for the end of empire in the middle of the twentieth century. Students end the course by considering how the dreams and opportunities of decolonization either narrowed or closed, and why in the decades that followed the exuberant 1960s.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in contesting empire: nationalism and decolonization in the afro-atlantic world and strengthens skills used in history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Search for the Divine: Hindu, Christian, Muslim, and Buddhist Ways in India
courseDescription: Down the ages, persons belonging to the Hindu, Christian, Muslim, and Buddhist faiths in India have searched for the Divine in myriad ways. This course presents a picture of this search woven around the lives, prayer, and writings of a significant number of Divine seekers. While showing the uniqueness of this unfolding search in the lives of individuals of different faiths, the course also points to its far reaching influence and attraction for people everywhere.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in search for the divine: hindu, christian, muslim, and buddhist ways in india and strengthens skills used in history work.

title: Crime and Punishment in Latin America
courseDescription: Crime, punishment, and the laws that define them are examined to provide a window onto the history of class, ethnic, and gender relations in Latin America. Courtrooms-and the documents they generate-are exceedingly important for historians writing about laboring classes, women, indigenous peoples, Africans, and other marginalized groups. Through books, articles, films, and primary sources, students study how laws and crime have shaped people's understandings of politics, morality, and social relationships.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in crime and punishment in latin america and strengthens skills used in history work.

title: History of the Police
courseDescription: Introduces the origins of modern police forces and their development over the nineteenth and twentieth centuries in Europe and the U.S. The course takes a particular interest in how police, as both a practice and an institution, emerged in dialog with other phenomena associated with democracy and state building, feminism, urbanization, surveillance technology, imperialism, racism, and anti-racism. The course addresses the role of the police in daily life and the ways that policing is a tool of social control.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in history of the police and strengthens skills used in history work.

title: Gender and Power in Modern Africa
courseDescription: Analyzes the impact of social, economic, and political change on gender relations in modern Africa. In particular, it explores the differential impact of colonization, wage labor, and cash crop production on women and men, which resulted in new forms of exploitation, as well as new opportunities. People's innovative response to opportunity, their resistance to negative social change, and how their changing identities informed their participation in nationalist and post-independence social movements are also considered.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in gender and power in modern africa and strengthens skills used in history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Gender and Sexuality in Latin America
courseDescription: Examines how the role of gender and sexuality in Latin American societies, cultures, economies, and religions has changed over time. Using sources such as books, articles, videos, images, oral histories, and primary documents, the course investigates the history of gender and sexuality with a particular emphasis on deconstructing such socially constructed binaries as femininity/masculinity, male/female, and homosexuality/heterosexuality. The course also focuses on the ways class, ethnicity, race, age, religion, and other identities affect men's and women's realities.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in gender and sexuality in latin america and strengthens skills used in history work.

title: The Middle East in the Media
courseDescription: Evaluates the figurative image of the Middle East produced by the American media industry. Despite the geographical distance, or perhaps as a result of it, students learn about the Middle East through narratives constructed by the media. In this course, students evaluate these narratives by juxtaposing them with the everyday life of Middle Easterners themselves.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the middle east in the media and strengthens skills used in history work.

title: Race and Geopolitics in the American Century
courseDescription: Examines how the global role of the U.S. intersected with the histories of race and democracy in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. The relationship between a global racial order formed through centuries of imperialism and the distinctive forms of democracy and racial hierarchy that have defined the modern history of the U.S. is explored. The course studies the ways racial inequality in the U.S. has shaped how different groups of Americans view the world beyond American borders—affecting decisions about when, where, and how to conduct warfare, whether to support or oppose movements for independence abroad, and how to promote economic development.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in race and geopolitics in the american century and strengthens skills used in history work.

title: The Modern Middle East through Film
courseDescription: Provides a nuanced historical understanding of the political, economic, social, and cultural changes that have occurred in the modern Middle East through the lens of film. Students engage in critical analysis of films produced in the Middle East or about the Middle East in order to understand how the lived experiences of women and men have been affected by European colonialism; the rise of nationalism and the creation of the modern nation-state; authoritarian regimes; the Palestinian-Israeli conflict; the politics of oil and U.S. hegemony in the region; the rise of Islamist movements; and the 2011 Arab uprisings.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the modern middle east through film and strengthens skills used in history work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

courseDescription: Explores Loyola Univeristy Maryland's relationship to slavery, Native American land dispossession, and Latin American immigrants and labor. title: Seminar: The U.S. in the 1960's
courseDescription: Examines the history of the U.S. in the 1960s, going beyond the mystique that surrounds "the '60s"—Camelot, rock 'n' roll, the hippies, and so on—to investigate the political, social, and economic forces that defined the era. What were the contradictions of the supposed "golden age" of postwar American capitalism? How did the decade's social movements (civil rights and Black Power, feminist, New Left, anti-war, among others) transform the meaning of American citizenship?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: the u.s. in the 1960's and strengthens skills used in history work.

courseDescription: Focuses on the British colonies in mainland North America and the West Indies during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: colonial british america and strengthens skills used in history work.

courseDescription: Key topics in the social and political history of the Civil War are explored with the goal of gaining deeper understanding of the human and policy dimensions of the conflict. courseDescription: Employs biography as a lens to explore the era of the American Revolution and Early American Republic. Biographies of the famous (e.g., Washington, Hamilton, Franklin, Paine) and not so-famous (e.g. a Boston shoemaker, a Maine midwife, and an enslaved African American in Charleston, SC) are used to examine how individuals shaped, and were shaped by, larger social, political, economic, and cultural shifts that occurred during these tumultuous years. The specific topics/biographies vary by year.

title: Seminar: European Imperial Societies
courseDescription: Explores the impact of imperialism on European societies. Rather than viewing imperialism as something that happened "over there", leaving Europe untouched, this course focuses on how Europeans and their metropolitan societies, political structures, laws, cultures, etc. were indelibly shaped by imperialism in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Topics may include gendered and racial conceptions of national and imperial identities, the intersections of science and colonialism, mass culture and propaganda, migration and citizenship, everyday encounters with empire in Europe, and the impact of decolonization, among others.

title: Seminar: Holocaust Memory in Germany and America
courseDescription: By the early twenty-first century, the Holocaust—the murder of six million European Jews—had come to represent the epitome of evil, an event in history that stands as the reference point for contemporary morality. In 1945, this was not as clear. This course explores how the meaning of the Holocaust as a singular event emerged and changed across generations after 1945 in two very different national contexts: Germany and America.

courseDescription: For many, mention of the Middle Ages brings to mind images of knights, kings, and castles. Few might think of republics, finance, and cosmopolitan sensibilities. But that is just a taste of what we find in the rich and varied societies of medieval Italy.

Study of their historicity, legendary use, and effect on medieval society proves a valuable tool to understanding the intellectual history of medieval Europe.

The course delves into how specific emotions such as fear, anger, love, sadness, pain, and happiness have been constructed, expressed, and regulated across different historical periods and societies. Case studies span a wide range of contexts, from ancient Greece and China to medieval and early modern Europe, pre-colonial Africa, and the modern U.S.

title: Seminar: East Asia in the Global 1960's
courseDescription: Examines the turbulent 1960s in China, Japan, and South Korea, with an emphasis on political, social, and cultural upheaval in all three countries. These movements are treated as arising from concerns specific to each place, and as part of a "global 1960s" during which people all over the world sought to re-imagine their societies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: east asia in the global 1960's and strengthens skills used in history work.

courseDescription: Explores the life of Margery Kempe, a fifteenth-century English woman. courseDescription: Examines canonical art works of the western tradition in the context of key intellectual and artistic developments through close reading of primary sources and the formal and iconographic readings of works of art. Fulfills the fine arts core requirement for Honors students. Closed to students who have taken AH 111.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in art and intellectual history: renaissance to modern and strengthens skills used in honors work.

title: Introduction to Theatrical Production
courseDescription: A comprehensive, experiential course in theatrical production. Students engage in major areas of production (acting, directing, design), as well as playwriting, theatre criticism, and the staging of an original theatre piece. Includes attendance at theatre productions on campus and in the Baltimore/Washington area.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to theatrical production and strengthens skills used in honors / theatre work.

title: Western Musical Traditions
courseDescription: Introduces the major forms and styles in the western musical tradition, with an emphasis on guided listening of masterworks and the study of issues in musical aesthetics through scholarly and primary source texts. Aims to develop a more perceptive and informed listener and to introduce skills in music scholarship. Fulfills fine arts core requirement for Honors students, Class of 2018 and beyond.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in western musical traditions and strengthens skills used in honors / music work.

title: Photographic Vision: Tools, Techniques, and Theories
courseDescription: Students work with film and digital single lens reflex (SLR) cameras in the studio, darkroom, and computer lab. Students learn to use their cameras to craft thoughtful, intentional photographs and to enrich their understanding through careful readings of core texts of photographic theory and analysis of historical and contemporary photographs. Fulfills fine arts core requirement for Honors students.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in photographic vision: tools, techniques, and theories and strengthens skills used in honors / photography work.

title: The Examined Life
courseDescription: Serves as a capstone for the Honors curriculum. It includes revisiting ethical concerns and issues raised in earlier Honors courses, rereading relevant texts, and introducing new texts and ethical issues when appropriate. Fulfills the Honors ethics course requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the examined life and strengthens skills used in honors work.

title: Climate Technology and Analytics
courseDescription: Introduces climate analytics analytics through the study of natural disasters such as wildfires, hurricanes, and flooding.
