Using ArcGIS and modern data tools, students analyze spatial and temporal climate data to understand how extreme events emerge, spread, and affect communities and infrastructure. The course emphasizes hands-on geospatial analysis, visualization, and model building, combining satellite imagery, environmental datasets, and real-time weather data.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in climate technology and analytics and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251 or DS 303 or ENV 232

title: Data Pipelines and Platforms
courseDescription: Focuses on the design, construction, and management of data pipelines that power information systems in organizations. Students learn how to collect, clean, integrate, store, and transform data from multiple sources to support machine learning models, analytics, and operational decision-making. The course emphasizes scalable data architecture, cloud-based platforms, data quality, governance, and automation, with attention to how data architecture choices affect artificial (AI) intelligence performance, reliability, and business value.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in data pipelines and platforms and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251 or CS 105 or DS 303; IS 353 or CS 485

title: Cyber Security and Networks
courseDescription: Explores the technologies underlying networking, multimedia, digital business, and entertainment industries. This course balances technical and managerial content while covering a broad range of topics, including the strategic role of telecommunications, networking infrastructure, cyber security, encryption, audio, video, intellectual property rights, artificial intelligence, and ethics associated with cyber security.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in cyber security and networks and strengthens skills used in information systems work.

title: Information Technology for Financial Services
courseDescription: At a time when information is critical to corporate success, financial service firms continue to be the largest consumers of information technology (IT). The impact of IT across U.S. and European equities markets, brokerage companies, bond trading, and electronic banking is examined. Trading platforms are examined in detail, particularly in the areas of algo trading and dark pools of liquidity.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in information technology for financial services and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251 or DS 303; FI 230

title: Management of Global Information Technology
courseDescription: Exposes students to the challenges of establishing a successful and globally competitive information technology (IT) industry outside the U.S. Students study historical, economic, political, labor, and social factors leading to the establishment of country-specific centers of IT excellence. In particular, students study what led multinational corporations to base their overseas activities within a specific location and the forces that govern the retention of those activities.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in management of global information technology and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: Restricted to students with a cumulative GPA of 2.500 or higher
Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Governance, Frameworks, and Risk Management
courseDescription: Integrates security governance, industry frameworks, compliance requirements, and risk management into a comprehensive understanding of how organizations manage cybersecurity at the enterprise level. Students learn to apply frameworks, assess and communicate risk, manage third-party security, and align security programs with business objectives. The emphasis is on practical application of governance concepts to organizational decision-making.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in governance, frameworks, and risk management and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251 or DS 303; IS 355

title: Identity, Privacy, and Access Management
courseDescription: Introduces identity governance, access management, and privacy program design as core elements of modern cybersecurity. Students learn how organizations control user access, manage digital identities, and protect personal data across systems and platforms. The course blends policy, risk, and regulatory perspectives with practical exposure to identity and privacy controls.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in identity, privacy, and access management and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251 or DS 303; IS 355

title: Endpoint Security
courseDescription: Examines steps take to protect devices and applications users rely on every day, including workstations, laptops, mobile devices, servers, and cloud-based applications. Students learn how organizations secure endpoints, manage access, protect data, and respond to threats in modern, distributed work environments. The course blends conceptual understanding with applied practice.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in endpoint security and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251 or DS 303; IS 355

title: Security Operations
courseDescription: This capstone course builds practical skills in security monitoring, threat detection, incident response, and day-to-day security operations. Students gain an applied understanding of how security operations centers (SOCs) operate, including roles, workflows, and decision-making during cyber incidents. Through guided exercises and simulations, students learn how to use security monitoring and analysis tools to detect threats, investigate alerts, and respond to incidents from initial identification through containment and recovery.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in security operations and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251 or DS 303; IS 355

title: Quantitative Risk Modeling
courseDescription: Quantitative representations of risk provide help when making informed decisions, comparing different scenarios, and identifying the sensitivities of a potential outcome to changes in conditions. The level of risk can be assessed by representing uncertainty in the factors contributing to an outcome and using a model to predict how those multiple uncertainties affect the solution. Sometimes the factors affecting an outcome are clear, and in other situations the factors are difficult to identify.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in quantitative risk modeling and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: EC 220 or ST 210; MA 151 or MA 251

title: Artificial Intelligence Systems Architecture
courseDescription: Explores the design, development, deployment, and monitoring of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in business settings. Students learn how to transform data into scalable, production-ready AI solutions using modern machine learning techniques, cloud-based tools, and MLOps practices. Emphasis is placed on data pipelines, model training and evaluation, system integration, performance monitoring, and life cycle management of AI applications.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in artificial intelligence systems architecture and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251 or DS 303; IS 420

title: Web-Enabled Entrepreneurial Project with Artificial Intelligence
courseDescription: Students explore and apply effective use of the technologies associated with responsive web applications and digital business including HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, Bootstrap, Responsive Design, and jQuery, all essential to modern companies. In this capstone course, students integrate skills from previous information systems courses, develop a plan for an entrepreneurial business using best practices, and create a sophisticated web-enabled senior project in a cloud and artificial intelligence environment. The course is interactive, team-oriented, and results driven.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in web-enabled entrepreneurial project with artificial intelligence and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251; IS 352 or CS 151; IS 353, IS 358

title: Research Project in Information Systems
courseDescription: Students develop individual research in a specific area of mutual interest with a faculty member. The student must begin with a written plan for the project and conclude with a written research report.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in research project in information systems and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the department chair

title: Sports Analytics
courseDescription: Big data continues to dominate the world of professional sports as exemplified by the movie Moneyball, which showcased the innovative use of data by the Oakland A's baseball franchise. This course examines the use of data and advanced modeling in professional football. Students use R platform alongside artifcial intelligence to analyze a variety of large player tracking data files from the National Football League (NFL).
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sports analytics and strengthens skills used in information systems work.
prerequisites: EC 220 or ST 210; IS 352 or CS 151 or ST 310

title: Introduction to Czech Business and Culture
courseDescription: The Prague Summer Study Abroad program is a one month study abroad experience based in Prague, the Czech Republic. The program usually occurs during the month of July. Students must enroll in two courses.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to czech business and culture and strengthens skills used in international business / management work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: International Management
courseDescription: Investigates business policy, strategy, structure, and process in an international context. Focuses on the international business environment and management practices outside the United States. Students develop an understanding of the complex and varied role of the general manager in a nondomestic environment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in international management and strengthens skills used in international business / management work.
prerequisites: IB 315: IB 282 or BH 282 ; MG 201 or BH 201; Restricted to sophomores, juniors, or seniors
IB 415: IB 282 or BH 282, 60 credits; Closed to students with catalogue year 2020-2021 or beyond
MG 315: IB 282 or BH 282, MG 201 or BH 201; Restricted to sophomores, juniors, or seniors
MG 415: IB 282 or BH 282, 60 credits; Closed to students with catalogue year 2020-2021 or beyond

title: Global Sustainable Business Case Study
courseDescription: Designed for students willing to work for, contribute to, and represent the department and the Sellinger School of Business and Management at case competitions at school, regional, and national levels. The course develops skills at analyzing strategically oriented cases in international business, sustainability, and/or management areas. In addition, students learn presentation skills in a supportive environment with feedback from peers, faculty, alumni, and board members.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in global sustainable business case study and strengthens skills used in international business / management work.

title: Cross-Cultural Interactions in Business
courseDescription: Due to globalization internationally-based employees working in multinational firms have become more connected. Many employees primarily work and collaborate with colleagues around the world. Yet, most managers have little, if any, understanding of how culture of employees impact interaction in the workplace.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in cross-cultural interactions in business and strengthens skills used in international business work.
prerequisites: IB 282 or BH 282 ; BH 201 or MG 201
Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Global Strategy
courseDescription: An upper-level seminar for international business students that brings together the managerial and environmental dynamics at work in the global economy. Incorporates all aspects of international business to enable managers to develop, implement, and evaluate a global strategy for the firm, be it family-owned, or a transnational corporation. Specific firms, industries and/or regions may be selected for study.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in global strategy and strengthens skills used in international business work.
prerequisites: IB 282 or BH 282, MG 201 or BH 201

title: Introductory Italian I
courseDescription: A thorough grounding in the four language skills: reading, understanding, writing, and speaking, as well as an understanding of the structure of the language and the literature and culture of the country. For students with no previous knowledge of the language. Laboratory study outside the classroom is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory italian i and strengthens skills used in italian work.

title: Introductory Italian II
courseDescription: A continuation of IT 101. Laboratory study outside the classroom is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory italian ii and strengthens skills used in italian work.
prerequisites: IT 101 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Intermediate Italian I
courseDescription: A systematic consolidation and expansion of the four basic skills: reading, understanding, speaking, and writing. To increase and perfect students' acquired abilities/proficiencies in the language, and broaden their understanding of the country's culture and literature. Laboratory study outside the classroom is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate italian i and strengthens skills used in italian work.
prerequisites: IT 102 or IT 161 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Comprehensive Beginning Italian
courseDescription: A review course for students who have had three years of language study in high school and for students who wish to begin a second modern language. The material covered is essentially the same as for the IT 101-102 sequence, except that it is covered in one semester instead of two. This includes a thorough grounding in the five language skills: reading, listening, speaking, writing, and cultural knowledge, as well as an understanding of the structure of the language, cultures, and literatures of the countries that speak Italian.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in comprehensive beginning italian and strengthens skills used in italian work.

title: Comprehensive Intermediate Italian
courseDescription: The material covered is essentially the same as for the IT 103-104 sequence, except that it is covered in one semester instead of two. It consists of a systematic consolidation and expansion of the four basic skills: reading, understanding, speaking, and writing. To increase and perfect students' acquired abilities/proficiencies in the language and broaden their understanding of the country's culture and literature, the second half is a capstone reviewing and reinforcing language skills to help students attain the intermediate level as defined by ACTFL guidelines in the five skills: reading, writing, speaking, comprehension, and culture of Italy and Italian-speaking areas.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in comprehensive intermediate italian and strengthens skills used in italian work.
prerequisites: Open to students who have completed IT 102 or IT 161 or placed into IT 103

title: Italian Composition and Conversation I
courseDescription: Students develop their ability to write and speak correctly and creatively in Italian through models of advanced linguistic structural patterns, related grammar, examples of usage, and composition exercises. Oral practice enhanced through the use of videos.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in italian composition and conversation i and strengthens skills used in italian work.

title: High Intermediate Italian: Meeting the Italian B2 Level
courseDescription: A continuing study of Italian language, literature, and culture at the high-intermediate/low-advanced level. Materials include newpaper readings, films, literary works, composition, and interviews to review and expand students’ knowledge in accordance with the vocabulary and format of the exam. At the end of the course, students should be ready to take the Italian CILS (Certificazione di Italiano come Lingua Straniera) exam at the B2 level offered each spring.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in high intermediate italian: meeting the italian b2 level and strengthens skills used in italian work.

title: Contemporary Italian Culture
courseDescription: Students explore modern Italian society and culture through readings, such as literary texts, articles, and reports concerned with contemporary issues. A variety of media are used to address fundamental aspects of Italian culture, perspectives, and social structures. By the end of the course students can produce clear, detailed text and discuss a wide range of subjects, explaining a viewpoint on relevant issues in contemporary Italian society.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in contemporary italian culture and strengthens skills used in italian work.

title: Exploring the Text
courseDescription: A preparatory course for students who will take advanced literature and culture courses where narrative texts are analyzed in Italian. Students watch films, read plays, poems, short stories, and novels and learn to analyze their structures and themes. All texts are read in the original Italian and placed within their historical, literary, and cultural contexts.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in exploring the text and strengthens skills used in italian work.

title: The Cinema of Italy
courseDescription: A comprehensive but selective overview and analysis of the landmarks of Italian cinema, predominantly from World War II onward. The course examines the ways in which Italian cinema reflects the evolution of modern Italy in terms of changing social, political, economic, and cultural developments which characterize twentieth-century Italian life. All lectures, assignments, and exams are in Italian.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the cinema of italy and strengthens skills used in italian work.
prerequisites: One IT 200-level course or written permission of the instructor

title: Advanced Grammar, Reading, and Composition
courseDescription: Expands students' ability to express and comprehend complex and nuanced concepts in reading, writing, and speaking. The study of grammar is in context at an advanced level. This course requires laboratory work outside of class in addition to reading, composition, and viewing videos.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced grammar, reading, and composition and strengthens skills used in italian work.

title: Italian Society and Culture
courseDescription: For students who have a knowledge of Italian sufficient to understand clear, standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc., and to deal with most situations likely to arise while traveling in Italy. Students explore modern Italian society and culture through readings, such as literary texts, articles, and reports concerned with contemporary problems. A variety of audio-visual materials are used to address fundamental facets of Italian mentality, culture, and social structures.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in italian society and culture and strengthens skills used in italian work.
prerequisites: One IT 200-level course or written permission of the instructor

title: Introductory Latin I
courseDescription: An enriched beginning course, intended for students with no previous knowledge of the language, which emphasizes grammar, syntax, vocabulary, and reading of easy passages from Latin authors. An introduction to the literature and culture of Rome.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory latin i and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Introductory Latin II
courseDescription: A continuation of LT 101.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory latin ii and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Intermediate Latin
courseDescription: Completion of Latin grammar and syntax.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate latin and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Latin Golden Age Prose and Poetry
courseDescription: Selected readings from authors of the golden age of Roman poetry (in particular) and prose. Analysis of styles/genres.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in latin golden age prose and poetry and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Latin Prose Composition
courseDescription: Exercises in the translation of sentences and connected passages into felicitous Latin prose. Development of knowledge of correct, idiomatic expression in written Latin.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in latin prose composition and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Roman Tragedy
courseDescription: An examination of selected plays of Seneca, with particular attention given to their literary precursors. Students study the language of the plays and also learn to appreciate them as pieces of living theater.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in roman tragedy and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Cicero on Friendship
courseDescription: Cicero's essay on Friendship has proven to be an influential discussion on the nature and characteristics of this most human of relationships. Students improve their Latin by reading Cicero's takes on having friends by looking at, among other things, what makes good and bad friends, how to recognize and distinguish them, and what the ideal might be.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in cicero on friendship and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Tacitus and Suetonius
courseDescription: Selections from the chief writers of history and biography of the Roman Empire. Discussions focus on the history of the emperors from Augustus to Nero, the differences between history and biography, and the authors' selection and presentation of material.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in tacitus and suetonius and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Sallust
courseDescription: A reading of the historical writings of Sallust with attention to his historical accuracy, his place in the development of Latin prose style and his description of the shortcomings of the Roman senatorial order.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sallust and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Roman Lyric
courseDescription: Studies the development of lyric poetry in Rome with special attention to the lyrics of Catullus and Horace.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in roman lyric and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Roman Comedy
courseDescription: An examination of selected plays of Plautus and Terence, along with notice of their precursors, backgrounds, and some descendants. Students study the language of the plays and also learn to appreciate them as hilarious, artful, and living theatre.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in roman comedy and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Pastoral Poetry
courseDescription: As Rome was on the brink of a political revolution in the 30's BCE, the poet Vergil decided to compose a series of ten poems about shepherds playing songs for each other. The course puts a focus on Vergil's Eclogues, which mark Latin's entrance into the pastoral genre. What do these poems have to do with Vergil's contemporary Roman world?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in pastoral poetry and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Petronius
courseDescription: Readings in one of ancient Rome's wildest and most extravagant authors and one of classical antiquity's few surviving novels. Students experience the seedy underbelly of Rome at its most decadent in the words of one of the Latin language's funniest and most brilliant prose stylists, while, among other delights, attending the most bizarre and hilarious banquet in literature. Werewolves, too.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in petronius and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Petronius and Apuleius
courseDescription: Close reading of sections of two underground classics, Petronius' Satyricon and Apuleius' Metamorphoses. Discussions focus on language, style, and subject matter along with the lure of the demimonde, sociocultural background, antihero, narrative technique, literary parody, and religious echoes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in petronius and apuleius and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Apuleius
courseDescription: Close reading of sections of Apuleius' underground classic Metamorphoses. Discussions focus on language, style, and subject matter along with the lure of the demimonde, sociocultural background, antihero, narrative technique, literary parody, and religious echoes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in apuleius and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Latin Elegy
courseDescription: Students are introduced to the themes and conventions of Latin elegy via select poems of Propertius, Tibullus, and Ovid (Amores, Ars Amatoria, Tristia). The course examines issues such as gender, genre, and the literary politics of Augustan Rome. It also situates elegy within its wider historical context through supplementary readings of love poetry from antiquity through the Renaissance and beyond.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in latin elegy and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Ovid
courseDescription: A reading of extensive selections from the brilliant poet of love and change; human psychology as seen through the lens of the classical myths.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ovid and strengthens skills used in latin work.

title: Thai History and Culture
courseDescription: Explores the history, diverse cultures, and contemporary life of Thailand and its neighboring Southeast Asian countries. Through an interdisciplinary approach, students explore the region's histories, religions, cuisines, artistic traditions, economic development, and sustainability initiatives. Class sessions provide context for cultural encounters and educational travel, while reflective discussions help students connect their experiences to broader historical and cultural understandings.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in thai history and culture and strengthens skills used in law work.
prerequisites: Restricted to students studying in Bangkok
Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Legal Environment of Business
courseDescription: Examines the legal environment of business activity. Students learn to explain basic legal terms; articulate legal rights and requirements in the managerial setting; identify how a particular legal issue fits into the legal system and how law develops and changes; and discuss managing an organization's legal matters, including ethical use of the law. Topics include classifications and sources of law, dispute resolution, agency, business associations, corporate governance, contracts, torts, product liability, securities, equal employment opportunity, artificial intelligence law and ethics, and intellectual property.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in legal environment of business and strengthens skills used in law / business honors work.
prerequisites: BH 305: 60 credits; Restricted to Sellinger scholars

title: Commercial Law
courseDescription: Examines the legal aspects of a commercial transaction. Students learn to explain the nature of a commercial transaction including formulating a contract for the sale of goods, paying for the goods, and financing the transactions. Topics include contract law, the uniform commercial code (sale of goods, negotiable instructions, secured transactions, bank collections and deposits), surety, and bankruptcy.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in commercial law and strengthens skills used in law / business honors work.
prerequisites: LW 406: Restricted to juniors and seniors or written permission of the instructor
BH 406: Restricted to junior and senior Sellinger scholars

title: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion at Work
courseDescription: Studies meritocracy, the American Deam, and the limits bias and discrimination place on both. What companies and organizations do in the areas of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) is highlighted. Students have the opportunity to pursue their individual interests in race, gender, class, disability, and more.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in diversity, equity, and inclusion at work and strengthens skills used in law work.

title: Cyberlaw
courseDescription: Examines the legal and regulatory environment governing data, digital infrastructure, and networked technologies in organizations. The course focuses on how cybersecurity, data protection, and privacy laws shape the design, deployment, and operation of information systems, including (but not limited to) artificial intelligence (AI) enabled tools and platforms. Students analyze real world cases involving data breaches, ransomware, cybercrime, surveillance, cross border data flows, platform governance, online speech and content moderation, as well as AI specific issues such as model theft, data poisoning, algorithmic misuse, and misinformation.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in cyberlaw and strengthens skills used in law work.
prerequisites: IS 251 or BH 251 or DS 303; LW 305 or BH 305

title: Exploring Language: Introduction to Linguistics
courseDescription: Investigates the study of linguistics, including sociolinguistics, with a focus on theoretical foundations and pragmatic, evidence-based implications for teaching and assessing reading, writing, spelling, phonics, and grammar in monolingual or multilingual contexts. Foundational concepts such as phonology, morphology, syntax, and pragmatics are explored with the goal of informing planning for teaching monolingual or multilingual students.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in exploring language: introduction to linguistics and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: Processes and Acquisitions of Literacy
courseDescription: Assists students in understanding the reading acquisition process. Course content is organized around current accepted research-based theoretical models that account for individual differences in reading. The Maryland State Department of Education has approved this course for the Processes and Acquisition requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in processes and acquisitions of literacy and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: Early Literacy Assessment and Instruction
courseDescription: Official credit range: 3-4 credits. Provides a research-based understanding of the cognitive, socio-cultural, linguistic, and motivational influences on early literacy and language development. Topics include: understanding reading research, cognitive psychology’s contributions to understanding the reading process, language development, the process of how the brain learns to read, literacy assessments to guide instruction, high leverage practices in each of the components of reading and writing instruction, and how to incorporate these components into culturally and linguistically diverse early elementary classrooms. Students are required to complete mandatory service-learning hours in a classroom or tutoring environment for students in grades K-2.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in early literacy assessment and instruction and strengthens skills used in education work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2023-2024 or beyond

title: Materials for Teaching Reading
courseDescription: Addresses selection and evaluation of print and electronic texts and identification of strategies used when teaching reading at children's instructional and developmental levels. The Maryland State Department of Education has approved this course for the Materials for Teaching Reading requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in materials for teaching reading and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: Intermediate Literacy Assessment and Instruction
courseDescription: Official credit range: 3-4 credits. Develops and utilizes foundational knowledge of literacy development for intermediate grades 3-5 using evidence based instructional and assessment approaches. Students explore literature and how to utilize it in their instruction. Students plan, modify, and implement interactive whole group and small group lesson plans for intermediate learners, taking into account the various literacy and multilingual needs of students in grades 3-5.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate literacy assessment and instruction and strengthens skills used in education work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2023-2024 or beyond

title: Methods for Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages
courseDescription: Focuses on the theories and methods of second language teaching and learning and develops the skills for applying the methods to classroom practice through lesson plan development and demonstration. Students explore the techniques, strategies, and materials for delivering ESOL-focused instruction across the content areas. Students develop appropriate, research-based teaching strategies for application across language proficiency levels and grade spans.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in methods for teaching english to speakers of other languages and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: Assessment and Instruction in Reading I with Field Experience
courseDescription: Addresses a variety of reading instruction methods and assessment measures for primary age children. A main focus of the course is to develop an understanding of how word recognition strategies develop and lead to comprehension. The Maryland State Department of Education has approved this course in conjunction with RE 420 for the Instruction in Reading and Assessment of Reading requirements.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in assessment and instruction in reading i with field experience and strengthens skills used in education work.
prerequisites: RE 219; RE 242 or written permission of the instructor

title: Literacy Assessment and Instruction for Multilingual Learners
courseDescription: Prepares students to understand, assess, and instruct multilingual students that are developing language and literacy in more than one language. Building on theory, research, and practice from the field of multilingualism, language acquisition, and education, students learn about the process of language and literacy development of diverse children who are exposed to more than one language and cultural contexts in which this development occurs. Students design lessons on English phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics to address multilingual reading, writing, listening, and speaking to promote academic and social language development.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in literacy assessment and instruction for multilingual learners and strengthens skills used in education work.
prerequisites: Open to students with catalogue year 2023-2024 or beyond

title: Second Language Acquisition Theory and Practice
courseDescription: Focuses on facilitating an understanding of language and language use, especially as it pertains to learning and teaching with emergent bilingual K-12 students. The course expands upon linguistic topics such as phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics. The interdisciplinary areas of psycholinguistics and sociolinguistics are also explored.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in second language acquisition theory and practice and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: Assessment and Instruction in Reading II
courseDescription: Addresses a comprehensive array of instructional and assessment techniques and strategies for independent readers with specific attention to comprehension, vocabulary, and fluency. The Maryland State Department of Education has approved this course in conjunction with RE 344 for the Instruction in Reading and Assessment of Reading requirements.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in assessment and instruction in reading ii and strengthens skills used in education work.
prerequisites: RE 219, RE 242, RE 344; or written permission of the instructor

title: Disciplinary and Digital Literacy for Diverse Elementary Learners
courseDescription: Addresses the theories, research, and scientific, evidence-based pedagogical practices related to the instruction, scaffolding, expansion, and assessment of foundational, intermediate, disciplinary, and digital (new) literacies with adolescent learners in the content areas (Art, Music, English Language Arts, World Languages, Mathematics, History, and the Sciences). Students explore reading research; how the brain learns to read; literacy assessments for universal screening, guiding instruction, and monitoring progress in the framework of Multi-Tiered Systems of Supports (MTSS) in the context of content area instruction.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in disciplinary and digital literacy for diverse elementary learners and strengthens skills used in education work.
prerequisites: RE 430: RE 345; ED 405 (must be taken concurrently); Open to students with catalogue year 2023-2024 or beyond; Restricted to elementary education majors

title: Literacy in the Content Area I
courseDescription: Introduces a wide variety of strategies which use reading, writing, speaking, listening, and viewing to support content learning. Particular attention is given to the development of vocabulary, comprehension, study skills, and writing strategies for all learners including struggling readers and English Language Learners. The Maryland State Department of Education has approved this course for the required Reading in the Content Area I course.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in literacy in the content area i and strengthens skills used in education work.
prerequisites: ED 205 or written permission of the instructor

title: Literacy in the Content Area II
courseDescription: Further explores the research and application that addresses literacy as a tool for negotiating and comprehending content area material. Students revisit and add to a wide range of literacy based content area strategies. Particular attention is given to the instruction/assessment cycle, uses of technology, and supporting diverse learners.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in literacy in the content area ii and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: Supporting Multilingual Learners in Secondary Education
courseDescription: Students develop and utilize scientific, evidence-based research on language and literacy development to support the academic success of multilingual learners in grades 7-12 in the content areas (Art, Music, English Language Arts, World Languages, Mathematics, History, and the Sciences). Building on theory, research, and practice from the field of multilingualism, language acquisition, and education, students learn about the process of language and literacy development of diverse children in secondary education who are exposed to more than one language and the cultural contexts in which this development occurs.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in supporting multilingual learners in secondary education and strengthens skills used in education work.

title: Introduction to Sustainable Business
courseDescription: Introduces sustainable business principles and methods, as well as examples of how they are used in real-world situations. Students learn how to integrate sustainable business into organizational management by investigating various business functions such as marketing, supply chain management, finance, accounting, political strategy, IT management, and human resource management. In addition, the course explores the role of ethical decision-making in sustainable business practices and the importance of corporate social responsibility.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to sustainable business and strengthens skills used in management work.

title: Managing Innovation and Entrepreneurship
courseDescription: Examines concepts and techniques about how innovation and entrepreneurship stages progress both within established organizations and start-ups. The course focuses on entrepreneurship at the individual level incorporating concepts and issues that spans from opportunity recognition to business model stage, and intrapreneurship at the organizational level incorporating concepts and issues related to innovation management and adaptation. At all levels, the course focuses on how development of an entrepreneurial mindset and techniques that support operationalization of innovative business decisions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in managing innovation and entrepreneurship and strengthens skills used in management work.

title: Global Strategy for Sustainability
courseDescription: Examines how corporations deliver value to people, planet, and profit while creating and sustaining competitive advantage. Students critically assess the relationship between environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices and the company’s financial performance, contingent on time-horizon (short-term vs. long-term), industry, region, and cultural context. Additionally, students learn and apply managing tools, industry standards, and metrics to plan and evaluate sustainability strategies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in global strategy for sustainability and strengthens skills used in management work.

title: Leadership in Organizations
courseDescription: Students advance their leadership capabilities through personal exploration, learning to understand and develop their leadership knowledge and skills. To achieve this goal, the course offers an extensive examination of leadership in organizations and provides students with a set of experiences that are designed to enhance their self-awareness and capacity for effective leadership. The learning method is experiential with a focus on self-assessment, class discussions, guest speakers, exercises and simulations, case studies, and team projects.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in leadership in organizations and strengthens skills used in management work.

title: Leading Change
courseDescription: Examines how organizations change, and how to be an agent for change in an organization. It explores the forces for change, the change implementation process, the behaviors and skills for successfully leading change initiatives, managing resistance to change, and the behavioral theories of how individuals and organizations change. The learning method is experiential with a focus on lectures, guest speakers, exercises and simulations, case studies, and team projects.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in leading change and strengthens skills used in management work.

title: Managerial and Communication Skills
courseDescription: Provides an opportunity for students to improve many key managerial and leadership skills. In particular it provides an opportunity for students to learn about their strengths and weaknesses with many of the traits and skills required of an effective manager and leader. These skills focus on the interpersonal competence required to work effectively with individuals and within teams.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in managerial and communication skills and strengthens skills used in management work.

title: Management Consulting Skills
courseDescription: Surveys the management consulting profession and practice with a subsequent emphasis on the issues consultants face in delivering client solutions. A focus is placed on developing proficiencies in a range of skills required to manage client interactions, assess problems, and present credible solutions. The course is delivered with a combination of academic and experiential elements that includes tests, oral presentations, and live cases.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in management consulting skills and strengthens skills used in management work.

title: Environmental, Social, and Governance Reporting
courseDescription: Provides an understanding of the key concepts and processes related to the management, measurement, and reporting of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) issues that local and global companies face. The course helps students develop their knowledge around: identifying and prioritizing material ESG issues; approaches to addressing ESG risks and opportunities; criteria for measuring ESG performance; and reporting frameworks and standards for corporate sustainability.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in environmental, social, and governance reporting and strengthens skills used in management work.
prerequisites: MG 201 or BH 201; IB 282 or BH 282; MG 222

title: Social Entrepreneurship
courseDescription: Develops student knowledge and interest in social entrepreneurship. Social entrepreneurship includes identifying and creating innovative solutions to solve social problems, empower people, and reduce poverty. Through experiential learning, research, and interaction with social entrepreneurship leaders, students learn to apply sound business and entrepreneurial practices.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in social entrepreneurship and strengthens skills used in management work.
prerequisites: MG 201 or BH 201 or BA 205 or IB 282 or BH 282

title: Negotiation and Conflict Resolution
courseDescription: Examines the theory and practice of negotiation and conflict resolution across a variety of settings. The course is designed to address a broad spectrum of negotiation and conflict-related problems. The learning method is experiential and provides students with the opportunity to develop their negotiation and conflict resolution skills experientially in a series of role-playing exercises that highlight various bargaining and negotiation processes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in negotiation and conflict resolution and strengthens skills used in management work.

title: Socially Responsible Marketing
courseDescription: Ethical decision making in marketing requires complex trade-offs that include consideration of immediate and long-term costs and benefits to the decision maker, the organization, customers, the community, and the world. Students develop moral awareness and reasoning capabilities to guide them in effectively making such decisions. This class involves working with a team to debate ethical marketing issues.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in socially responsible marketing and strengthens skills used in marketing work.

title: Branding and Packaging
courseDescription: Provides an in-depth understanding of how branding and packaging are used to gain the target audience's attention in the competitive retail environment. Students learn to utilize product packaging as a critical strategic element for brand identity and differentiation. Key topics include brand recognition, branding a service, consumer research, brand extensions, emotional branding, global brands, legal issues, and store brands versus national brands.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in branding and packaging and strengthens skills used in marketing work.

title: Retail Marketing
courseDescription: Examines the strategic role of retailing in the distribution of consumer goods and services. Students learn why consumer insight and superior execution are critical factors for building retail brands that will be successful in the future. Key topics include retail formats, multichannel retailing, merchandise assortments, retail locations, holiday sales trends, supply chain management, customer relationship management, pricing, store layout and design, retail communication mix, and customer service.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in retail marketing and strengthens skills used in marketing work.

title: Services Marketing
courseDescription: The United States, as well as much of the world economy, is dominated by services. In the United States, approximately 80 percent of the labor force and 78 percent of the gross domestic product is accounted for by services. The primary theme of the course is that service organizations require a distinctive approach to marketing strategy-both in its development and execution.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in services marketing and strengthens skills used in marketing work.

title: Precalculus Lab
courseDescription: Emphasizes problem solving as applied to topics from Precalculus. Class time is spent on computer generated problem sets, workbooks in a question and answer format, and individualized work with the instructor. Topics covered include: Linear equations in one variable, graphing lines, finding equations of lines, functions, function notation, graphing functions, polynomials, exponents, and radicals.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in precalculus lab and strengthens skills used in mathematics work.

title: Mathematics for Elementary Teachers: Algebraic
courseDescription: Provides an inquiry-based examination of basic concepts, operations, and structures occurring in numbers, number sense, and algebraic reasoning. Students develop a deeper understanding of the numeric, arithmetic, and algebraic concepts required to teach elementary school mathematics. Does not fulfill mathematics and statistics core requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in mathematics for elementary teachers: algebraic and strengthens skills used in mathematics work.

title: Mathematics for Elementary Teachers: Geometric
courseDescription: Provides an activity-based exploration of informal geometry in two and three dimensions as well as probability and statistics. Emphasis is on visualization skills, fundamental geometric concepts, the analysis of shapes and patterns, and analyzing and displaying data. Students develop a deeper understanding of mathematical concepts required to teach mathematics in elementary school.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in mathematics for elementary teachers: geometric and strengthens skills used in mathematics work.

title: Precalculus
courseDescription: The study of functions from an algebraic, graphical, and numerical perspective. Concepts and procedures are emphasized, focusing on connections between equations, inequalities, and the analysis of function behavior. Algebraic, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions are examined and applied to problems from science and business.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in precalculus and strengthens skills used in mathematics work.
prerequisites: A score of 50 or better on ALEKS or a math SAT score of 560 or better or a math ACT score of 24 or better. Students not meeting the prerequisite will take corequisite MA 005 in addition to MA 109. Students who place into Calculus need department chair's permission to take this course (may be taken concurrently)

title: Mathematics and Politics
courseDescription: A mathematical and historical perspective on representation, voting, and power. The layers of the electoral system are considered, including voting systems, apportionment, redistricting, and the electoral college. Criteria for fairness in these topics and associated impossibility theorems are discussed.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in mathematics and politics and strengthens skills used in mathematics work.
prerequisites: No prior credit for MA/ST 200-level courses

title: Introduction to Combinatorics
courseDescription: A basic introduction to counting and its relationship to combinatorial structure. Topics may include sets, enumeration, permutations and combinations, probability, graph theory - colorability, planarity, and trees. Closed to students who have credit for MA/ST 200-level courses.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to combinatorics and strengthens skills used in mathematics work.
prerequisites: No prior credit for MA/ST 200-level courses

title: Mathematics, Numbers and the Real World
courseDescription: The nature of mathematical reasoning and the concept of proof in relation to concrete problems. Topics may include inductive reasoning, deductive reasoning, various number systems and their history, everyday arithmetic, financial management, introductory probability, and statistics. Topics are often discussed with a view toward practical applications and interesting real world examples.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in mathematics, numbers and the real world and strengthens skills used in mathematics work.
prerequisites: No prior credit for MA/ST 200-level courses

title: Applied Calculus
courseDescription: A one semester introduction to calculus. Definition, interpretation, and applications of the derivative especially in business and social sciences. Degree credit will not be given for both MA 151 and MA 251.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in applied calculus and strengthens skills used in mathematics work.
prerequisites: MA 109 or a score of 65 or higher on ALEKS or one year of high school calculus

title: Programming in Mathematics
courseDescription: The basics of MATLAB programming are covered through the investigation of various mathematical topics, including functions, conditional statements, loops, and plotting.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in programming in mathematics and strengthens skills used in mathematics work.
prerequisites: Restricted to mathematics or statistics majors

title: Techniques of Mathematical Modeling
courseDescription: Covers basic mathematical tools for quantitative descriptions of practical problems arising from physics, biology, economics, and engineering. Mathematical models are an important way of obtaining quantitative solutions to these problems. Emphasis is on the formulation, analysis, and testing of mathematical models through some elementary examples and effective communication of quantitative results.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in techniques of mathematical modeling and strengthens skills used in mathematics work.

title: Physical Training Lab
courseDescription: Fulfills ROTC's physical fitness lab requirements. Students who have declared intent to be a cadet in ROTC cannot progress through ROTC without completing this lab each semester. (Pass/Fail).
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in physical training lab and strengthens skills used in military science work.
prerequisites: MS 101 or MS 102 or MS 201 or MS 202 or MS 301 or MS 302 or MS 401 or MS 402 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Leadership Lab
courseDescription: Provides an environment for practicing leadership skills taught in the classroom and hands-on training with military equipment. Outcome-based training simulating military operations and public speaking are used as the vehicle for feedback-delivery and development for students in the leadership categories of character, presence, intellect, leads, develops, and achieves. Cadets apply, analyze, and evaluate military science course knowledge by prioritizing, planning and preparing, executing, evaluating, and assessing training during this lab.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in leadership lab and strengthens skills used in military science work.
prerequisites: MS 101 or MS 102 or MS 201 or MS 202 or MS 301 or MS 302 or MS 401 or MS 402 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Introduction to the Army
courseDescription: Focuses on introductng the Army and basic Soldier skills. Students receive an introduction to the Army Profession and examine what it means to be a professional in the U.S. Army, committed to the ideal that America and its founding documents remain the most powerful force for good in human history.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to the army and strengthens skills used in military science work.

title: Foundations of Leadership
courseDescription: Introduces the personal challenges and competencies that are critical for effective leadership and being committed to the ideal that America and its founding documents remain the most powerful force for good in human history. Students learn the importance of personal development in life skills such as critical thinking, resilience, holistic health and fitness, and the communication process. Students receive awareness training in Antiterrorism and introductory classes in tactics, beginning with Team and Squad Basic Components, Basic Movements, Basic Patrolling, and Battle Drills that are foundation throughout their military careers.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in foundations of leadership and strengthens skills used in military science work.

title: Leadership and Ethics
courseDescription: Focuses on leadership and ethics. The course adds depth to the cadet's knowledge of different leadership styles. Cadets conduct a leadership analysis of famous leaders and a self-assessment of their own leadership style.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in leadership and ethics and strengthens skills used in military science work.

title: Army Doctrine and Decision-Making
courseDescription: Focuses on Army Doctrine and Decision-Making. The course begins with cadets gaining an insight to analytical techniques, creative thinking skills, and the Army problem-solving process as related to situations faced by leaders committed to the ideal that America and its founding documents remain the most powerful force for good in human history. TLPs and OPORD lead cadets to an understanding of Army Doctrine and Symbology.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in army doctrine and decision-making and strengthens skills used in military science work.

title: Foundations of Tactical Leadership
courseDescription: Examines the challenges of leading teams in the complex contemporary operating environment (COE). The course highlights dimensions of the cross-cultural challenges of leadership in a constantly changing world and applies these to practical Army leadership tasks and situations. Health, wellness, and fitness instruction occurs outside the classroom.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in foundations of tactical leadership and strengthens skills used in military science work.

title: Training Management and the Warfighting Functions
courseDescription: Focuses on training management and the warfighting functions. The course is academically challenging, requiring cadets to study, practice, and apply the fundamentals of Training Management and how the Army operates through the Warfighting Functions. At the conclusion of this course, cadets are capable of planning, preparing, and executing training for a squad and platoon conducting small unit tactics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in training management and the warfighting functions and strengthens skills used in military science work.

title: Applied Leadership in Small Unit Operations
courseDescription: Focuses on applied leadership in small unit operations. It is an academically challenging course where cadets analyze, test, and relate the fundamentals of direct-level leadership and small-unit tactics at the platoon level. At the conclusion of the course, cadets are capable of planning, coordinating, navigating, motivating, and leading a platoon in the execution of a mission.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in applied leadership in small unit operations and strengthens skills used in military science work.

title: The Army Officer
courseDescription: Focuses on the development of an Army officer committed to the ideal that America and its founding documents remain the most powerful force for good in human history. It is an academically challenging course where cadets develop knowledge, skills, and abilities required of junior officers pertaining to the Army in multidomain operations. Cadets also learn to plan, resource, and assess training at the small unit level using the Training Management Process.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the army officer and strengthens skills used in military science work.
prerequisites: MS 009, MS 099, MS 499 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Company Grade Leadership
courseDescription: Focuses on the development of a company grade officer committed to the ideal that America and its founding documents remain the most powerful force for good in human history. It is an academically challenging course where cadets develop the knowledge, skills, and abilities required of junior officers pertaining to unit level leader roles and responsibilities. Cadets learn about Army programs that support counseling subordinates and evaluating performance, values and ethics, career planning, and legal responsibilities.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in company grade leadership and strengthens skills used in military science work.
prerequisites: MS 009, MS 099, MS 499 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Command and Staff Simulation Lab
courseDescription: Provides senior ROTC cadets with a practical environment to apply the principles of mission command, organizational leadership, and unit management. Cadets serve in battalion and company-level leadership positions, executing the duties of command and staff officers. Through structured command and staff meetings, training meetings, and operational planning sessions, cadets synchronize unit activities, manage training calendars, and coordinate resources in support of the battalion's mission.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in command and staff simulation lab and strengthens skills used in military science work.
prerequisites: MS 401 or MS 402 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Study Abroad Immersion Research Project
courseDescription: All students studying abroad through a Loyola program or exchange are required to complete an immersion research project. Students may choose to participate in a well-documented community service project while abroad or complete an independent research portfolio on their interaction with their host cultures. The project must be submitted to the Office of International Programs no later than 30 days after the student's program abroad ends.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in study abroad immersion research project and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.
prerequisites: Restricted to students participating in a Loyola study abroad program or exchange

title: Introduction to Chinese Literature in Translation
courseDescription: Introduces the rich history of Chinese literature and literary culture. Literary works in various genres and registers are analyzed in their broader sociocultural contexts along with an examination of their connections with human experiences and world communities. Text selections (pre-modern or modern Chinese literature) may vary by semester.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to chinese literature in translation and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Exploring Language: An Introduction to Linguistics
courseDescription: Investigates the study of linguistics, including sociolinguistics, with a focus on theoretical foundations and pragmatic, evidence-based implications for teaching and assessing reading, writing, spelling, phonics, and grammar in monolingual or multilingual contexts. Foundational concepts such as phonology, morphology, syntax, and pragmatics are explored with the goal of informing planning for teaching monolingual or multilingual students.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in exploring language: an introduction to linguistics and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Modern Chinese Literature
courseDescription: Since the late nineteenth century, China has witnessed a history of radical transformations. Literature in modern and contemporary China became a battleground for competing political, cultural, and aesthetic discourses. Through a close reading of the literary texts and a review of the socio-historical background, this course provides diverse approaches to understanding the ever changing lives of the Chinese people.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in modern chinese literature and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Old Wine in a New Bottle: Modern Film and Classical Chinese Tales
courseDescription: Modern films adapted from premodern Chinese historical and literary works connect the past and present, and sometimes also China and the West. By examining famous stories and their cinematic representations, students investigate how these films demonstrate the value of the past in contemporary society, and how they have influenced society's understanding of the cultural past of China. Selected historical, literary, archaeological, and cinematic works are used to analyze the origin and development for each story.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in old wine in a new bottle: modern film and classical chinese tales and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Gender, Peace, and Justice in East Asia: Texts and Context
courseDescription: Provides a survey on the gendered representations and experiences in East Asia (China, Japan, North Korea, and South Korea), as well as in other Asian regions and countries. Situating East Asian men and women in both regional and global contexts, this course investigates how gender in East Asia has been (re)constructed, (re)institutionalized, (re)appropriated, as well as (re)interpreted in different socio-historical discourses and/or under the global influence.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in gender, peace, and justice in east asia: texts and context and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Introduction to Traditional Chinese Culture
courseDescription: The unique features of Chinese literature, society, and culture are introduced through the examination of masterworks of history, literature, philosophy, and the arts in order to help students understand the origins and development of Chinese culture, as well as its influence on modern society. All written works are provided in English translation.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to traditional chinese culture and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Language and Identity
courseDescription: Language both determines and is an expression of identity. The connection between the construction of social identity and language use within the context of the United States is investigated. Students explore how discourse is structured to shape the identity of various ethnic groups (e.g., Black, Native, Asian, and Latin Americans), examining common language myths and evaluating the language stereotypes and attitudes reflected in books, film, newspapers, advertisements, etc.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in language and identity and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Paris Then and Now
courseDescription: Intensive study of how Paris and France are represented in literature and in the news media compared to how today’s Parisians of diverse social and cultural backgrounds and neighborhoods view themselves. Students read two novels featuring Paris as a main character, watch and read daily news and interview various Parisians in order to determine how certain stories, representations and myths are created about a city and how they compare to reality. This work is discussed in relationship with the current representation of French national identity and the role of France in the world today.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in paris then and now and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.
prerequisites: Restricted to students with cumulative GPA of 2.500 or higher

title: Popular Culture in Contemporary China: Transformation, Consumption, and Exchange
courseDescription: Critically examines popular culture and everyday life in Chinese society and the cross-cultural significance between China and the West in the context of globalization. Students study film to literature, music to fashion, and culinary arts to entertainment. They investigate the historical, sociopolitical, and aesthetic impacts of selected cultural topics through assigned readings and videos, in-class discussions, a field trip, and interactions with Chinese people.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in popular culture in contemporary china: transformation, consumption, and exchange and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Liberation Theology from Its Origins
courseDescription: Examines the origins of liberation theology during the Renaissance, comparing European and Latin American paradigms developed in association with the European conquest of the Americas. The course concludes with a liberation theologian from the twentieth century. Themes studied are mortality; charity versus charity; charity and justice; God versus the Church; the nature of the soul; temporal power; spiritual power; division of power; virtue; theology and history; the Gospels; the evangelization of Native Americans; the Counter-Reformation; the Church; Utopian visions (Saint Thomas More, Erasmus, Las Casas, and Guamán Poma de Ayala); immanence and transcendence; and revolutionary appropriations of Christ.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in liberation theology from its origins and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Dante's Divine Comedy (in translation)
courseDescription: An examination of Dante's major opus. Focuses on the historical, political, and philosophical aspects of Dante's masterpiece. Appreciation of Dante's place in world literature.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in dante's divine comedy (in translation) and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: China through Film
courseDescription: Explores Chinese culture through award-winning movies recently produced in mainland China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, and other Chinese-speaking communities. Lectures and discussions focus on the representations of Chinese history, family, and society and further examine how the Chinese identity is constructed in these movies. Aesthetic styles and cinematic themes are also investigated.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in china through film and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: The Early Latino Experience in the United States
courseDescription: Traces early Latino experiences and history in the lands that would become the United States. Three milestones are included: the first encounters between the Spanish and indigenous Americans during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; the Anglo incorporation of California, New Mexico, and Texas, during which Spanish-speaking peoples suddenly found themselves to be citizens of the English-speaking United States; and the first Pan-American conference (the origins of the Organization of American States), when Puerto Ricans and Cubans began to realize that their struggle for independence from Spain was being diverted and that they, like the upper-Californians, were coming under United States control.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the early latino experience in the united states and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Italy and Italians in Today's World
courseDescription: Studies Italian issues in Europe and the world, with history and culture being of primary concern. Students are encouraged to view these diverse realities through the lens of their major discipline, linking the language and culture studied with their major discipline, the courses taken in the minor, and study abroad. Includes readings, films, videos, and a final paper about an issue concerning Italian Studies examined in an interdisciplinary manner.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in italy and italians in today's world and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Introduction to Latin American and Latino Studies
courseDescription: Studies Latin America and Latino issues in the United States, with history and culture being of primary concern to determine how identities and nations are constructed and how they interact with each other. Students are encouraged to view these diverse realities through the lens of their major discipline. Closed to students who have taken HS 392.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to latin american and latino studies and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: Medieval Studies Capstone Project
courseDescription: An independent study accompanying a concurrently taken three-credit elective approved for the Medieval Studies minor. The interdepartmental subject and title must be approved by the instructor and Medieval Studies Consortium.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in medieval studies capstone project and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: CCLS Capstone Paper
courseDescription: An independent study accompanying a concurrently taken, three-credit elective approved for the CCLS major. Students research and write a senior project paper integrating the course topic into the specific orientation chosen for their comparative studies. Written or electronic permission of the CCLS director.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ccls capstone paper and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.

title: CCLS Capstone Research Paper
courseDescription: Students research, write, and present a senior research paper drawing from two or more of their CCLS courses within the specific orientation chosen for their comparative studies. Written or electronic permission of the CCLS director. Topics must be approved by the CCLS director, in consultation with the CCLS Steering Committee and the course instructor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ccls capstone research paper and strengthens skills used in modern languages work.
prerequisites: Two FR, ML, or SN courses at the 300-level

title: Class Piano I
courseDescription: Group instruction in musical technique and repertoire for the beginning student. Covers basic skills including music reading. Students work both in groups and individually with the instructor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in class piano i and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Musicianship II
courseDescription: A continuation of MU 205.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in musicianship ii and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: MU 205 or written permission of the instructor

title: American Musical Theatre: Uptown and Down
courseDescription: Studies the variety found in American musical theatre, including musical drama, opera, and musical comedy. Through readings, recordings, and video tapes, students investigate this lively art. At least one live performance is viewed during the semester.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in american musical theatre: uptown and down and strengthens skills used in music / theatre work.

title: Jazz Ensemble I
courseDescription: The Loyola Jazz Ensemble is open to all instrumentalists by audition. Repertoire includes jazz standards and original compositions. Students are given opportunities for solo playing.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in jazz ensemble i and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Chamber Ensemble I
courseDescription: Provides performance opportunities for instrumentalists who wish to play as soloists or as members of small groups (two to eight players), with a concert performance at the end of the semester. An audition with the instructor. May be repeated for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chamber ensemble i and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Concert Choir I
courseDescription: Concert Choir is a large, mixed ensemble that performs a varied and challenging program of choral repertoire from across time and place. Known for their diverse repertoire, and for a blended, unified sound, Concert Choir is the department's flagship choral ensemble, performing at venues both on and off campus. An audition with the instructor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in concert choir i and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Guitar Ensemble I
courseDescription: Designed for guitarists to perform in small groups of two to eight players. There are performance opportunities each semester. Open to students, faculty, and staff by audition.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in guitar ensemble i and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Steel Pan Ensemble I
courseDescription: Repertoire from Trinidad and Tobago. Panorama, transcription, calypso, soca, latin, jazz, ragtime, classical, and island favorites are performed with a full steel pan orchestra. An audition with the instructor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in steel pan ensemble i and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Repertoires of Western Music
courseDescription: Through a study of influential and representative works, students become acquainted with important theoretical, stylistic, and generic touchstones of the Western art music tradition from circa 500-2000.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in repertoires of western music and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: MU 201 or MU 302 (may be taken concurrently)

title: American Jazz
courseDescription: Traces the origin and development of a truly American musical phenomenon: jazz. Topics include prejazz, ragtime, New Orleans and Chicago jazz, big band, bop, and contemporary styles. Discusses the effect of jazz on the popular music of the time.
