whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in american jazz and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Music and Medicine
courseDescription: Examines the historical intersections of music and health, with a consideration of how music has been used to improve wellbeing, how myths about maladies have been represented in musical works, and how disabilities of composers and performers have been received by audiences. No training in music necessary. Open to all students.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in music and medicine and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Music in the Twentieth Century
courseDescription: A survey of European and American art music since 1900.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in music in the twentieth century and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Music History II: Classical to Contemporary
courseDescription: Traces the evolution of Western art music from the Classical era to the present (c. 1750–today). Beginning with the musical ideals of balance and clarity in the Classical period, the course follows music through the expressive expansion of Romanticism, the technological and cultural upheavals of the twentieth century, and the diverse experimental movements of contemporary music.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in music history ii: classical to contemporary and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: MU 201 or MU 202 (may be taken concurrently)

title: Structure of Music: Theory II
courseDescription: Third music theory course in the curriculum. Students begin working with advanced techniques of analysis and composing short works. Topics include modulation, melodic development, and chromatic harmony.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in structure of music: theory ii and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Jazz Ensemble II
courseDescription: A continuation of MU 211. An audition with the instructor. May be repeated for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in jazz ensemble ii and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Class Piano II
courseDescription: Continuation of MU 202. Group instruction in musical technique and repertoire. Covers more advanced techniques and music reading skills.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in class piano ii and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: MU 202 or written permission of the instructor

title: Conducting
courseDescription: Students study the art of conducting. Topics include score preparation, conducting, and rehearsal techniques. Students work with choral and/or instrumental ensembles in preparation for performance.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in conducting and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Chamber Ensemble II
courseDescription: A continuation of MU 220. An audition with the instructor. May be repeated for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chamber ensemble ii and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Concert Choir II
courseDescription: A continuation of MU 221. An audition with the instructor. May be repeated for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in concert choir ii and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Jazz Combo
courseDescription: An instrumental jazz group of four to eight players, representing the top jazz musicians on campus. The combo performs repertoire from lead sheets, requiring performers to create arrangements collectively and to develop a musically mature improvisational language. Members must be active in the jazz ensemble.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in jazz combo and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: MU 211 or MU 311 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Composition
courseDescription: Student study the process of musical composition by examining masterworks and by completing a series of composition assignments and original works. Assignments progress from basic melody writing, through two- and three-part writing, to multivoiced works for piano or small ensemble.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in composition and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Counterpoint
courseDescription: Students study the art of imitative and nonimitative counterpoint by studying examples of polyphonic music from the Renaissance and Baroque.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in counterpoint and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Songwriting
courseDescription: Introduces the fundamental methods, techniques, and practices of songwriting. Study includes a survey of styles such as pop, folk, hip hop, singer-songwriter, rhythm and blues, and country, including such artists as George Gershwin, The Beatles, Radiohead, Kendrick Lamar, and others based on student interest. Students have the opportunity to develop their own original material, work in collaboration with others, and receive individual feedback on their work.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in songwriting and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: MU 110 or MU 201 or MU 202 or written permission of the instructor

title: Cantorei
courseDescription: Cantorei is a smaller vocal ensemble that specializes in the vocal jazz repertoire, delving into both traditional vocal jazz, jazz arrangements of popular tunes, and repertoire from the American Songbook. Participants must also be active members of the Concert Choir. An audition with the instructor is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in cantorei and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: MU 221 or MU 321 (must be taken concurrently)

title: Guitar Ensemble II
courseDescription: A continuation of MU 230. May be repeated for credit. Open to students, faculty, and staff by audition.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in guitar ensemble ii and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: Two semesters of MU 230 or an audition with the instructor

title: Steel Pan Ensemble II
courseDescription: A continuation of MU 231. May be repeated for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in steel pan ensemble ii and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Recording Studio II
courseDescription: A continuation of MU 350. Focuses on the application of advanced techniques in digital recording. Students complete recording assignments in live stereo recording, studio tracking, mixing, equalization, the use of effects, and basic mastering.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in recording studio ii and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: MU 350 or written permission of the instructor

title: Applied Music (1/2 hour)
courseDescription: Private instruction in musical instruments and voice. Each lesson is one-half hour per week with independent practice as prescribed by the teacher. May be repeated 2 times for degree credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in applied music (1/2 hour) and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: MU 360: Open to first-years and first semester sophomores
MU 370: Restricted to majors and minors; Closed to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

MU 380: Two semesters of MU 370 or MU 375 and a passed jury. Permission is granted by the coordinator of the music program; Restricted to music majors and minors; Closed to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Applied Music (1 Hour)
courseDescription: Private instruction in musical instruments and voice. Each lesson is one hour per week with independent practice as prescribed by the teacher. May be repeated 2 times for degree credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in applied music (1 hour) and strengthens skills used in music work.
prerequisites: MU 375: Restricted to music majors and minors; Closed to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

MU 385: Two semesters of MU 370 or MU 375 and a passed jury. Permission is granted by the coordinator of the music program; Restricted to music majors and minors; Closed to students with catalogue year 2022-2023 or beyond

title: Musical Writing for the Public
courseDescription: Students bring together their historiographic and analytical skills and compile a set of program notes for their final recital or jury in this senior capstone course. In consultation with the music faculty and studio instructor, students research the history, social context, and reception of the works and their composers, and analyze the structures of their pieces. Students then learn to craft notes that are compelling and accessible to a general audience.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in musical writing for the public and strengthens skills used in music work.

title: Lean and Green Supply Chains
courseDescription: Explores Lean Six Sigma and business simulations under the lens of collaboration, innovation, and data-driven decisions. The course focuses on process improvement and data analysis to eliminate waste, reduce variability, and add value to operational processes. These basic principles can dramatically affect services and supply chains to improve quality, productivity, customer satisfaction, financial performance, and sustainability (including ESG reporting).
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in lean and green supply chains and strengthens skills used in operations and supply chain management work.

title: Global Supply Chain Strategy and Logistics
courseDescription: Introduces global supply chain issues. Topics include understanding global supply chain structure, key tensions in designing a supply chain, and cultural issues when dealing with global supply chains. Logistics topics include planning, implementing, and controlling the efficient and effective flow and storage of goods, services, and related information between the point of origin and the consumer.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in global supply chain strategy and logistics and strengthens skills used in operations and supply chain management work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, or seniors

title: Sourcing and Supply Chain Analytics
courseDescription: Explores the strategic and operational aspects of procurement and supply management within supply chains, with particular emphasis on both direct and indirect spend categories. Students examine how organizations plan and execute procurement processes, manage supplier relationships, and integrate purchasing decisions with overall organizational strategy and performance objectives. The course emphasizes data-driven decision-making by applying supply chain analytics to sourcing, spend management, supplier evaluation, and risk assessment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sourcing and supply chain analytics and strengthens skills used in operations and supply chain management work.

title: Evidence-Based Practice and Research in Nursing
courseDescription: Examines the role of qualitative and quantitative evidence in improving patient care and outcomes, emphasizing the integration of scientific evidence into nursing practice and focusing on nursing informatics for quality improvement. Students demonstrate competency in evaluating and applying evidence, summarizing scholarly articles, and presenting research findings using critical and analytical reasoning. The course explores ecological concepts related to human health, such as homeostasis, stress responses, and environmental factors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in evidence-based practice and research in nursing and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 101
ST 210 or ST 265 (may be taken concurrently)

title: Nursing Health Assessment
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment and reasoning skills in health assessment across the lifespan, integrating genetic, developmental, and nutritional perspectives. The course emphasizes taking health histories, conducting systematic physical examinations, and integrating assessment data into nursing diagnoses and care plans. Students demonstrate competency in using electronic medical records and collaborating with other healthcare providers.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nursing health assessment and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 101, NUR 102

title: Nursing Health Assessment Clinical
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment and competencies in patient-centered, compassionate care through goal setting, observation, practice, feedback, self-evaluation, and reflection. Students practice conducting comprehensive health assessments, including taking health histories, performing systematic physical examinations, and documenting findings in electronic medical records. The course emphasizes integrating cultural, spiritual, and social factors into clinical judgment to ensure holistic, patient-centered care.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nursing health assessment clinical and strengthens skills used in nursing work.

title: Fundamentals of Nursing
courseDescription: Builds on clinical judgment and reasoning, focusing on how these skills guide nurses working with diverse patients across various care settings. The course emphasizes the nursing process, basic nursing skills like monitoring physiological adaptation, and principles of safe patient care, including infection control and risk reduction. Students explore molecular genomics' basic principles and applications, understanding how these insights are used across various fundamental and applied fields.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in fundamentals of nursing and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 210, NUR 211

title: Fundamentals of Nursing Clinical
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment and competencies in providing patient-centered, compassionate care. Students apply basic nursing skills and the nursing process in clinical settings, emphasizing safety, privacy, and dignity in patient care and professional interactions. Student competency is assessed through clinical practice, skills checklists, direct observation, and feedback, with evaluations based on communication, critical thinking, clinical judgment, psychomotor skills, safety, professional behavior, and self-reflection.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in fundamentals of nursing clinical and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 210; NUR 211

title: Nursing Care of Adults and Older Adults Clinical
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment and competencies for patient-centered, compassionate care through goal setting, observation, practice, feedback, self-evaluation, and reflection. Students practice clinical judgment in the direct nursing care of adults and older adults, emphasizing safety, medication administration, medical-surgical procedures, and monitoring physiological adaptation. The course emphasizes psychosocial care and interprofessional collaboration within clinical settings, fostering critical thinking and clinical judgment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nursing care of adults and older adults clinical and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 215; NUR 216
NUR 371, BL 362, BL 370 (may be taken concurrently)

title: Nursing Care of Families: Maternal Health and Childbearing
courseDescription: Focuses on providing nursing support to women and childbearing families across the reproductive spectrum, from prenatal care to childbirth, perinatal care, and infant care. The course emphasizes clinical judgment in balancing the physiological needs of mothers and newborns while addressing the psychosocial needs of the entire family. Key topics include genetics, childbirth, well-woman and well-baby screenings, maternal mental health, lactation, parental risk behaviors, and domestic safety, with a focus on culturally sensitive care.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nursing care of families: maternal health and childbearing and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 310, NUR 311

title: Nursing Care of Families: Maternal Health and Childbearing Clinical
courseDescription: Allows students to apply clinical judgment and develop competencies in the patient-centered, compassionate care of childbearing families. Students engage in goal setting, observation, practice, feedback, self-evaluation, and reflection as they deliver nursing care focused on prevention, screenings for physiological, developmental, and mental health, neonatal safety, and psychosocial adaptation. An emphasis is placed on integrating teaching-learning practices and addressing the family's unique needs in relevant practice settings to meet course objectives.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nursing care of families: maternal health and childbearing clinical and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 310; NUR 311

title: Nursing Care of Families: Children and Adolescents
courseDescription: Focuses on the nursing care of children and adolescents, emphasizing health promotion, growth, development, and disease prevention. The course covers well-childcare, including vaccinations and developmental screenings, from infancy through adolescence. It also addresses pediatric pharmacology, medication adaptations, and care for acutely or chronically ill children.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nursing care of families: children and adolescents and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 310, NUR 311

title: Nursing Care of Families: Children and Adolescents Clinical
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment and competencies in providing patient-centered care for children and adolescents. Students practice clinical reasoning, emphasizing child development, preventive care, and the management of acute or chronic conditions, with a focus on pediatric pharmacology, medication adaptations, and family-centered care. The course highlights interprofessional collaboration and the referral of families to supportive services, addressing the holistic needs of children and their families.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nursing care of families: children and adolescents clinical and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 310; NUR 311

title: Pharmacology Clinical Laboratory
courseDescription: Focuses on nursing skills and clinical judgment related to pharmacological and parenteral therapies. Students practice "the eight rights of medication administration," drug calculation methods, routes of medication administration, devices used in venous access, monitoring patient reactions to medications, and safe handling of controlled substances. The course aims to establish practices for delivering high-quality and safe patient care in medication administration.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in pharmacology clinical laboratory and strengthens skills used in nursing work.

title: Nursing Care of Adults and Older Adults with Complex Health Problems
courseDescription: Focuses on the curative and rehabilitative care of patients with dual or multiple diagnoses and complex social circumstances, such as homelessness or lack of health insurance. Students learn to coordinate care across agencies, understand the role of nurses in rehabilitative care, and develop effective interprofessional partnerships. The course emphasizes patient dignity, advocacy, psychosocial adaptation, and addressing the challenges of aging populations and social determinants of health.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nursing care of adults and older adults with complex health problems and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 310, NUR 311

title: Nursing Care of Adults and Older Adults with Complex Health Problems Clinical
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment and competencies in patient-centered, compassionate care for adults and older adults with complex health problems, including dual diagnoses and socioeconomic challenges. Students practice their clinical judgment and reasoning in direct nursing care, emphasizing patient safety, establishing evidence-based priorities, coordinating care, and advocating for vulnerable populations. The course integrates skills in managing rehabilitation, addressing psychosocial needs, and collaborating with interprofessional teams.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nursing care of adults and older adults with complex health problems clinical and strengthens skills used in nursing work.

title: Mental Health Promotion and Psychiatric Nursing
courseDescription: Focuses on reducing mental health stigma, advocating for patients, and supporting the development of healthy personal habits to integrate mental health maintenance and well-being across the lifespan. Students develop clinical judgment skills to respond to grief, loss, trauma, substance abuse, and psychiatric conditions such as depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. The course covers pharmacotherapeutics commonly used in the treatment of psychiatric disorders and addresses mental health needs from childhood through adulthood.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in mental health promotion and psychiatric nursing and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 310, NUR 311, NUR 315, NUR 316, NUR 320, NUR 321

title: Mental Health Promotion and Psychiatric Nursing Clinical
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment and competencies for patient-centered, compassionate care in community health settings. Students practice mental health promotion and psychiatric nursing clinical reasoning and skills, incorporating safety, therapeutic communication, psychosocial integrity, and dignity into all direct patient care and professional interactions. The course emphasizes targeted nursing interventions to address population health concerns, reduce health disparities, and promote health while preventing disease.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in mental health promotion and psychiatric nursing clinical and strengthens skills used in nursing work.

title: Population Health and the Catholic Tradition of Social Justice
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment and patient education informed by community health measures, such as injury prevention, harm reduction, and nutrition. Students examine health systems, economics, culture, health legislation, and infectious disease management, while applying the ecological model of health promotion and place-based learning principles to address social determinants of health in Baltimore. The course emphasizes nursing interventions to reduce health disparities and promote health equity.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in population health and the catholic tradition of social justice and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 310, NUR 311, NUR 315, NUR 316, NUR 320, NUR 321

title: Population Health and the Catholic Tradition of Social Justice Clinical
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment and competencies in patient-centered care within the context of population health. Through goal setting, practice, feedback, and reflection, students focus on nursing interventions that promote health, reduce risk, and prevent disease in diverse communities and clinical settings, while addressing health disparities and emphasizing health promotion, disease prevention, and harm reduction. Competency is assessed through clinical practice, peer feedback, self-reflection, case studies, group projects, and structured evaluations, measuring students' ability to apply clinical judgment, engage in evidence-based practices, and demonstrate the core competencies required to promote health equity.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in population health and the catholic tradition of social justice clinical and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 310, NUR 315, NUR 320; NUR 311, NUR 316, NUR 321

title: Leadership and Management Nursing
courseDescription: Examines leadership theories and practices in advocacy, management, teaching, and research, focusing on safe delegation of care, staffing best practices, feedback strategies, and evidence-based conflict management. The course emphasizes diversity, equity, and inclusion as integral to just leadership, guided by Catholic tradition and Jesuit principles of discernment, continuous improvement, and lifelong learning. Students develop competencies in delegation, conflict management, and leadership strategies, with assessments through group projects, case studies, written exams, role-playing exercises, simulations, and peer feedback, measuring their ability to apply leadership theories, manage teams, and promote inclusivity and equity in leadership.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in leadership and management nursing and strengthens skills used in nursing work.

title: Leadership and Management Nursing Clinical
courseDescription: Develops clinical judgment and competencies for patient-centered care within leadership and management contexts. Students apply clinical reasoning and leadership skills through goal setting, observation, feedback, and reflection, with an emphasis on prioritizing care, safe delegation, and engaging in quality improvement and nursing research. In clinical practice, students develop competencies in delegation, leading teams, and managing care, aiming to improve patient outcomes and communication.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in leadership and management nursing clinical and strengthens skills used in nursing work.
prerequisites: At least a C or better in NUR 420; NUR 421

title: Transition into Professional Nursing Clinical
courseDescription: Focuses on actualizing the student's professional identity through an immersive clinical experience in a placement of their choice. Students reflect on the Jesuit values of Magis and the constant challenge to improve, deepening their ethical commitment to patients and the common good. The course includes the Health Equity Capstone Project, which emphasizes social justice in nursing professionalism and serves as a competency-based assessment of students' skills, knowledge, and abilities.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in transition into professional nursing clinical and strengthens skills used in nursing work.

title: Foundations of Philosophy
courseDescription: A one semester introduction to philosophy. Three focal points are covered: the emergence and development of rational theories on the nature of reality (metaphysics); questions concerning the grounds for distinguishing between knowledge and opinion (epistemology); and the nature and status of values (ethical, aesthetic, religious, etc.). Special attention is paid to the origins of philosophy and its historical beginnings in the ancient world.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in foundations of philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: The Project of Modernity
courseDescription: Examines distinctive aspects of the modern philosophical project as it relates to questions of science, politics, society, history, or morals. Philosophical theories ranging from the seventeenth through the twentieth centuries are treated in their historical development and/or their opposition to ancient teachings.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: the project of modernity and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: Methods of Reasoning
courseDescription: Introduces the principles of clear and effective reasoning through the analysis of argument structure, deductive and inductive inferences, common logical fallacies, rhetorical strategies, and everyday reasoning patterns. The course serves as a foundational tool for critical thinking across fields such as science, law, business, and public policy.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: methods of reasoning and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: Politics and Society
courseDescription: Addresses the basis and goals of human society, including issues concerning the structure of the good community as balanced against the interests of the individual.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: politics and society and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: Asian Thought
courseDescription: Introduces the philosophical and spiritual traditions of Asia, such as Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, and Daoism. Comparisons with Western thought are explored.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: asian thought and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: Art and Imagination
courseDescription: An exploration of the parallel development of philosophy and art as truth-disclosing activities.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: art and imagination and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: Soul and Psyche
courseDescription: An examination of the philosophical foundations of psychology from Plato to Freud.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: soul and psyche and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: Philosophy and Genocide
courseDescription: Examines the challenges that genocide poses for philosophy and what philosophy and philosophers might do to confront and even prevent genocide.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: philosophy and genocide and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: Humanity and Divinity
courseDescription: A philosophical investigation of the nature and meaning of the religious life.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: humanity and divinity and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: Gender and Nature
courseDescription: Examines the history of Western concepts of nature and science with particular attention to how ideas about hierarchy, gender, and violence have affected our relationship to the natural world. Introductory course for the Gender Studies minor.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: gender and nature and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: Philosophy and Science
courseDescription: A philosophical examination of science. Explores topics such as confirmation of the scientific method, the possibility of scientific progress, and the value of scientific inquiry.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: philosophy and science and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophical Perspectives: Environmental Philosophy
courseDescription: Explores the place of human beings within the much larger natural world and the fundamental conceptions of nature. Is nature savage, a resource for our use, or a mindless machine? Special topics may include animal consciousness, sustainability, indigenous cultures, global climate change and other ecological crises, and the effects of contemporary technologies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophical perspectives: environmental philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Modern Histories of Philosophy
courseDescription: Introduces key concepts and figures from the history of modern European Philosophy, while also enabling students to critically examine the contested nature of ‘philosophical canons’. Students consider cultural perspectives and historical developments (such as colonialism, race, gender or non-western philosophical traditions) that complicate dominant narratives of the European philosophical tradition. Recommended for philosophy majors and minors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in modern histories of philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Ethics
courseDescription: Explores, both historically and topically, the basic questions about values and obligation, the social and individual influences on moral judgement, the application of general guidelines to particular situations, and the search for a personal moral life.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethics and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Ethics of Humanitarian Intervention
courseDescription: The language and idea of “human rights,” “the rights of man,” and “natural rights” enter into political and moral discourse in the late eighteenth century. In 2005 the United Nations adopted the Responsibility to Protect, intended to protect all populations from human rights abuses. Ethics demand humanitarian intervention.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethics of humanitarian intervention and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Ethics of Race and Gender
courseDescription: Examines how relations of race and gender construct ethical subjects and change the way we understand what it means to live a good life. The course begins by offering some historical context for ethics of race and gender. The course then uses contemporary texts to explore how ethical subjects feel, act, and live their lives within the structures of violence, oppression, domination, and privilege.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethics of race and gender and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Business Ethics
courseDescription: Studies the relevance of ethics to business, with special emphasis on the similarities and differences between business and personal life. Case studies and special readings cover such topics as the social responsibilities of business and the notion of the economic common good.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in business ethics and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Bioethics
courseDescription: Studies the moral problems and uncertainties connected with biomedical research. Theoretical questions on the nature of morality and methodological foundations of science lead to a discussion of current topics, such as recombinant DNA, cloning, organ transplants, definitions of death, and death therapy.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in bioethics and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Ethics after Auschwitz
courseDescription: When philosopher Theodor Adorno wrote that “to write a poem after Auschwitz is barbaric,” it was a profound recognition that the Holocaust changed everything. This course explores ways in which philosophy might be implicated in the Holocaust and other genocides. It then turns to the failures of traditional philosophical ethics that we are forced to confront in the wake of the Holocaust.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethics after auschwitz and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Logic
courseDescription: Studies the basic principles and types of reasoning as they function in such fields as business, politics, law, and the natural and social sciences. Attention to the various ways in which language, argument, and persuasion can be used/misused.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in logic and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Cross-Cultural Philosophy
courseDescription: In today's multicultural societies, with increasingly frequent cross-cultural interaction taking place on a global scale, there is greater need than ever for philosophical reflection on how cultures have interacted and should interact. This course examines major theories and debates regarding the ethics and politics of cross-cultural relations and the hermeneutics of cross-cultural dialogue.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in cross-cultural philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Religion
courseDescription: An examination of phenomenological descriptions of religion, and a discussion of the possibility of metaphysical statements about God. Topics include contemporary problems of God-talk, secularization, the relationship between philosophy and theology.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of religion and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of War
courseDescription: Examines war through Tolkien’s Lord of the Rings and von Clausewitz’s On War. Tolkien describes Lord of the Rings as ‘a tale about war.’ To explore this claim, the course pairs Tolkien with the classic Western analytics of war, von Clausewitz’s On War. As Clausewitz was a veteran of the Napoleonic Wars and Tolkien was a veteran of World War I, both authors raise critical philosophical questions about the nature of war born from real experience.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of war and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Social and Political Philosophy
courseDescription: Addresses fundamental issues pertaining to the nature, shape, principles, and norms of the social and political order. Focuses on one or more special topics such as power, political authority, conflict, violence, oppression, marginalization, justice, equality, liberty, solidarity, rights, inclusion, and plurality.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in social and political philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Law
courseDescription: An examination of some basic systems of law, including legal positivism, common law, and natural law. Places where these systems come into conflict-for example, the tort law of wrongful birth-are a special focus of this course. By way of a central theme, students are introduced to the kinds and scope of laws governing homicide and how these apply domestically and internationally.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of law and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Contemporary Political Philosophy
courseDescription: Introduces the fundamental ideas which shape the way we think politically such as power, politics, political action, conflict, cooperation and contestation, authority, legitimacy, identity, resistance, and democracy. While exploring these ideas, we discuss some of the central questions of contemporary political philosophy: Does democracy need a common identity which unites the 'body' politic? In what ways does the pluralistic nature of democratic societies challenge the identity of the people?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in contemporary political philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Political Philosophy: Justice and Mass Incarceration
courseDescription: The United States imprisons more people per capita than any other nation in the world. A disproportionate number of those incarcerated are people of color, particularly Black, Latino, and indigenous men. How can mass incarceration in the United States be understood?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in political philosophy: justice and mass incarceration and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Comparative Philosophy: East-West Dialogues
courseDescription: Places in dialogue Western philosophical topics or figures with those drawn from Asian traditions. One or more specific themes are chosen as the focus of the course; for example, Eastern and Western conceptions of being and nothingness; human nature; the problem of evil; or mind and body.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in comparative philosophy: east-west dialogues and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy and Feminism
courseDescription: Treats analyses of oppression, conceptions of agency and autonomy, and accounts of the relationship between politics and social reality developed from several feminist philosophical perspectives. Taken together, the course texts challenge students to approach issues in moral and political theory in light of an understanding of how power dynamics involving gender function across cultural-historical contexts.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy and feminism and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Psychoanalysis and Philosophy
courseDescription: Examines recent interpretations of psychoanalysis, informed by existential philosophy and new conceptions of the nature of language. These perspectives restore the fertility and sophistication of Freud's thought and present new opportunities/challenges for philosophical questioning.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in psychoanalysis and philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Science
courseDescription: Introduces major themes in the philosophy of science, starting with a historical overview of key developments in twentieth century analytic philosophy. The course explores papers in contemporary philosophy of science, which may include topics such as theory change, scientific inference, the laws of nature, the role of creativity in science, the relationship between science and values, and how to distinguish good science from bad. Readings and case studies may be drawn from the physical, life, or social sciences.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of science and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Human Rights
courseDescription: Addresses basic questions about the nature, content, and philosophical foundations of human rights, with a specific emphasis on the philosophical-historical development of the idea of human rights. Various contemporary human rights problems are explored, including ethnic cleansing and genocide, poverty, and humanitarian intervention.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of human rights and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Peace
courseDescription: Studies the nature, aims, and possibility of peace. Students read what philosophers have had to say about peace and war from ancient to contemporary times. Some of the issues examined include just war theory, conscientious objection, nonviolent protest, and the current Iraq war.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of peace and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy and Art
courseDescription: Explores the relationship between philosophy and art, such as how philosophical concepts shape artistic expressions and, conversely, how art influences and molds philosophical discourse. Students explore key philosophical themes, including aesthetics, epistemology, phenomenology, and the nature of creativity, and develop the skills to articulate the interplay between philosophy and art. Questions covered may include: How do we define and distinguish art from non-artistic expressions?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy and art and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Economics
courseDescription: A critical and historical inquiry into economic theory from a philosophical perspective. The emergence of the field, its development through the lens of colonialism, its solidification in contemporary market capitalism, and dissenting voices along the way are examined, ending with a look into Green economics. Major figures from the field are also studied.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of economics and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Freedom
courseDescription: A philosophical and historical analysis of the multiple meanings and uses of the concept of freedom through text, literature, and film, including some cross-cultural exploration. What does the mythic land of freedom look like? Topics include emancipation and incarceration, political liberty and fascism, individual and collective rights, existential freedom, and Gaia.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of freedom and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Experience
courseDescription: Examines the major Western articulations of holism with emphasis on the experience of unity and the unity of experience, including the Neoplatonic philosophy of Plotinus; the Christian mystical tradition inspired by Pseudo-Dionysius; the early modern philosophies of Spinoza and Leibniz; the philosophical idealism of Hegel and Bradley; and the phenomenology of Merleau-Ponty.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of experience and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Chinese Philosophy
courseDescription: Students are introduced to some of the major themes and figures of philosophical thought in China. Major attention is given to the classical schools of Chinese philosophy, especially Daoism and Confucianism. Recent works on Chinese philosophy in comparison with Western philosophy may also be examined.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chinese philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of History
courseDescription: History is a central theme of philosophical inquiry. The study of the philosophy of history raises the question as to whether there is meaning in events over time and space, granting regularity and human freedom. Some key authors are Cicero, Augustine, Vico, Kent, Herder, Hegel, Marx, Dilthey, Ricoeur, and Danto, each of whom contributed to shaping the understanding of history.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of history and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Biology
courseDescription: Explores fundamental issues in the philosophy of biology: What is life? What is consciousness, and how does it arise? What is evolution, and how did Darwin initially formulate it?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of biology and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Kant's Revolutions
courseDescription: Introduces the revolutionary contributions made by the great German thinker Immanuel Kant to the fields of metaphysics, ethics, and aesthetics. Kant shifts the focus of inquiry from reality in itself to the role of the mind in constructing experience; from moral emotions to rational moral principles; and from the artist's poetic making to judgments of beauty.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in kant's revolutions and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Japanese Philosophy
courseDescription: Students are introduced to some of the major themes and figures of philosophical thought in Japan. The focus is on traditional thought, such as that of the Zen Buddhist philosopher Dogen, and/or on modern thought, such as that of the Kyoto School.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in japanese philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Medieval Philosophy
courseDescription: The Middle Ages is a period which not only excels for its cultural richness-in architecture (e.g., the emergence of the Gothic cathedral), literature (e.g., the vibrant innovations in love poetry), and intellectual life (e.g., the rise of universities)-but also for its profound concern with regard to philosophical issues. The scholastic period (approximately c. 1300-1500) particularly stands out for its vigorous and engaged discussion of profound philosophical questions such as time and eternity, being and thinking, soul and intellect, language and truth.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in medieval philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy/The Enlightenment
courseDescription: Studies the major questions of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century thinkers, such as Descartes, Voltaire, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke, Hume, Rousseau.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy/the enlightenment and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Nature
courseDescription: Examines the changing view of nature from the period of the early modern philosophers of nature, Newton and Bacon, through the Cartesian mechanization of nature adopted and extended by Enlightenment scientists and its rejection by Goethe and Schelling, who defended an organic and holistic view of nature. The basic opposition between the idea of nature as no more than mere natural resources to be exploited for human profit and nature as both alive and the source of all life is shown to be indispensable for understanding contemporary approaches to environmental ethics as well as the looming threat of a global ecological crisis.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of nature and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Marx and Marxism
courseDescription: Studies the philosophical writings of Marx and of the views on man and society presented by some contemporary Marxist authors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in marx and marxism and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: German Idealism
courseDescription: German idealism is the name usually given to the explosive series of developments in philosophy during the period immediately after Kant. Seldom in the history of philosophy has so brief a space of time produced so many philosophical innovations, many of which live on today, albeit under other names. Provides an introduction to the seminal role of Kant's thought as it influenced three of the most important thinkers of the time-Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in german idealism and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Existentialism
courseDescription: Studies some of the philosophical and literary works of thinkers such as Kierkegaard, Heidegger, Sartre, Marcel, and Camus.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in existentialism and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Phenomenology
courseDescription: Introduces phenomenology through a study of its major representatives, notably Husserl, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, and Sartre.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in phenomenology and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: The Thought of Heidegger
courseDescription: Traces the path of Heideggerian philosophy, focusing both on the existential, hermeneutic approach of Being and Time, as well as on the later, more meditative period. Questions will be raised about the implications of Heidegger's thinking for our understanding of the nature and history of philosophy.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the thought of heidegger and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Nietzsche
courseDescription: Nietzsche is the first major figure in the history of philosophy to repudiate the tradition of Western thought that began with Plato. The nature of this repudiation and Nietzsche's attempt to inaugurate a new mode of philosophical thinking are examined.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nietzsche and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Technology and the Crisis of Nature
courseDescription: Is the human use of technology rooted in a kind of thinking or way of being? Through a reading primarily of Martin Heidegger's work, students look at the dark side of technology and the devastating effects of human technical manipulation of the natural world.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in technology and the crisis of nature and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Process Philosophy
courseDescription: Studies the basic principles of process philosophy through Whitehead's Process and Reality. Topics include actual entities and their formative principles, the phases of feeling, the concrescence of an actual entity, actual entities, nexus and societies, the theory of perception.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in process philosophy and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy and Film
courseDescription: Our culture has been reshaped by the new technologies of cinema and television. Examines a range of philosophical issues surrounding the audio-visual structure of these media, and their impact upon society. Also uses films, like written texts, as a medium for addressing significant issues in philosophy.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy and film and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy of Mysticism
courseDescription: Many traditions and authors through history have set forth "mystical" insights, often accompanied by rigorous argument—for example, that beneath the chaotic diversity of experience there is an ultimate source of meaning and/or unity. This course examines a selection of such accounts, seeking to understand their domains of evidence, philosophical implications, and experiential applications.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy of mysticism and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Peace and Justice Studies Capstone
courseDescription: Designed to integrate students' experiences in the Peace and Justice Studies minor, this course consists of a senior capstone project and other work selected by the instructor. Both the course and the capstone project seek to foster reflection, integration, and action. Required for peace and justice studies minors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in peace and justice studies capstone and strengthens skills used in philosophy / theology work.
prerequisites: PL 401: Restricted to peace and justice studies minors
TH 401: Senior standing; Peace and justice studies minors

title: Imagination
courseDescription: Imagination has been variously conceived as a necessary aid to cognition (Aristotle), an "inferior kind of perceiving" (Berkeley), a "blind but indispensable function of the soul" (Kant), and "reason in its most exalted form" (Wordsworth). In this seminar, students investigate the history of the concept of imagination, with particular attention given to the philosophical significance of shifts in its characterization and its role in our contemporary self-understanding. Which kinds of human cognition are imaginative and in exactly what sense?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in imagination and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.

title: Philosophy and Work: Career Discernment
courseDescription: This course is designed for those who want to participate in the career discernment aspect of PL 499, but are not interested in or unable to participate in the internship.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in philosophy and work: career discernment and strengthens skills used in philosophy work.
prerequisites: Restricted to philosophy majors and minors
Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Photocraft
courseDescription: An intermediate, technical introduction to photography concentrating on the fundamentals of imagemaking, editing, and presentation in both silver and digital processes. Students gain a wide range of technical skills and experiences in both the darkroom and digital labs, focusing on in-camera exposure techniques, film/digital printing, and project-based work. A basic introduction to the Zone System, studio lighting, and image presentation is also provided.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in photocraft and strengthens skills used in photography work.
prerequisites: PT 270 or written permission of the instructor

title: Spirit Photography
courseDescription: Do you believe in ghosts? Spirits? The metaphysical?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in spirit photography and strengthens skills used in photography work.

title: Artist in Residence Seminar
courseDescription: A seminar led by and related to the work of the current semester’s Artist in Residence at the Julio Fine Art’s Gallery. Students collaborate with the artist on a project of a group or individual nature related to the artist’s exhibition and practice. Varies by semester.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in artist in residence seminar and strengthens skills used in photography / studio art work.

title: Silver Processes
courseDescription: An intermediate study of black and white silver photography. Students produce their own darkroom work. Exposure, development, and printing are explored in detail in the darkroom.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in silver processes and strengthens skills used in photography work.

title: Directed Workshop
courseDescription: Designed to allow students to pursue an interest in a specific area of photography such as sports, portraits, landscape, nature, etc. Weekly critiques of ongoing projects and a final exhibition portfolio required. May be repeated twice for credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in directed workshop and strengthens skills used in photography work.

title: Landscape and Nature Photography
courseDescription: An intensive workshop in photographing the landscape and elements from it as an expression of personal statement. Some weekend field trips required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in landscape and nature photography and strengthens skills used in photography work.

title: Alternative Photographic Processes
courseDescription: Studies the early processes by which photographic images were recorded and displayed. Students make their own pinhole cameras and light sensitive materials, and produce original photographs. Explores the aesthetic and expressive possibilities of alternative photographic processes, including cyanotype, Van Dyke brown, and wet-plate collodion.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in alternative photographic processes and strengthens skills used in photography / studio art work.

title: The Photographic Essay
courseDescription: Under the instructor's direction, students develop a body of photographic images exploring, in depth, a specific photographic subject. Frequent classroom critiques of the ongoing project, technical demonstrations, and museum/gallery visits.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the photographic essay and strengthens skills used in photography work.

title: Image and Text
courseDescription: Explores the dynamic relationship between photographic imagery and text. Students study the history of art that combines text and visual imagery. They also explore in their own work the ways that text as an interactive, subversive, or antithetical element can conspire with the photographic image to construct or deconstruct opinions and provoke new responses.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in image and text and strengthens skills used in photography work.

title: Portraiture
courseDescription: Provides a basic foundation for students interested in portraiture. By examining the evolving roles of the photographer and the person being photographed, students are acquainted with contemporary trends in portraiture. Students work on projects that explore different ways of making portraits.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in portraiture and strengthens skills used in photography work.

title: The Body in Photography
courseDescription: Throughout history the human image has been the most important subject through which artists have expressed their personal visions and identities. This course offers students an opportunity to study the human form as an artistic, photographic topic.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the body in photography and strengthens skills used in photography work.

title: Senior Capstone for Artists
courseDescription: Students are introduced to the working world of the professional artist. Students create a cohesive body of work that is critiqued throughout the semester and exhibited at the end of the semester. Students produce a portfolio of digital images of their artwork with accompanying professional materials aimed at being able to participate in the art world in some form upon graduation.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior capstone for artists and strengthens skills used in photography / studio art work.
prerequisites: PT 400: PT 270 or PT 300 or PT 301; Senior standing; Visual arts major
SA 400: SA 224 or SA 227; SA 225; Senior standing; Visual arts major

title: Introductory Physics II with Lab
courseDescription: A continuation of PH 101 which includes wave motion, sound, electrostatic and electromagnetic fields, DC and AC circuits, geometric and physical optics, and selected topics in atomic and nuclear physics. Lab component introduces basic principles of experimentation, error analysis, and report writing. Fulfills one math/science core requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory physics ii with lab and strengthens skills used in physics work.

title: Introduction to the Universe
courseDescription: A survey of the history of astronomy and the current state of this science. A look at the probabilities of, and search for, extraterrestrial life. A study of our solar system, stars and their evolution, our galaxy and other galaxies, supernovas, pulsars, black holes, quasars.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to the universe and strengthens skills used in physics work.

title: Practical Meteorology
courseDescription: Teaches students the science behind what causes weather. Course content highlights cloud types, storm systems, weather instruments, and foundations of forecasting. Throughout the course, students analyze the most up-to-date computer models, radar, satellite, and forecast discussions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in practical meteorology and strengthens skills used in physics work.

title: Energy and Environment
courseDescription: An examination of energy sources for the future: nuclear power, breeder reactors, gasoline substitutes, the future of coal, solar and geothermal sources are studied in view of the laws of thermodynamics. Studies the impact of energy use on resource conservation, water resources, air quality, waste disposal, and land use. Fulfills one math/science core requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in energy and environment and strengthens skills used in physics work.

title: Light and Color
courseDescription: Light and its behavior influences our perception of the world around us. Reflection, refraction, polarization, diffraction and interference are investigated, as well as optical instruments, vision and the phenomena of color. Fulfills one math/science core requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in light and color and strengthens skills used in physics work.

title: General Physics II
courseDescription: A continuation of PH 201 which includes classical electromagnetic theory and geometrical optics. Fulfills one math/science core requirement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in general physics ii and strengthens skills used in physics work.
prerequisites: MA 252; PH 292 or written permission of the department chair (must be taken concurrently)

title: General Physics Lab II
courseDescription: A continuation of PH291 with experiments taken from sound, wave motion, electrostatics, DC and AC circuits, and geometrical optics. Basic electronic instrumentation introduced.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in general physics lab ii and strengthens skills used in physics work.
prerequisites: PH 291 or written permission of the department chair

title: Intermediate Laboratory I
courseDescription: A variety of illustrative and sometimes classic experiments in optics, thermal physics, mechanics, electricity and magnetism, and quantum physics; also introduces the rigorous analysis of experimental errors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate laboratory i and strengthens skills used in physics work.
prerequisites: PH 202 and PH 292, or written permission of the department chair

title: Intermediate Laboratory II
courseDescription: A continuation of PH 293, with further experiments in optics, thermal physics, mechanics, electricity and magnetism, and nuclear and quantum physics. Extends discussion of error analysis to include use of partial derivatives and statistical distributions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate laboratory ii and strengthens skills used in physics work.
prerequisites: PH 293 or written permission of the department chair

title: Haig Scholars Seminar
courseDescription: Offers students from all disciplines within the Natural and Applied Sciences the opportunity to partake in professional and social activities planned to enrich the academic experience, develop professional skills, foster entrepreneurial mindset, nurture community engagement, and expose students to leaders in technical fields with proven social impact. The activities designed for this seminar course mainly take place on campus but may also include events in the Baltimore-Washington metropolitan area. Students must enroll in this course only once and after they have been admitted as a Haig scholar.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in haig scholars seminar and strengthens skills used in physics work.
prerequisites: Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Mathematical Methods in Physics
courseDescription: Development of the mathematical methods needed to describe waves and vector fields. Topics include power series, complex numbers, linear algebra, Fourier series, and vector calculus. Physical examples cover harmonic oscillations, coupled oscillations, and traveling waves.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in mathematical methods in physics and strengthens skills used in physics work.

title: Quantum Mechanics II
courseDescription: Studies the formal structure of quantum mechanics including matrix mechanics, operators, and spin. Includes more advanced applications such as scattering theory, perturbations, and quantum statistics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in quantum mechanics ii and strengthens skills used in physics work.

title: Electricity and Magnetism II
courseDescription: Electric and magnetic fields in matter and the relativistic formulation of electrodynamics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in electricity and magnetism ii and strengthens skills used in physics work.

title: Quantum Computing
courseDescription: Studies advanced topics and applications in quantum computing. Topics include quantum Fourier transformation, eigenvalue estimation, and their applications such as Shor's algorithm and the HHL algorithm. Other topics may include an introduction to quantum machine learning using quantum kernels and quantum variational methods, quantum computing as applied to quantum chemistry, and quantum error correction.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in quantum computing and strengthens skills used in physics work.

title: Advanced Laboratory
courseDescription: A laboratory that emphasizes extended experiments requiring equipment design and originality. A public presentation of results is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced laboratory and strengthens skills used in physics work.

title: Chinese Politics
courseDescription: China is likely the most important country rival for the U.S. in the twenty-first century. The economy has greatly developed in the last 25 years but the ruling Chinese Communist Party faces enormous political challenges today. What major political events from the past shape China's political culture today?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in chinese politics and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Latin American Politics
courseDescription: Latin America is a land of contrasts. It is rich in natural resources such as oil and copper, and is also a leading exporter of foodstuffs such as soybeans, meat, and coffee. Despite this, social inequality, poverty, and increasing violence are prevalent.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in latin american politics and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Natural Law in Political and Legal Thought
courseDescription: Studies natural law doctrines from Greek and Roman speculations to contemporary debates on the possibility and content of a natural law. A review of the writings of various natural law thinkers is undertaken from both an historical and analytical perspective.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in natural law in political and legal thought and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Politics of Russia
courseDescription: Introduces Russia in the twenty-first century, emphasizing its political system and foreign policy. An independent research paper on one aspect of this fascinating country is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in politics of russia and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: China and Globalization
courseDescription: The US-China trade war grabs headlines, while the Chinese Communist Party quietly sells surveillance technologies and spreads authoritarian values across the world as it secures access to critical oil and mineral resources. Taking advantage of the "global war on terror," the Party has imprisoned as many as a million Uighur Muslims in camps at home in the name of security while it propagates Chinese versions of "human rights" and "democracy" that no longer have their usual meanings.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in china and globalization and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Political Economy of Development
courseDescription: There is a growing realization among academics and policy-makers that economics and politics are deeply interconnected. Political economy is a field of study that engages both disciplines in order to better understand important questions such as: Are some political institutions more conducive to economic development than others? Under what conditions does economic development foster political development and democratization?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in political economy of development and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Protest and Mobilization in Authoritarian Regimes
courseDescription: Popular movements and protests mobilize aggrieved citizens under repressive authoritarian regimes but they face a number of obstacles to success. Activists seek to fashion slogans that resonate with the discontented, employ new communication technologies to outflank regime controls, and draw supporters from the existing collectives in society. What explains how these movements get off the ground, how they develop over time, and what outcomes they achieve?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in protest and mobilization in authoritarian regimes and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: African Politics
courseDescription: Africa is often described as the “last frontier of development.” It is a continent full of challenges but also full of opportunities and fast-paced political and socioeconomic change. We examine why African countries are poorer and less democratic on average than those of other continents. We also investigate why some African countries, such as Botswana or Mauritius, are much more developed and democratic than others, such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in african politics and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Introduction to Security Studies
courseDescription: Examines core theories and policy debates in international security, including great power competition, the causes of war and civil conflict, the roles of terrorist groups and armed non-state actors, and challenges such as climate change and human security in weak and fragile states. An emphasis is placed on conflict prevention, stabilization, and strategic decision-making in a rapidly evolving global environment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to security studies and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: American Economic Inequality and the Law
courseDescription: The United States has one of the highest levels of economic inequality in the developed world. While some level of economic inequality is inherent and even desirable in a capitalistic economy, many scholars believe that the level of inequality that prevails in the U.S. erodes generalized levels of trust, poisons interpersonal relationships, and ultimately makes it far more difficult to govern a democratic society. This course examines the roots of American economic inequality, with a tight focus on how laws adopted through democratic processes have resulted in a huge transfer of wealth from the hands of the many to the hands of the few.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in american economic inequality and the law and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Public Opinion and American Democracy
courseDescription: Deals with the origins, nature, content, and impact of American public opinion. Role of demographics and economics on the distribution of public sentiment is noted; so are surprising departures from "conventional wisdoms" regarding its character.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in public opinion and american democracy and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: American Political Development
courseDescription: What factors explain the "exceptional" character of the American state and American politics more generally? What roles have America's political institutions as well as its political ideas and rhetoric played in society and the economy? What are the dominant patterns, causes, and consequences of political change in American history?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in american political development and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: American Political Parties
courseDescription: The continuing combat between Democrats and Republicans in the electoral arena. Focus on contemporary studies of the American electorate and its behavior. Attention to congressional and other elections as well as those at the presidential level.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in american political parties and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Media and Politics
courseDescription: What impact do media institutions and actors have on public opinion, governing, and the substance of public policy? Students examine how media routines affect what constitutes news; how political elites use media strategies for campaigning and governing; and how the public consumes and perceives media messages about politics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in media and politics and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Organizing in America in the Digital Age
courseDescription: Collective action is one way in which individuals can participate in political change in the U.S., but effective action is rarely spontaneous. This course discusses strategies for building grassroots power and how they have changed since the mid-twentieth century. Students explore how digital technologies have shaped prospects for bottom-up change through reading in American social movements, the political economy, and technology.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in organizing in america in the digital age and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Religion and Politics in America
courseDescription: Examines the attempts by religious groups, movements, and interests to influence American politics through agenda setting, lobbying, lawsuits, and electoral activities. Includes case studies following litigants who pursued their vision of the First Amendment to the Supreme Court.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in religion and politics in america and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Mock Trial
courseDescription: Students gain a hands-on appreciation of trial court practice and procedures. In this course, students participate in a mock criminal or civil trial, playing the role of an attorney in one and a witness in the other. Students learn how to work with statutes and precedents and rules of evidence, and they also do opening statements, direct and cross examine witnesses, and present documentary and physical evidence.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in mock trial and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Politics of Asian Religions and Environmental Sustainability
courseDescription: The environmental health of the planet depends to a great extent on what happens in Asia, because China and India are the most populous countries and produce a massive share of global pollution. At the same time, these and other Asian countries have varying religious traditions, religion-state relationships, and levels of religious practice. How do the politics of religion in Asian countries, including China, Taiwan, India, and other countries affect the possibilities for global environmental sustainability?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in politics of asian religions and environmental sustainability and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Congress: The Legislative Process
courseDescription: Explores the political and institutional factors that determine how and whether legislation becomes law. The role of parties, committees, and other House and Senate legislative institutions in the legislative process are examined. What factors promote and hinder Congress' ability to pass laws in the public interest?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in congress: the legislative process and strengthens skills used in political science work.

title: Congressional Politics
courseDescription: Explores the politics of Congress, both as a collection of individual members and as an institution. Using the whole of congressional history, students examine changes in congressional representation and elections, the politics of lawmaking, the role of Congress in the separation of powers, and Congress' impact on society.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in congressional politics and strengthens skills used in political science work.
