title: Health and Society
courseDescription: Introduces macro-, micro-, and meso-sociology with particular emphasis on the social causes, social distribution, and social responses to health/illness. Topics include cultural conceptions of disease and its treatment (including roles and norms); the consequences of social inequality (especially race/ethnicity, class, and gender); and the social organization of care. Historical-evolutionary and cross-national comparisons supplement a primary focus on the contemporary situation in the United States.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in health and society and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Social Problems
courseDescription: Studies common social problems using sociological, theoretical, and conceptual frameworks. Individual deviance, patterns of social injustice, specific problems affecting major U.S. institutions, and international issues are investigated. Various mechanisms and resources for solving and preventing social problems are explored.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in social problems and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Introducing Gender and Sexuality Studies
courseDescription: Students gain an overview of the role of gender and sexuality in society. Questions explored: How are our expressions of gender and sexuality tied to our biology and to economics, educational systems, and political ideology? How do gender and sexuality exist as elements of both the structure of society and individual identities?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introducing gender and sexuality studies and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Introduction to Social Work
courseDescription: Objectives are to understand the concept of human services; to know the fields of practice in which human services are delivered; to understand the social worker's role in the service delivery system; to be exposed to problems experienced by people and the issues addressed by social service workers; and to understand the concepts of social work practice with individuals, groups, and communities.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to social work and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Sociology of Race, Class, and Gender
courseDescription: The social construction and intersection of race, social class, and gender is examined. Particular attention is paid to privilege, economics, historical and legal contexts, and systems that act to perpetuate these categories. Fulfills social science core.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociology of race, class, and gender and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Sociology of Asian Americans
courseDescription: Challenging the myth of a monolithic Asian American experience, sociological and interdisciplinary frameworks are used to ask what Asian America means and how such meanings have changed through history. Through a range of case studies, students situate Asian America within the global and local contexts of war, colonialism, environmental racism, migration, labor, and social movements. The course explores how social inequality, culture, and politics shape the lives of Asian Americans utilizing examples such as COVID-19 and anti-Asian racism, affirmative action, and pop culture.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociology of asian americans and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Juvenile Delinquency
courseDescription: Introduces the field of juvenile delinquency. Covers the history of juvenile crime, prevalence and trends in youth crime, and risk factors within the family and schools. Peers and gang violence are also discussed.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in juvenile delinquency and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Introduction to Criminal Justice
courseDescription: Introduces the structure and operation of the criminal justice system in the United States. Topics include criminal law, prevalence and trends, the police, the judicial system, and corrections.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to criminal justice and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: The Sociology of Food and Foodscapes
courseDescription: Introduces the sociological study of modern "foodscapes" as simultaneous structures of community and inequality. The course examines how food production links human societies to the natural world and how food distribution ensures social reproduction. The food system as a commodity chain along with shared and contested food practices, meanings, and unequal realities of food access and food sovereignty are also studied.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the sociology of food and foodscapes and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Child Welfare
courseDescription: Exploration of issues related to the child welfare (social service) system which responds to children who have service needs as a result of a dysfunctional family or from experiencing traumatic events in their childhood. Issues addressed include child abuse and neglect, foster care, adoption, impact of chemical dependent or mentally ill caretakers on childhood development, impact of family violence on childhood development, and teen suicide. Highlights the role of the social worker and response by child welfare agencies and the juvenile court for each topic discussed.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in child welfare and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Sociology of Religion
courseDescription: Engages students in the sociological study of religion. The field of sociology provides a distinctive manner by which religion can be understood to interact with both people and the wider environment. Specifically, sociology provides useful language, methods, ways of thinking, and other tools for describing, understanding, and explaining the nature and function of religion in relation to the increasingly interconnected world in which we live.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociology of religion and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Artificial Intelligence: Social Implications
courseDescription: Examines how artificial intelligence (AI) technologies shape and are shaped by social structures, norms, and power dynamics. The ethics of AI, algorithmic bias, and how AI affects criminal justice surveillance, healthcare, education, labor, governance, and identity are explored to better understand the impact on racial, class, and gender inequalities. Students engage with critical theories of technology, drawing on the works of scholars in sociology, critical data studies, and ethics to analyze the promises and perils of AI in society.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in artificial intelligence: social implications and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, or seniors

title: Deviance and Social Control
courseDescription: An examination of the relationship between deviance and social control, including how and why certain forms of behavior come to be defined as deviant, the nature of formal and informal response to deviance, and the interaction of different social control institutions. An overview of general theories of deviance and the particular forms it takes, with special attention to issues that cut across the whole range of deviance.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in deviance and social control and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: The Sociology of Crime and Criminals
courseDescription: An historical and contemporary overview of the nature of crime and the causes of criminal behavior. Examination of the measurement of crime and crime trends.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the sociology of crime and criminals and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Conflict and Peace Studies
courseDescription: War and large-scale violent conflicts are unfortunately a pervasive feature of our global landscape. While conflicts are inevitable, violent conflicts are not. In this course, students increase their understanding of the conditions under which social conflicts tend to become destructive and how they can be waged (and transformed) constructively.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in conflict and peace studies and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors sociology majors and minors

title: Social Research Methods
courseDescription: Students learn social science vocabulary and techniques necessary to step into a position where they can contribute to an ongoing study; to critically evaluate social science research completed by others on both methodological and ethical terms; to frame a sociological question of interest, seek out and obtain literature relevant to it, and construct an essay that coherently synthesizes trends in the body of material; and to conceptualize a research question and a basic framework that would be appropriate for pursuing an empirical investigation in an ethical manner.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in social research methods and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to junior or senior sociology majors or minors

title: Sociological Theory
courseDescription: An overview of classical, modern, and contemporary theories. Classical theory stresses the contribution of scholars whose work most strongly influenced modern theory. Modern theory includes varieties of structuralism, Marxian theory (historical materialism), and Weberian theory (sociology of institutions).
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociological theory and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to junior or senior sociology majors or minors

title: Critical Analysis of Criminal Justice Outcomes
courseDescription: Explores sources of inequity in the U.S. criminal justice process, focusing on court-related processes: bail, arraignment, plea bargaining, trial, and sentencing decisions. Students develop understanding of the independent and interlocking roles of race, gender, and class in the perpetuation of inequality through reading empirical research and exploring alternative justice systems.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in critical analysis of criminal justice outcomes and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Social Inequality
courseDescription: Examines economic, political, gender, racial, and ethnic inequality in the United States. Extensive descriptive materials are presented on various systems of social inequality, and the major theoretical and ideological perspectives on inequality are considered.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in social inequality and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Sociology of Health, Illness, and Medicine
courseDescription: Through classic and contemporary empirical works, students are encouraged to reflect on the structural determinants of health, the limitations of Western medicine, and the perspectives and practices of complementary and alternative medicines. Topics include cultural influences on understandings of health, mental illness stigma, epigenetics, and the quality of doctor-patient relationships. The course consists of lectures and student-led discussions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociology of health, illness, and medicine and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Neighborhood and Community in Urban America
courseDescription: Examines the social aspects of urban life in modern America. Topics include patterns of city growth; the loss of traditional community; the growth of the underclass; social disorder; economics; and the welfare state. Special emphasis is given to the social organization within the community (e.g., neighborhood associations, faith congregations, business and political coalitions, and interpersonal networks).
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in neighborhood and community in urban america and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Sociology of Sexuality
courseDescription: A sociological perspective is used to examine human sexuality, focusing on how sexuality reflects the societies in which we live. Although it is often assumed that sexual attitudes and behaviors are biologically based, they are strongly shaped by society. This course examines the history of sexuality in Western society, the acquisition of sexuality, and alternative forms of sexuality.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociology of sexuality and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, or seniors

title: Masculinities
courseDescription: Critiques of masculinity barrage us with the notion that men are dangerous and distressed; yet, men's experiences are various, ranging from powerful and confident to marginal and frightened. This course examines the many ways men live, how literature describes them, and how scholars interpret them. Feminist, multicultural, and transnational perspectives are utilized.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in masculinities and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomore, junior, or seniors

title: Mining the Gap: Determinants of Educational Outcomes
courseDescription: Using the lens of Critical Race Theory, this course examines the influence of “color-blind” educational models on racial achievement gaps. Using local, state, and national level data, students interrogate the role of educational policies and practices in the production and reproduction of educational inequalities on the bases of race, class, gender, special education, and immigration status.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in mining the gap: determinants of educational outcomes and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Sociology of Serial and Mass Murder
courseDescription: Sociologically analyzes typologies, theories, patterns, and motives of serial and mass murder. Cross-cultural comparisons are made, myths versus facts are addressed, and data is analyzed to view the known and predicted occurrences of these crimes. At the end of the course students are able to distinguish between serial and mass murder, separate fact from fiction, analyze crime patterns, and apply a sociological lens to the perceived motives for serial and mass murder.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociology of serial and mass murder and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Sociology of Human Rights
courseDescription: Human rights are approached from a comparative historical and interdisciplinary perspective. Students learn about foundational notions of human rights as they are interpreted in accordance with various belief systems and secular humanist philosophy; the UN-based human rights regime; and contemporary challenges to the realization of human rights in the global era. Taught from a sociological perspective, this course takes a critical approach to the study and analysis of the human rights system, with special focus on contradictions, failures, and collective mobilization.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociology of human rights and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Sociology of Development
courseDescription: The topics of political and economic development are approached from a comparative historical perspective. Students learn about the history of modern development practices; the postulates and assumptions of various theories of development; and the various criticism/critiques of development regarding European colonialism, Cold War geopolitics, and contemporary global integration and backslashes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociology of development and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Health and the Environment in Times of Crisis
courseDescription: Explores social, political, and cultural responses to disasters and crises and the implications of such responses for health and the environment. Taking a transnational and multidisciplinary view, a range of cases are explored, including nuclear accidents, global pandemics, and government restrictions on scientific knowledge. The course also takes an intersectional approach to consider how legacies of exploitation such as racial capitalism and colonialism shape the meaning of disaster and crisis.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in health and the environment in times of crisis and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Israel-Palestine: Conflict Narratives, Media Framing, and Peace-Building
courseDescription: Students gain extensive knowledge of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict through exposure to the different historical narratives, conflict frames, and social psychological realities on the ground. More broadly, the course deepens students' understandings of the characteristics and dynamics of deep-rooted conflict, the challenges posed by conflicting narratives, the role of media, education, and other institutions in perpetuating protracted conflicts, and the social, psychological, and structural processes inherent in transforming protracted violent conflict and building a just and sustainable peace.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in israel-palestine: conflict narratives, media framing, and peace-building and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Social Movements and Social Protest
courseDescription: Explores national, international, and transnational efforts by organized civil society groups to bring about political, social, and cultural change. The grievances, goals, tactics, and achievements of a wide range of social movements are examined. Students explore when and why movements occur, who joins them, how they are organized, what strategies they use, how they are influenced by different institutions like the state and the media, and what impact they have on society.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in social movements and social protest and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors

title: Social Power and Social Change in the Modern Middle East
courseDescription: Examines the political and economic development of the region commonly called the "Middle East". Coined as a geopolitical term in 1902, the name is often used to oversimplify an incredibly diverse area. While popular media frequently equates the region solely with "Islam" or "Arab" culture, this course moves beyond those stereotypes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in social power and social change in the modern middle east and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Gender and Sexuality Studies Capstone
courseDescription: Addresses a selected topic from a particular disciplinary perspective to explore the construction and meaning of gender and sexuality in specific times, places, and institutional spaces in relation to other social categories, identities, and structures such as race, class, ethnicity, and ability. Topics and the disciplinary home of the instructor vary by semester. This course is intended to engage senior Gender and Sexuality Studies minors in collaborative feminist and/or queer analysis and cross disciplinary dialog about the substantive topic as the culmination of their undergraduate study in Gender and Sexuality Studies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in gender and sexuality studies capstone and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Sociology Practicum
courseDescription: Students develop career-relevant skills through participation in supervised work experience. Agency placements include courts, social services, counseling centers, research centers, and federal/state/local government. Relevant issues are discussed in a weekly seminar.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociology practicum and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to junior and senior sociology majors
Written or electronic permission of the instructor

title: Social Work Practicum
courseDescription: Students develop social work skills through participation in supervised social work setting. A weekly seminar provides a forum for discussion of relevant issues and professional development toward a career in social work. Seminar format with limited enrollment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in social work practicum and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to junior and senior sociology majors
Written or electronic permission of the department chair

title: Gender and Sexuality Studies Practicum
courseDescription: Students develop career-relevant skills through participation in supervised work experience. Placements are in agencies/organizations that explicitly address issues of gender and/or sexuality, and may be governmental, nonprofit, or political entities. Relevant issues are discussed in weekly seminars or in tutorial, dependent upon course enrollment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in gender and sexuality studies practicum and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: SC 210, two 300-level or 400-level gender and sexuality studies minor courses

title: Seminar: Qualitative Data Analysis
courseDescription: Students collect qualitative data and engage in collaborative interpretive analysis using relevant software. Readings exemplify analytic strategies and focus on techniques and ethical concerns in ethnography and related methodologies. Seminar format with limited enrollment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: qualitative data analysis and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Seminar: Quantitative Data Analysis
courseDescription: Students use quantitative data to answer questions about the social environment. This course familiarizes students with computer applications and presents the logic underlying the analysis of survey data. Students work with existing data sets in the conceptualization and examination of causal relationships.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: quantitative data analysis and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Seminar: Social Construction of Opportunity
courseDescription: Among American core ideals is the notion that opportunities are equally available for all. Nevertheless, the lived reality is that opportunity is profoundly impacted by demographic factors such as race, class, and gender. This course examines the role of social and cultural capital (trust, civic, engagement, community attachment, and social networks) in shaping life chances and provides a critical understanding of how structural positions and social relationships affect the distribution of social opportunities such as educational and occupational attainment, health, and wealth.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: social construction of opportunity and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Sociology of Mental Health and Illness
courseDescription: Examines mental health and illness from a sociological perspective. In addition to learning about different conceptualizations of mental health and illness, students learn about the social distribution of mental illness and the consequences of having a mental illness and acquiring a mental illness label. The course also explores popular discourse on mental health and how that influences how mental illness is perceived.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociology of mental health and illness and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Seminar: Gender and Justice
courseDescription: Examines how legislation, interpretation, and application of criminal law reflect gendered, raced, and classed assumptions about human nature, appropriate roles, and positions in society. The course focuses on the processing of victims and offenders. Readings and assignments provide students with multiple perspectives on gender and with qualitative and quantitative investigations of the criminal justice system, explore intersectionality within the context of the available literature, and engage students in making sense of and critically analyzing empirical methods.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: gender and justice and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Seminar: Forensic Sociology
courseDescription: Considers the use of sociological data and its interpretation in decisions made by courts and other agencies of the judicial system. Areas considered may include profiling in law enforcement and corrections, insanity, competency, intimate partner violence, stalking, the death penalty, and the CSI effect. Seminar format with limited enrollment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: forensic sociology and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to junior and senior sociology or forensic science majors and minors

title: Seminar: Global Sociology
courseDescription: A reading and writing intensive seminar that engages with global social theory and the writings of sociologically informed thinkers who critically analyze the processes of global connectivity, global movement, and global social change from a macro, longue dureé perspective. Global social formations include the capitalist economic system that is anchored by private property relations the world over, a political system organized by and for territorially bound nation-states and in the name of a legally sanctioned citizenry, and a cultural system enamored by processes of service-driven consumerism.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: global sociology and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Seminar: Conflict Transformation and Reconciliation in Divided Societies
courseDescription: Explores what enables societies to move from violent social division to a sustainable peace. The characteristics and dynamics of protracted conflicts, and the structural and cultural processes inherent in conflict transformation in divided societies are analyzed. Students learn about various contemporary conflicts, peace processes, and reconciliation initiatives.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in seminar: conflict transformation and reconciliation in divided societies and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Food Fight: Inequality, Injustice, and Resistance
courseDescription: Interrogates food as an economic, social, and political domain that requires the study of macro processes of regional and class marginalization, exploitation, conformity, oppression, resistance, and revolution. The course studies "food fights", which includes farm-worker strikes, consumer calls for boycotts, campaigns to ban harmful pesticides and fertilizers, debates about labeling genetically modified food, and national policies to encourage citizens to eat specific foods.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in food fight: inequality, injustice, and resistance and strengthens skills used in sociology work.

title: Feminisms Across Borders
courseDescription: Explores feminisms as a series of overlapping political projects that move across diverse geographies and social contexts. The course combines practical case studies with feminist theory to examine topics such as feminist waves in North America, intersectionality, postcolonial feminisms, queer theory, international human rights, and the ways in which border crossings and legacies of transnational exchange are central to the history of feminisms. Seminar format with limited enrollment.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in feminisms across borders and strengthens skills used in sociology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to junior or senior sociology or global studies majors or sociology or gender and sexuality studies minors

title: Introductory Spanish I
courseDescription: A thorough grounding in the four language skills: reading, understanding, speaking, and writing, as well as an understanding of the structure of the Spanish language, as well as the national literatures and cultures of Spanish American countries and Spain. For students with no previous knowledge of the language. Not recommended for students who have taken three years of high school Spanish.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory spanish i and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Introductory Spanish II
courseDescription: A continuation of SN 101. Laboratory study outside the classroom is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introductory spanish ii and strengthens skills used in spanish work.
prerequisites: SN 101 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Intermediate Spanish I
courseDescription: A systematic consolidation and expansion of the four basic skills: reading, understanding, speaking, and writing. To increase and perfect students' acquired abilities/proficiencies in the language, and broaden their understanding of the country's culture and literature. Laboratory study outside the classroom is required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate spanish i and strengthens skills used in spanish work.
prerequisites: SN 102 or SN 161 or appropriate score on placement exam

title: Spanish Composition and Conversation
courseDescription: Increases students' oral and written proficiency through assimilation of advanced structural patterns, stylistic analysis, discussion of contemporary topics. Summer sections Closed to students who have taken SN 203, SN 217, or any SN 300-level course.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in spanish composition and conversation and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Introduction to Reading Literature
courseDescription: Transition from SN 201 to advanced classes. Develops reading skills with emphasis on class discussion and new vocabulary. Introduces Hispanic literature: basic terms, genres, detailed analysis, and themes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to reading literature and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Spanish for the Professions: Healthcare
courseDescription: Introduces the use of Spanish in healthcare and social services fields. The course provides functional Spanish designed for students preparing for a career in healthcare (speech pathology, psychology, pre-health, forensics, etc.) who need to be familiar with vocabulary, conversational Spanish, basic translation, and cultural practices. With an emphasis on aural and oral interactions, the variety of vocabulary and phrasal expressions used by Latinx populations living in the U.S.A. are covered.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in spanish for the professions: healthcare and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: The Culture and Civilization of Spain
courseDescription: Studies the historical, political, literary, and artistic development of Spain including an examination of the characteristic traditions and customs of their social context.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the culture and civilization of spain and strengthens skills used in spanish work.
prerequisites: SN 201 or SN 203 or one SN 300-level course

title: Introduction to Mexican Culture
courseDescription: Offers an interdisciplinary survey to the foundation of Mexico, its peoples, their origins, historical legacies, and present-day cultural productions. It combines disciplines such as history, literature, visual arts, cultural studies, music, culinary appreciation, and anthropology. Discussion topics include identity formation, migration, social disparity, gender violence, and political divide.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to mexican culture and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Contemporary Central America
courseDescription: With civil wars in Nicaragua, El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras during the 1980s, Central America endured class struggle in its most extreme form. After the peace accords of the 1990s and the repatriation of Central Americans who had assimilated the gang culture of large U.S. cities, the situation degenerated into nonpolitical, extreme social violence that continued to rip at the social fabric of the Central American region. Students examine a series of texts and videos which define the conflict and the violence related to it in terms of economics, gender, and race.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in contemporary central america and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Visual Culture in Colonial Latin America
courseDescription: Examines the visual production of the colonial period considering race, sexual gender, space, and religion as the analyzing factors. Readings consist of a variety of texts and images including chronicles, autobiographies, journals, paintings, maps, and plates. Visual sources come from Gillain Rose's Visual Methodologies, Serge Gruzinski's La colonizacion de lo imaginario, and Magli Carrera's Imaging Identity in New Spain.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in visual culture in colonial latin america and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Music and Latin American Social Movements
courseDescription: Given the historical importance of musical expressions in relation to several great struggles and transformations of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries in Latin America, this course analyzes the relationships between music and key moments of social, political, and cultural change in the region. Beginning in the sixties, the course encompasses the protest song, the new Cuban trova, the new Chilean song, and Argentine rock in their role against dictatorships. Additionally, popular music in the national liberation movement of El Salvador is explored, among other topics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in music and latin american social movements and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Violence and Culture: Columbia in the Twentieth Century
courseDescription: Cultural territories that represent the complex and unique political, economic, and social realities of Columbia are explored. Starting with the eighties, students examine important events in the history of the country as recreated by writers Laura Restrepo, Fernando Vallejo, and Jorge Franco Ramos. Modern conflicts such as social violence, guerrilla resistance, and marginality are addressed, as portrayed in testimonial writings, documentaries, painting, and music.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in violence and culture: columbia in the twentieth century and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Introduction to Spanish Linguistics
courseDescription: Introduces the basic linguistic issues concerning the Spanish language. Students explore the basic concepts of the principle areas of linguistics, such as phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, sociolinguistics, dialectology, and historical linguistics. Focus is placed on understanding of the basic tools involved in linguistic analysis and their application in the analysis of the Spanish language.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to spanish linguistics and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Spanish Phonetics and Phonology
courseDescription: Focuses on the linguistic study of the Spanish sound system and explores articulatory phonetics (how sounds are pronounced) and phonology (how sound patterns are formed and organized). Theoretical and practical comparisons between Spanish and English are made to illustrate relevant concepts.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in spanish phonetics and phonology and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Bilingualism in the Spanish-Speak World
courseDescription: Explores the nature of bilingualism, focusing on concepts of language acquisition and the structure of Spanish in contact with other languages. In addition, the class examines bilingual and multilingual contexts of the Americas, Spain, and Equatorial Guinea, focusing on topics of bilingual education, language policy, and contemporary sociolinguistic issues.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in bilingualism in the spanish-speak world and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Spanish Applied Linguistics
courseDescription: The processes of learning and acquisition of Spanish as a second or world language are studied. Students study the history of this field, as well as the approaches and methodologies that have developed the field throughout its history. During the second half of the course, students focus on the concepts of the linguistic system of the Spanish language which present themselves as the most challenging for learners of Spanish, as well as pedagogical questions and issues associated with the learning and acquisition of Spanish as a second or world language.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in spanish applied linguistics and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Spanish in the United States
courseDescription: Explores various aspects of the Spanish language in the United States. Sociolinguistic issues of language variation, change, contact, use, attitudes, and maintenance are examined by studying multiple bilingual communities located in the United States.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in spanish in the united states and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Contemporary Spanish Literature: 1975 to the Present
courseDescription: A survey of literature in Spain from the death of Francisco Franco in 1975 to the present, covering the major figures in narrative, poetry, and theatre. Focuses on the relationship between literary structure and political context of the period, with particular attention to the rise of post-modernism as well as feminist and gay literature. Readings include Lourdes Ortiz, Manuel Vázquez Montalván, Paloma Pedrero, Antonio Gala, Pere Gimferrer, Ana Rossetti, and others.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in contemporary spanish literature: 1975 to the present and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Rewriting the Self: Women's Literature in Contemporary Spain
courseDescription: How has women writers' perception of themselves and their country evolved following the Spanish Civil War (1936-1939)? This course is a survey of literature written by Spanish women writers from the 1940s to the end of the century. Students focus on first person fictional accounts of women's lives, the changing meaning of womanhood, the struggle for gender equality, and the experience of cultural and political exile.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in rewriting the self: women's literature in contemporary spain and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: A World in Crisis: Writing Contemporary Spain
courseDescription: Studies literary texts in contemporary Spain since the 1990s that comment on crises from different perspectives that include: the relationship between the individual and society (gender and race); the distrust of language; the historical revision after the Spanish civil war; political, economic, and ecological crises; immigration; and the covid-19 pandemic. The work of literary authors Javier Marías, Rosa Montero, Soledad Puértolas, Desirée Bela-Lobedde, Chenta Tsai, Sara Mesa, and Lorenzo Oliván are included in this course.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in a world in crisis: writing contemporary spain and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Short Latin American Fiction
courseDescription: Reading and discussion of short stories and very short novels (novellas) by Latin American writers. Topics include sociopolitical, familial, or imaginary worlds in relation to the strategies of fiction. Authors include García-Márquez, Borges, Cortázar, and Fuentes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in short latin american fiction and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: The Golden Age
courseDescription: The most important period in this country's literary heritage surveys Spain's golden age through an examination of representative works such as the anonymous Lazarillo de Tormes, Cervantes' Don Quijote, Tirso de Molina's El Burlador de Sevilla, and Lope de Vega's Peribáñez. Texts for the course are in the Spanish language of the period.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the golden age and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Contemporary Latin American Literature
courseDescription: Studies representative, contemporary Latin American writers such as Asturias, Borges, Cortázar, Fuentes, García, Márquez, and Vargas Llosa. Special attention given to works which exemplify innovation in form and the artist's involvement in contemporary social problems.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in contemporary latin american literature and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Spanish Postwar Literature
courseDescription: Studies representative works which bear witness to and examine the contradictions of postwar Spain. Emphasis placed on sociohistorical context and literary analysis.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in spanish postwar literature and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: A Survey of Spanish Theatre
courseDescription: Surveys the theatre of Spain from its beginnings to the twentieth century. Aims at providing some insight into major periods in Spanish literature through the study of works by such representative writers as Miguel de Cervantes, Lope de Vega, Calderon de la Barca, Tirso de Molina, Jose Zorrilla, Federico Garcia Lorca, Alejandro Casona, and Antonio Buero Vallejo.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in a survey of spanish theatre and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Latin American Short Story
courseDescription: Studies this important genre in Latin America from its development in the nineteenth century to the present.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in latin american short story and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Civilization and Barbarism in Argentine Literature
courseDescription: Examines the theme of civilization versus barbarity during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries in Argentine literature, as well as the subthemes of liberalism versus authoritarianism; Francophilia versus the Pampa; the city versus the rural; man versus woman; and man versus himself. Readings are chosen from representative works of Argentine literature including Mármol, Sarmiento, Gorriti, Borges, and Giardinelli.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in civilization and barbarism in argentine literature and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: The Origins of Contemporary Spain: 1898-1920
courseDescription: Examines the various responses among Spanish writers to the loss of the last colonies after the war of 1898 and the paradoxical entrance of Spain into the twentieth century. Focuses on the major intellectual trends in Europe and the Americas which influenced radical changes of style and structure in the narrative, poetry, and theatre of the period. Readings include works by Miguel de Unamuno, Pío Baroja, Ramón María del Valle-Inclán, Azorín, and Antonio Machado.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the origins of contemporary spain: 1898-1920 and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Contemporary Spanish Literature: The Generations of 1914 and 1927
courseDescription: A survey of Spanish literature at the beginning of the twentieth century (1910-1936), covering the major figures in poetry, drama, and narrative fiction. Particular attention is paid to the relationship between literary structures and the innovations in technology and social and political organization which characterize the period. Readings include Ramón Gómez de la Serna, Carmen de Burgos, Ramón Pérez de Ayala, Pedro Salinas, Federico García Lorca, Ernestina de Champourcin, and others.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in contemporary spanish literature: the generations of 1914 and 1927 and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Spanish Literature of Exile: 1939-1975
courseDescription: A survey of literature written by Spanish exiles after the Civil War (1936-1939), covering the major figures in narrative, poetry, and theater. Focuses on the meaning of exile and the relationship between literary structure and political context of the period. Readings include Francisco Ayala, Rosa Chacel, Max Aub, Rafael Alberti, and others.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in spanish literature of exile: 1939-1975 and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: The Latin American Essay and Early Cultural Studies
courseDescription: Examines political, social, anthropological, and philosophical speculation from nineteenth-and twentieth-century Latin America. Studies authors such as Sarmiento (Argentina), Martí (Cuba), González Prada (Perú), Cabello de Cabonera (Perú), Hostos (Puerto Rico), and Paz (México). Special emphasis is given to the notion of the nation in its relationship to culture, cultural studies, and cultural history.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the latin american essay and early cultural studies and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Latin American Testimony
courseDescription: An overview of twentieth century testimonial writings in Latin America. Particular emphasis is given to development, trends, and controversies. The relevance of testimony within Latin American literature and historiography is highlighted.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in latin american testimony and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: The Short Story in Spain Since 1936
courseDescription: A survey of the short story form, beginning with the Spanish Civil War and continuing through the postwar period and the transition to democracy after 1975. Readings and class discussion focus on the short story, both as a literary form and as a means to address the changing relationship between the individual and society over the course of the twentieth century. Authors include Manuel Chaves Nogales, Camilo José Cela, Ana Maria Matute, Ignacio Aldecoa, and Álvaro Pombo.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the short story in spain since 1936 and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Travelers and Migrants in Twentieth-Century Colombian Literature
courseDescription: Examines representations of travel, migration, and displacement in Colombian narratives, starting in the 1920s and continuing through various decades of the twentieth century. The readings include fictional narratives such as novels and short stories. From the experience of the characters within the literary works, the course focuses on new identities shaped by traveling throughout geographical and symbolic territories.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in travelers and migrants in twentieth-century colombian literature and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: From Baroque to Enlightenment: Novo-Hispanic Perspectives
courseDescription: Examines texts written by Criollo authors from New Spain whose works demonstrate the ongoing construction of identities in colonial Mexico. These narrations intertwine personal, fictional, and collective events and show the diversity of the colonial reality observed and constructed by these writers. Texts are studied in light of cultural, social, and historical contexts.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in from baroque to enlightenment: novo-hispanic perspectives and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Nineteenth-Century Latin American Novel
courseDescription: Focuses on the relationship between love and social institutions in nineteenth-century Latin America. Special attention given to the power of love, social norms, dictatorship, and the institution of slavery. Also examines gender/racial issues within their social context.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in nineteenth-century latin american novel and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: The Short Story in Spain, 1875-1925
courseDescription: The theory and evolution of the short story from romanticism through realism and modernism. Students read representative short story collections from each of the important literary movements of the period with a focus on the evolution of aesthetic ideas and structures. Authors include the Duque de Rivas, Cecilia Böhl de Faber, Pereda, Clarín, Pardo Bazán, Baroja, and Valle-Inclán.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the short story in spain, 1875-1925 and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: The Nineteenth-Century Spanish Novel
courseDescription: A fascinating journey through the Spanish novel in the second half of the nineteenth century, focusing on the representation of gender roles and social class in the context of the construction of contemporary Spain as a nation. Readings include works by Juan Valera, Benito Pérez Galdós, Emilia Pardo Bazán, and Leopoldo Alas, Clarín.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the nineteenth-century spanish novel and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Literature and Identity Politics in Peru
courseDescription: Examines what Martin Stabb so aptly called the "quest of identity." Works written over five centuries are compared to see how ethnicity, politics, religion, and gender negotiate with each other in their pursuit of identity. Five hundred years of scripted ideological activity is brought into focus: the Conquest, the Colonial Era, the Early Republican Era, and the twentieth century. A diverse sampling of genre types, chronicles, poetry, testimonio, fiction, and essay is included.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in literature and identity politics in peru and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: The Romantic Revolution in Spain
courseDescription: Spanish Romanticism emerges as a direct response to the conflicts and concerns of a country undergoing a series of rapid transformations during the first half of the nineteenth century. The most important authors of the period explored the idea of individual freedom in social, political, and artistic contexts while at the same time reflecting the struggle between traditional values and newer forms of thought and expression. This course covers important examples of the prose, poetry, and theater of the period with emphasis on major authors such as Larra, Espronceda, Bécquer and Rosalía de Castro.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the romantic revolution in spain and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Spanish Literature of Fantasy, Mystery, and Terror
courseDescription: Literature devoted to the exploration of the irrational in human experience, whether in the form of fear of the unknown or the examination of criminal impulses, forms an essential part of modern culture. In this course, the evolution of this tendency in Spain from the Gothic literature that appears as a reaction to the Enlightenment at the end of the eighteenth century to the new aesthetics of irrationality that arises at the close of the nineteenth century with Modernismo is studied.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in spanish literature of fantasy, mystery, and terror and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Crime Fiction in Spain
courseDescription: Since the 1970's, many Spanish authors have turned to the crime novel as a vehicle for chronicling the social and political evolution of the country. This course provides an introduction to how some of the genre's most important works have addressed such issues as the growth of major cities, urban crime, and corruption in all of its forms. Authors studied include Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, Andreu Martín, Lorenzo Silva, and Alicia Giménez Bartlett, among others.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in crime fiction in spain and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Modernismo
courseDescription: Development, trends, and influences; study of the works of representative writers of this Latin American literary renaissance, from the initiators to Ruben Dario and the second generation of modernistas.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in modernismo and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Latin American Avant-Garde
courseDescription: Examines both formal experimentation and social commitment of Latin American writers as portrayed in works created between 1916 and 1935. Focuses on poems and cultural manifestos that reflect a high aesthetic awareness and an aspiration to define national and continental identities. Representative writers include Vallejo, Huidobro, Villaurrutia, Girondo, Neruda, and Vidales, among others.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in latin american avant-garde and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Women Against the Current in Latin America
courseDescription: Discusses important events in the recent history of four Latin American countries (Mexico, Ecuador, Guatemala, and Uruguay) as reflected in the personal histories and testimony of women. In the case of Ecuador and Guatemala, the focus is on the experience of Quichua and Mayan women in their struggle to overcome the discrimination encountered in many aspects of their lives, including the family, the community and the larger political arena.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in women against the current in latin america and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Women Take the Floor: Mexican Female Writers
courseDescription: Focuses on texts written by Mexican women from the Baroque Period to present times. Novels, poetry, periodical excerpts, and short stories that discuss social and cultural issues central to Mexico through the lens of women are read. The texts studied aim to deconstruct the idea that women were not subjects in Mexican literature.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in women take the floor: mexican female writers and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: The Conquest of the New World
courseDescription: Provides the building blocks for understanding the encounter between the Spanish and indigenous cultures during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Special attention is given to two regions: Meso-America and the Andes.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the conquest of the new world and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Travel Writings of the New World
courseDescription: Examines the role of travel in colonial Spanish America and how it contributed in the creation of the idea of the New World. Special attention is placed on the "ways of seeing" of the authors who represented colonial territories and their inhabitants. Primary texts include works from the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth centuries, by authors with diverse backgrounds-military, bureaucrats, businessmen, and scientists-like Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, Catalina de Erauso "The Second Lieutenant Nun," Antonio de Ulloa, and Alexander Von Humboldt.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in travel writings of the new world and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Extirpation of Idolatries
courseDescription: Studies the practice of eliminating pre-Hispanic religious traditions in Peru and Mexico, beginning in the sixteenth century, as part of the Christianization process. Examines the religious conquest of Amerindian groups as a fragmentary process since many kept practicing activities that evoked their ancestral traditions, despite the Spanish efforts to change and even suppress them. Texts discussed include works from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries by Joseph Arriaga, S.J., Pedro Calderón de la Barca, Bernardino de Sahagún, O.F.M., Cristóbal Albornoz, and Father Diego Durán.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in extirpation of idolatries and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Periodical Texts of the Americas
courseDescription: Examines the role of newspapers and gazettes in the Spanish American territories, focusing on the history of the press and the logistical obstacles editors faced in printing and distribution, by analyzing periodical documents dated between 1750 and 1810, including the Gazeta de México, Mercurio Peruano, Papel Periódico de Santafé de Bogotá, Gazeta de Guatemala, and Diario de México. The course explores topics such as medicine, the role of women, the job market, and the image of Spain.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in periodical texts of the americas and strengthens skills used in spanish work.

title: Introduction to Special Education
courseDescription: Provides an introduction to the terminology, identification, and issues commonly encountered when addressing the needs of diverse students with disabilities. Emphasis is placed on inclusion, diversity issues, federal and state legislative mandates pertinent to nondiscriminatory assessments, parental involvement, individualized education programs, and professional practice and foundations in special education. Participants investigate the major areas of exceptionality, addressing the characteristics and educational needs of students with orthopedic, visual, hearing, speech, emotional, cognitive, and health impairments, including Autism Spectrum Disorder, and those with learning disabilities.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to special education and strengthens skills used in special education work.

title: Assessment and Evaluation for Special Education
courseDescription: Teacher candidates demonstrate understanding of the principles, ethics, and limitations of assessment, as well as the process of special education eligibility, progress evaluation, and dismissal. Candidates demonstrate understanding and knowledge of various formal and informal assessment instruments, their administration, and their interpretation. Candidates construct goals and objectives for students with learning and behavior problems by using assessment information and input from parents and other professionals.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in assessment and evaluation for special education and strengthens skills used in special education work.

title: Collaboration and Consultation for Students with Special Needs
courseDescription: Students explore the full continuum of special education service delivery models, including inclusive education, resource services, team teaching, and consultation. Learners gain insight into the intricacy of collaboration with other professionals and families. Through the use of formal measures and self-reflection, students explore the factors that influence their ability to collaborate and refine their interpersonal communication skills.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in collaboration and consultation for students with special needs and strengthens skills used in special education work.

title: Principles of Behavior Management for Special Education
courseDescription: Provides a foundation for behavior management, applied behavior analysis (ABA), and positive behavior interventions and supports (PBIS) for use by special educators or behavioral specialists. Students examine behavioral definitions and measurement procedures, prompting and reinforcement strategies, systematic behavior change methods, targeted interventions, and school-wide behavior support processes. Students use data from functional behavior assessment methods to discover the function of a child’s problem behavior, modify environments to reduce or prevent problem behavior, implement positive behavioral interventions, and program functional alternatives for school settings.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in principles of behavior management for special education and strengthens skills used in special education work.

title: Curriculum and Instruction for Special Education
courseDescription: Designed to give teacher candidates a thorough understanding of specially designed instruction and is focused on IEP development and instructional methods for teaching exceptional learners. Candidates are prepared to meet the instructional needs of exceptional students in a variety of settings. They learn how to use data to make instructional decisions and monitor student growth; gain an understanding of effective approaches to learning and teaching; prepare instruction, modify curriculum and materials, and review behavior management strategies to meet the unique needs of individual learners.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in curriculum and instruction for special education and strengthens skills used in special education work.

title: Introduction to Human Communication
courseDescription: Effective communication is a critical skill affecting most, if not all, areas of our personal and professional lives. In this first-year, Messina course, the principles surrounding human communication are addressed, connecting them to basic processes of speech, language, and hearing. Students invest time and energy exploring the impact of perception, difference, and language on human communication, both inside and out of the classroom.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to human communication and strengthens skills used in speech-language-hearing sciences work.

title: Professional Development in Speech-Language-Hearing Sciences
courseDescription: Introduces the scope of practice within the Speech-Language-Hearing Sciences through guest speakers who work in different areas of the fields. Additional focus on oral communication skills, resume writing, career discernment, and graduate school preparation. (Pass/Fail)
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in professional development in speech-language-hearing sciences and strengthens skills used in speech-language-hearing sciences work.

title: Introduction to Sign Language
courseDescription: Provides an introduction to American Sign Language (ASL) and explores Deaf culture and its history. Designed for students with no prior signing experience, the course focuses on developing foundational receptive and expressive communication skills.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to sign language and strengthens skills used in speech-language-hearing sciences work.

title: Sociolinguistics
courseDescription: The field of sociolinguistics deals with the ways in which language serves to define and maintain group identity and social relationships among speakers. Students learn to describe relationships between language and society, including regional and social variation and gender differences. Language variations are compared through the lens of phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sociolinguistics and strengthens skills used in speech-language-hearing sciences work.

title: Professional and Technical Writing in Speech-Language Pathology/Audiology
courseDescription: Students gain knowledge and experience in the area of professional writing for the field of speech-language pathology/audiology. This course is a writing intensive course where students learn the process for writing technical papers and are required to research and write a professional literature review. Students also develop skills for writing clinical reports, including the skills for writing goals and objectives.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in professional and technical writing in speech-language pathology/audiology and strengthens skills used in speech-language-hearing sciences work.

title: Intermediate Sign Language
courseDescription: Expands the student's sign language vocabulary and increase speed, accuracy, and fluency of sign language communication. Students develop more complex skills related to grammar, idioms, role shifting, and classifiers. Deaf culture and issues impacting the Deaf and hard of hearing community are explored through lecture and participation in local community events.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intermediate sign language and strengthens skills used in speech-language-hearing sciences work.
prerequisites: SP 214 or written permission of the undergraduate program director

title: Clinical Methods and Management in CSD
courseDescription: Students gain knowledge and clinical skills related to methods and procedures in communication sciences and disorders (CSD). Topics include roles and responsibilities of a speech-language pathologist including prevention, assessment, and intervention specific to CSD. Practical experience related to clinical procedures and requirements (e.g., simulated case studies, direct experiences, collaborative projects) are used in instruction to promote critical thinking and problem-solving designed to develop clinical skills.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in clinical methods and management in csd and strengthens skills used in speech-language-hearing sciences work.
prerequisites: Restricted to junior or senior majors

title: Clinical Research in Communication Sciences and Disorders
courseDescription: An overview of research theories and methods used in the field of communication sciences and disorders. Strategies for reading, understanding, and evaluating research literature for the purpose of becoming critical consumers are presented, and opportunities for exposure and involvement in research are provided.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in clinical research in communication sciences and disorders and strengthens skills used in speech-language-hearing sciences work.

title: Field Experience: Communication Sciences and Disorders
courseDescription: Designed to introduce students to clinical practice in communication sciences and disorders (CSD). Students work with CSD professionals in a variety of locations allowing them to become acquainted with and participate in various aspects of clinical practice. Students are responsible for transportation.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in field experience: communication sciences and disorders and strengthens skills used in speech-language-hearing sciences work.

title: Clinical Practice in Audiology II
courseDescription: Advanced supervised clinical practice; clinical experience at on-campus clinical centers and off-site screening settings. Clinical practice involves advanced participation in clinical diagnostic and assessment procedures, as well as administering preventative hearing screenings. Students are expected to interpret results of audiological test procedures.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in clinical practice in audiology ii and strengthens skills used in speech-language-hearing sciences work.

title: Introduction to Statistical Methods and Data Analysis
courseDescription: An introductory statistics course requiring no calculus. Statistical methods are motivated through real data sets. Topics include graphical summaries of data, measures of central tendency and dispersion, chi-squared tests, regression model fitting, normal distributions, and sampling.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to statistical methods and data analysis and strengthens skills used in statistics work.

title: Biostatistics
courseDescription: A non-calculus-based course covering descriptive statistics, regression model fitting, probability, distributions, estimation, and hypothesis testing. Applications are geared toward research and data analysis in biology and medicine. Degree credit will not be given for more than one of EG 381 or ST 210 or ST 265 or ST 381.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biostatistics and strengthens skills used in statistics work.
prerequisites: MA 109 or a score of 65 or higher on ALEKS or one year of high school calculus

title: Statistical Quality Control
courseDescription: Quality has become an integral part of the lives of both the consumer and the producer. Covered topics include the ideas of W. Edwards Deming; six sigma; Shewhart concepts of process control; control charts for attributes and variables; CUSUM, EWMA, and MA charts; and factorial experimental designs.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in statistical quality control and strengthens skills used in statistics work.
prerequisites: EC 220 or EG 381 or PY 292 or ST 210 or ST 265 or ST 381

title: Two-Dimensional Design
courseDescription: Students learn the essential elements of design through hands-on creation of artworks and verbal/written expressions of design concepts. Composition is addressed through employing the Elements of Art (line, shape, value, color, texture, and space) in combination with the Principles of Design (including movement, harmony, scale, and contrast). Students work with a range of media and learn to solve creative problems that include drawing, painting, and collage.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in two-dimensional design and strengthens skills used in studio art work.

title: Drawing
courseDescription: Through the education of hand and eye, students learn to draw in a manner that mirrors visual reality as well as to compose fully realized works that involve the imagination. Basic drawing principles and techniques are explored through line and tone in graphite, felt-tip pens, charcoal, and pastel on paper. Requirement for visual arts majors with a concentration in studio arts and studio arts minors.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in drawing and strengthens skills used in studio art work.

title: Life Drawing
courseDescription: A comprehensive introduction to the concepts and techniques for realistically and expressively drawing the human form. Skeletal and muscle sketches familiarize students with the structure of human anatomy leading to drawings of nude models. Media includes graphite, charcoal, ink, and pastel on paper.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in life drawing and strengthens skills used in studio art work.
prerequisites: SA 225 or written permission of the instructor

title: Drawing with Color
courseDescription: Color as a vehicle for drawing and composing expressive imagery using colored pencils and inks. Subject matter drawn from nature and man-made forms.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in drawing with color and strengthens skills used in studio art work.
prerequisites: SA 225 or written permission of the instructor

title: Introduction to Painting
courseDescription: Introduces basic painting techniques and theory. Students work both from life and conceptually.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to painting and strengthens skills used in studio art work.
prerequisites: SA 224 or SA 227 or written permission of the instructor

title: Watercolor
courseDescription: An exploration of the techniques of watercolor painting. Through various projects involving composition, perspective, color theory, and creative experimentation, landscape, still life, figure, and abstraction take on a new meaning.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in watercolor and strengthens skills used in studio art work.
prerequisites: SA 224 or SA 225 or SA 227 or written permission of the instructor

title: Abstract Painting
courseDescription: Looking at the tradition of abstraction in cubism, neoplasticism, abstract expressionism, color field painting, and minimalism, students create original works that focus on form, color, and texture. Through a series of painting explorations, critiques, field trips, and examination of work by well-known abstract artists, students gain a better understanding of what is meant by "content in abstraction."
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in abstract painting and strengthens skills used in studio art work.

title: Portraits and the Figure
courseDescription: Using the technique of painting in a single sitting ("alla prima" or "wet into wet"), students learn to paint the human face and figure, working from life. The course covers the preparation of grounds and supports and understanding of the tools, techniques and concepts of life painting. Students are encouraged to experiment and to emphasize the tactile quality of paint, concentration, and keen observation.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in portraits and the figure and strengthens skills used in studio art work.
prerequisites: SA 224 or SA 225 or SA 227 or written permission of the instructor

title: Landscape
courseDescription: Explores drawing and painting the landscape. Deals with naturalistic ideas, light being a primary concern. Students improve drawing and painting skills and media as they work in the classroom and at locations around the Loyola community.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in landscape and strengthens skills used in studio art work.
prerequisites: SA 224 or SA 227 or written permission of the instructor

title: Printmaking: Screenprint and Nontraditional Lithography
courseDescription: Introduces the materials, techniques, concepts, and equipment used in planographic (drawing and painting based) and stencil printing methods. In the nontraditional lithographic method, hand-drawn and/or photographic images are exposed on plates that are printed uniquely, in multiple layers, and/or in editions. Screens allow the printing of solid colors and detailed digital imagery through stencils mounted on fabric.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in printmaking: screenprint and nontraditional lithography and strengthens skills used in studio art work.
prerequisites: SA 224 or SA 225 or SA 227 or written permission of the instructor

title: Printmaking: Alternative Processes
courseDescription: Introduces the materials, techniques, concepts, and equipment used in the practice of printmaking, with an emphasis on mixed media methods and monotype- the closest printmaking form to painting. Processes that can be done without a press and some transfer methods are included. Water- and oil-based, black and white, and color inks are used.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in printmaking: alternative processes and strengthens skills used in studio art work.

title: Drawing from Observation
courseDescription: Through class work and independent assignments, the nature of observation and representation are the critical focus of this course. Working with a variety of drawing materials and conceptual formats, students explore subject matter and narrative with an emphasis upon observation. In successive projects designed to cultivate technical competence and conceptual autonomy, this course challenges students to develop a personal approach to space, form, composition, and content.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in drawing from observation and strengthens skills used in studio art work.

title: Drawing: A Conceptual Approach
courseDescription: For conceptual artists, the idea of a work of art matters as much–if not more–than its physical identity. In this course, students learn to produce drawings intended to convey an idea using both traditional and nontraditional media. Various artists' works that have influenced this art movement are studied as inspiration for students' creative solutions to assigned problems.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in drawing: a conceptual approach and strengthens skills used in studio art work.

title: Clay
courseDescription: Creativity and honesty in design is emphasized through handbuilding with clay. Students learn to make original works of glazed clayware and small sculptures using slab, coil, relief, and mold methods.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in clay and strengthens skills used in studio art work.

title: Sculpture
courseDescription: Students learn to recognize and use the elements that embody a three-dimensional work of art, defining and using those principles in a variety of media. Students are encouraged to discover new methodologies of visual thinking that reflect the interdisciplinary nature of art today. The problem-solving nature of this course includes both conceptual and observations-based assignments.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sculpture and strengthens skills used in studio art work.

title: Introduction to Theatre History
courseDescription: The evolution of theatre as an art form is explored, from ancient Greek to contemporary performance. Major theatrical genres/movements, playwrights, directors, actors, and designers are covered. An emphasis is placed on the link between society and theatre, focusing on key moments in the Theatre's development.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to theatre history and strengthens skills used in theatre work.

title: Experience of Theatre
courseDescription: Students experience theatre by performing different roles associated with theatrical production. Students act as readers, audience members, actors, reviewers, playwrights, directors, and designers. An emphasis is placed on students understanding and experiencing all aspects of the theatrical process.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in experience of theatre and strengthens skills used in theatre work.

title: Introduction to Dance
courseDescription: Students are introduced to a variety of dance styles including ballet, modern, and some social and ritual dance. In addition to training students in dance technique, improvisation, and composition, the course is also recommended to actors for training in movement. Includes visits to dance performances and screening of dance videos.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to dance and strengthens skills used in theatre work.

title: Modern Dance
courseDescription: The multifaceted dance form known as Modern Dance was born out of rebellion at the beginning of the twentieth century.
