This course considers how each subsequent generation has promulgated new rebellions yielding radical changes in subject, composition, presentation, and ways of moving. A commitment to continuous creative research is the through line driving modern dance.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in modern dance and strengthens skills used in theatre work.

title: Theatre Practicum
courseDescription: Requires supervised, hands-on experience in a particular area of theatrical production for a main-stage Evergreen Players, Poisoned Cup, or Spotlight Players production. Areas of concentration include acting, directing, set construction, lighting, prop and costume construction, stage management, and running crews. The faculty supervisor details responsibilities.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in theatre practicum and strengthens skills used in theatre work.

title: Theatre Practicum Capstone
courseDescription: Provides students the opportunity to apply the skills they have learned during their academic program to demonstrate fulfillment of the learning aims. (Pass/Fail).
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in theatre practicum capstone and strengthens skills used in theatre work.
prerequisites: Performing arts majors with theatre or comprehensive concentration

title: Improvisation
courseDescription: Focuses on listening and responding, freeing the instrument, and collaborative problem solving in the creation of spontaneous performances. Improvisation is also applied to rehearsal of scripted material and actor training. Topics include scene building, character development, comedy, and storytelling.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in improvisation and strengthens skills used in theatre work.

title: Directing II
courseDescription: An in-depth, hands-on study of directing which builds on DR 351. Students work with professional designers and hone their skills in all parts of the directing/production process. The course culminates in the public performance of a fully produced, one-act play directed by each student in the class as part of the Evergreen Players' regular season.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in directing ii and strengthens skills used in theatre work.

title: Solo Performance
courseDescription: The history, theory, and creation of the one-person show. Topics include historical and contemporary solo performances; biographical solo works; multicharacter solo works; autobiography in solo performances; and the development of frames, concepts, and approaches to the solo format. Students present part of a work-in-progress to the Loyola community.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in solo performance and strengthens skills used in theatre work.
prerequisites: DR 350 or written permission of the instructor

title: Stage Management
courseDescription: A thorough analysis of the technical, organizational, and interpersonal aspects of stage management. The focus is on preparing for, running, and archiving rehearsals and performances. Students observe productions, create a prompt book, and complete a major technical management project on a Loyola production.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in stage management and strengthens skills used in theatre work.
prerequisites: DR 251 or written permission of the instructor

title: Queer Theatre and Film
courseDescription: Examines plays and films from the 1960s to the present that tell stories about alternative sexualities including lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer identities. The course examines a wide range of texts while asking the questions: what makes a play, or a film, queer? How do we define this genre?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in queer theatre and film and strengthens skills used in theatre work.

title: Evergreen Players Production
courseDescription: Engages students in the cast and crew of the April Evergreen Players production in a learning experience that spans the entire Spring semester. In addition to a substantial involvement in the creation of a major play or musical production, students are involved in learning about the play through the study of dramaturgy, production history, time period, and other avenues. This course blends the studio instruction of the rehearsal and production process with the more traditional academic learning of the theatre discipline.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in evergreen players production and strengthens skills used in theatre work.

title: Introduction to Christian Theology
courseDescription: Introduces the Jewish and Christian scriptures, the history of Christianity, and the way these texts and traditions challenge, and are challenged by, the contemporary world.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to christian theology and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Theology and Catholic Autobiography
courseDescription: Why have Catholics produced an astonishing number of autobiographies? Is it because of Augustine, often credited with creating the genre? Or is it because of the place of spiritual journey in Catholic tradition?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in theology and catholic autobiography and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Catholic Church: Life and Thought
courseDescription: A survey of the seminal events of the two-thousand-year history of the Catholic Church. Because the Church's history is so vast and complex, and its membership so various, key events are presented through the prism of the lives and thought of major figures. Generally, the persons selected are canonized saints or those proposed for canonization; whether pope or lay woman, each is acknowledged to have lived a Christ-like life, sometimes under the most trying circumstances.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in catholic church: life and thought and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Friends and Foes: Jews and Christians through the Ages
courseDescription: The almost two-thousand-year relationship between Christianity and Judaism has often been characterized, at best, by fear and mistrust, and at worst, by violence and antagonism. Studies the relationship between Church and Synagogue from its beginnings in the first century to the current day.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in friends and foes: jews and christians through the ages and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Ignatius and the Jesuits: History and Spirituality
courseDescription: A theological and historical investigation of the Society of Jesus, arguably the most influential order in the history of the Catholic Church. From the religious conversion of Saint Ignatius Loyola in Renaissance Spain to the state of the Jesuit order in contemporary America, this course endeavors to clarify and interpret the intellectual, spiritual, and pedagogical vision of Ignatius and his followers.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ignatius and the jesuits: history and spirituality and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: The Reformations
courseDescription: A theological and historical introduction to the history and ideas of the period of Reformation. This course covers the end of the fifteenth to the middle of the seventeenth century. Students consider key cultural and social changes, from the printing press to revolutions; leading thinkers, from Martin Luther to Ignatius of Loyola; important historical moments, from the Farmers Revolt to the Council of Trent; and the theology, both Protestant and Catholic, undergirding these events.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the reformations and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: The Catholic Church in the United States
courseDescription: From the Colonial Era to the present. Examines the relationship between the Catholic Church and American culture. Special attention devoted to Catholic attitudes toward independence and the Revolutionary War; the trusteeship controversy; nativism; post-Civil War movements; American imperialism and neutrality prior to United States entrance into World War I; positions on foreign affairs, e.g., the Spanish Civil War, Fascism, and World War II; domestic background of the Second Vatican Council and ecumenism.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the catholic church in the united states and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: The Bible in the Twenty-First Century
courseDescription: Develops a student’s ability to read and to interpret biblical texts today with attention to theological interpretation, reading in community, traditional and postmodern theories of biblical interpretation, ethical reading practices, and reading the Bible as history, as text, and as Scripture.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the bible in the twenty-first century and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Race and Ethnicity in Scripture
courseDescription: Examines historical, literary, and cultural contexts of race and ethnicity in Scripture with particular attention to early Christianity and to modern biblical interpretation in America.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in race and ethnicity in scripture and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Forgiveness and Reconciliation
courseDescription: Explores Jewish and Christian traditions of forgiveness and reconciliation at several levels: in the aftermath of violent conflicts, through the lens of restorative justice in communities, and in personal relationships. From war crimes to race relations to the betrayal of friends, students dive into the question of when forgiveness is owed, and to whom. Concrete cases of local, national, and global conflict are analyzed from a theological perspective.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forgiveness and reconciliation and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: American Feminist Theologies
courseDescription: A survey of contemporary American female theologians. Students read major works from white feminist, Black womanist, Asian American, and Latina theologians to examine the ways gender and race inform theological reflection. While there is substantial engagement with theological doctrines, the class also engages topics that shape the lives of many women, such as patriarchy, environmental racism, intimate partner abuse, poverty, immigration, and family.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in american feminist theologies and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Christian Sacraments
courseDescription: Explores Christian sacraments - holy signs and holy things – in Christian history and contemporary life. Specific issues include the place of Israel and the Christian community in the teachings of Jesus and the early Church, the historical development of the practice and theology of the sacraments, and the past and present controversies over the nature of both Church and sacraments. Special attention is paid to the Roman Catholic tradition, but Protestant and Eastern Orthodox perspectives are also included.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in christian sacraments and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Theology of Happiness
courseDescription: Everyone wants to be happy, yet what actually is happiness and what are its sources? Is happiness a disposition or is it dependent upon external factors? And what happens when life does not go as planned?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in theology of happiness and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Introduction to Judaism
courseDescription: Evolution of Jewish belief and practice from Abraham to modern times; the historical relationship between Judaism and Christianity.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to judaism and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: African American Religious Thought
courseDescription: Americans of African descent have accumulated a variety of religious experiences and thought since the 1600s. This course places those experiences and thoughts in historical context and seeks to uncover their impact on and importance for theology, politics, society, literature, and the arts. Selected readings in Cone, Raboteau, Hurston, Thurman, and others.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in african american religious thought and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Christianities in Asia
courseDescription: Explores the major historical and theological moments for the maturation of Christianities in Asia, beginning with colonialism and the fifteenth century arrival of Spanish ships on Filipino shores. The course critically examines the work and legacies of Christian missionaries from colonialism until today in addition to identifying the most urgent cultural, economic, political, and ecclesial concerns within Asian contexts and the contemporary church's response. The course considers how Christian thinkers have engaged the other great religions of East Asia.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in christianities in asia and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Theology and Children's Literature
courseDescription: Explores such tropes as the good life (and death), family, power, God, etc. The extent to which theological reflection and children's literature can mutually illuminate one another is also explored. Readings include works of fiction and theological sources.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in theology and children's literature and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: World Christianity
courseDescription: Christianity is a global phenomenon. There are far more Christians living outside of the United States than inside of it. Diverse forms of Christianity from around the world are presented.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in world christianity and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Theology and Literature
courseDescription: Studies major themes in Christian theology which juxtaposes works of modern fiction and poetry with theological writing.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in theology and literature and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: The Christian Imagination
courseDescription: Is there a distinctively Christian imagination? What is the relation between faith and human creativity? Do, or should, Christians have a particular way of understanding artistic and literary expression?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the christian imagination and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Martyrs and Martyrdom: Theology and Ideology
courseDescription: Examines martyrdom and martyrs in the Christian tradition and its meanings, and then explores ideas of martyrdom prevalent among Christian, Muslim, and Jewish fundamentalist groups today. How have the notions of martyrdom been used to legitimate violence against the self and others? Topics discussed include imperialism, colonialism, apocalyptic groups, suicide bombings, and school shootings.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in martyrs and martyrdom: theology and ideology and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Sustainability and Community
courseDescription: Involves travel to and week-long participation in the work of Bethlehem Farm, Alderson, West Virginia, experiencing sustainable farm practices and serving the local rural community. Course material covers a range of issues in sustainability, and the role of community in supporting intentional lifestyles.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in sustainability and community and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Religion and Healthcare in Baltimore's History
courseDescription: Catholic, Jewish, and other religious communities have contributed to the creation of Baltimore's hospitals and community health initiatives since the nineteenth century. Students explore the unique ways in which faith communities promoted the emergence of modern medicine and healthcare in Baltimore, a world-renowned medical city with a vibrant presence of diverse faiths. Students learn about the impact of historic immigration on the creation of Baltimore's Catholic, Jewish, and other medical institutions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in religion and healthcare in baltimore's history and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Christianity and Islam
courseDescription: Examines the theological encounter of the world’s two largest religious traditions. Students in the course learn about fundamental aspects of Islamic thought and practice in the contemporary world, from Islamic law (Shari’a) to Islamic mysticism (Sufism). A special focus of the course is on the history and contemporary directions of Christian-Muslim dialogue.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in christianity and islam and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Ethics: Theology and Ethics of Hospitality
courseDescription: Examines theological sources and foundations for hospitality. Practices of hospitality such as monastic life, pilgrimages, and hospitals are contrasted with vices of inhospitality such as wrath, gluttony, and bribery. The class considers topics like individualism, friendship, and vulnerability that are applicable to issues like ethnocentricism, health care, and urban planning.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethics: theology and ethics of hospitality and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Ethics: Economics and Ethics: The Catholic Tradition
courseDescription: Examines key ethical issues in economic life from a theological perspective. Central questions include work, capitalism, socialism, entrepreneurship, just wage, just price, family economics, unionization, and the common good. The central resources for the course are the church documents and concepts known as Catholic Social Thought.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethics: economics and ethics: the catholic tradition and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Ethics: Introduction to Christian Ethics
courseDescription: Introduces the Christian understanding of the moral life through a critical examination of some of the classical texts concerned with this issue.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethics: introduction to christian ethics and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Ethics: Contemporary Moral Issues
courseDescription: An inquiry into the process of deliberate and voluntary moral decision, into the ways in which persons assume and assess responsibility for such decisions, and into the formation of conscience and character. Practical applications are made to questions of peace and violence, resources and poverty, marriage and sexuality, education, medicine and politics. Endeavors, through discussion, to share values, insights, and experience with a view to growth in freedom and responsibility.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethics: contemporary moral issues and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Ethics: Comparative Wisdoms
courseDescription: Examines central themes and questions of ethics through the study of various Wisdom traditions. It focuses on the study of wisdom literature in the Jewish and Christian Scriptures for their teachings about moral character. It also conducts a comparative investigation of wisdom literature from other traditions such as Confucian, Daoist, Buddhist, Greek, and Egyptian.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in ethics: comparative wisdoms and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Diverse Ethics in a Global Church
courseDescription: Analyzes debates in Christian ethics from a global perspective. While there is no shortage of ethical disagreement among Christians, this course focuses on key ethical divides that cut across our world today, such as gender, sexuality, race, and ethnicity. Disagreements over women's ordination, abortion, and LGBTQ+ inclusion have led to global rifts among many Christian bodies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in diverse ethics in a global church and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Christian Environmental Ethics
courseDescription: How are human beings to value non-human creation? Possible answers are considered to this question by drawing on both Christian theological/ethical sources and contemporary environmental science. The focus is especially on: 1) how to construct an environmental ethic in light of the constant flux of nature; 2) the relationship between ecological justice and social justice; and 3) the relationship between the global economy and the biosphere.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in christian environmental ethics and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: The Ethics of Disability and Trauma in the Christian Tradition
courseDescription: The body is a nexus of social, medical, and religious ideas. This course looks at how the Christian tradition, both in theology and practice, has engaged issues of disability. Specifically, the course examines disability in the Bible, medieval western Europe, and modern disability and trauma theologies.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the ethics of disability and trauma in the christian tradition and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Conversations/Controversies in Catholic Ethics and Morality
courseDescription: Spirituality is understood in its functional connotation, as referring to the world of the American Catholic Church in its social, ethnographic, geographical, and even political and economic dimensions and ramifications as they related to formal ecclesiastical life, sacramental practice, ritual activity, contemporary theologies, popular piety-common and persistent beliefs and practices, the line where religion shadows off into superstitions, attitudes toward death, conceptions of hell and visions of the afterlife, parish life, and regional contrasts among different parts of America. Accents what it was like to be an ordinary Catholic in diverse places at various points in American history.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in conversations/controversies in catholic ethics and morality and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Christianity and Its Critics
courseDescription: Beginning with the earliest followers of Jesus, Christianity has responded to criticism from those outside the faith and from dissenters within. This course investigates historical, theological, political, sociocultural, and philosophical problems related to Christianity and asks students to evaluate ancient and modern critiques of Christianity and judge the adequacy of Christianity’s response.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in christianity and its critics and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Health and Healing in Early Christianity
courseDescription: Explores the interplay between medicine, philosophy, psychology, and religion in antiquity and how these fields may overlap today. This course compares medical treatises from the Hippocratic corpus and Galen to early and medieval Christians who saw physical and spiritual health as intimately connected. It concludes by examining the possible benefits of these ancient insights for contemporary healthcare professionals.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in health and healing in early christianity and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Medieval Women Authors
courseDescription: An exploration of the social setting and theologies of medieval women authors, including such figures as Catherine of Siena and Julian of Norwich.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in medieval women authors and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Finding God in All Things: Spirituality and Prayer in the Christian Tradition
courseDescription: How do we find God? How does God find us? Introduces students to a wealth of prayerful practices, from the traditional to the innovative (e.g., "Jesuit breadmaking").
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in finding god in all things: spirituality and prayer in the christian tradition and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: The Theology of Thomas Aquinas
courseDescription: Thomas Aquinas was a major medieval theologian who remains as controversial in the twentieth century as he was in the thirteenth century. Studies Aquinas' life and social context, his exegesis of Scripture, and selections from his major theological works. Focuses on how Aquinas might be a resource for responding to contemporary theological, philosophical, and political questions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the theology of thomas aquinas and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Wrestling with the Old Testament
courseDescription: Engages a number of the problems readers confront when reading the Old Testament as Scripture. Explores interpretive approaches that help make sense of these texts and allow them to speak as a word of God for today. Topics examined include ethical lapses on the part of biblical saints; God’s representation as vengeful and punishing; violence; exclusion; and discrimination on the basis of gender, ethnicity, and disability.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in wrestling with the old testament and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: New Testament Survey
courseDescription: Students are introduced to the text of the New Testament, as well as a variety of historical concerns related to Second Temple Judaism and the Greco-Roman worlds in which the story of the New Testament is set and from which its text emerges.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in new testament survey and strengthens skills used in theology work.
prerequisites: Restricted to junior or senior theology majors

title: Old Testament Survey
courseDescription: Students are introduced to the content of the Hebrew Bible or Old Testament (the Torah, prophets, writings, and Deuterocanonical books) and to the history of its interpretation, including scholarly approaches since the rise of historical criticism. Also includes study of the history of ancient Israel.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in old testament survey and strengthens skills used in theology work.
prerequisites: TH 201 and one additional TH 200-level course
Restricted to junior or senior theology majors

title: Saint Paul and Early Christian Letters
courseDescription: Devoted to reading the letters of Paul in literary, historical, and theological contexts. Attention is also given to relevant topics in other early Christian literature, including economic issues and the relationship between faith and good works.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in saint paul and early christian letters and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Hope, Death, and the End of the World
courseDescription: This seminar studies the partly overlapping and partly opposed claims about the endtime among Catholics and Protestants, Christians and Jews, members of other religions, and unbelievers. Will everyone be saved, or will some go to heaven and some to hell? What do Christians mean when they confess that Jesus Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead or that they look forward to the resurrection of the body and eternal life?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in hope, death, and the end of the world and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Theology and Art
courseDescription: What is beauty? What does it mean to be a beautiful person? Can there be an image of a beautiful God?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in theology and art and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Faith and Reason
courseDescription: An investigation of the ways faith has reasoned about itself in relation to challenges in the ancient, medieval, modern, and postmodern worlds. The course eventually focuses on select problems in contemporary theology such as the nature and tests of truth; theology and scientific reasoning; reasoning about Scripture and tradition; God's own reason or logos; the truth of traditional claims about creation, incarnation, resurrection, and so forth.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in faith and reason and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Liberation Theology: Roots, Branches, and Critiques
courseDescription: Liberation theology emerged as one of the most important theological movements of the twentieth century. From its beginning, this movement has focused especially on explicating what it means to follow Jesus in a world marked by staggering poverty and structural injustice. Students examine the social and ecclesial contexts out of which liberation theology was born; consider closely several seminal liberationist texts; analyze various critiques of liberation theology; and consider the present and future of the movement.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in liberation theology: roots, branches, and critiques and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: The Resurrection
courseDescription: The Resurrection of Christ is central to the message of the Gospel. But what does the Resurrection of Christ mean for us? How do Christians understand what God has done for the world in and through this pivotal moment in history?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the resurrection and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Comparative Theology: Christian Encounters with World Religions
courseDescription: Surveys the theological encounter of Christianity with non-Christian religions, including Hinduism, Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism, Judaism, and Islam. The course examines a central text of a non-Christian religion as well as an example of Christian engagement with that text, either historical or contemporary. Students complete the course with a foundational understanding of major world religions, and are trained in the history and contemporary methods of Comparative Theology – the theological discipline of Christian engagement with non-Christian religions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in comparative theology: christian encounters with world religions and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Faith and Film: The Apostle's Creed in the American Cinema
courseDescription: Frank Capra, one of the truly great directors of cinema's first century, left us this testimony from the artist's viewpoint to the consequences of film's power: "Only the morally courageous are worthy of speaking to their fellow men for two hours in the dark. And only the artistically incorrupt will earn and keep the people's trust." The twofold purpose of this course is to analyze the meaning of the fundamental truths of the Christian faith and to explore the American cinema's capacity to convey those truths.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in faith and film: the apostle's creed in the american cinema and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: The Theology of Dante's Divine Comedy
courseDescription: Dante's Divine Comedy is widely regarded as one of the greatest literary works in the Western canon. But it is also a remarkable contribution to Catholic theology. This course surveys the Comedy's theology by attending to Dante's understanding of the nature of humanity and human language, sin and salvation, the relationship between justice and politics, and the possibility of knowledge of God.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the theology of dante's divine comedy and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: The Theological and the Religious in International Cinema
courseDescription: Going beyond a narrow evaluation of the morality of films or the mere recognition of their explicit religious subject matter, this course considers specifically religious or theological issues raised in non-American cinema. It also explores the theological implications of some international films that do not deal explicitly with religious issues, events, or even symbols. Finally, recurring theological and religious references are investigated, such as cinematic analogues of both redemption and damnation and figures of Christ and Satan.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in the theological and the religious in international cinema and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Poverty and Wealth in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam
courseDescription: Examines wealth and poverty from Jewish, Christian, and Islamic perspectives. Examples of topics covered include charity and financial ethics, voluntary poverty movements, the preferential option for the poor, usury and antisemitism, and Islamic banking. After completing the course, students are able to reflect theologically upon the economic conditions of the world as well as understand the distinctive contributions of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam in the realms of economic justice and financial ethics and practice.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in poverty and wealth in judaism, christianity, and islam and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: International Catholic Literature in the Twentieth Century
courseDescription: As the twentieth century comes to a close, perceptive readers of world literature are confronted with an amazing, some might even say bewildering, reality: a sizeable amount of this "secular" century's most significant and compelling literary works have been penned by confessing Catholic authors. Far from ignoring or even masking their beliefs, these writers go to great lengths to portray and dramatize them, frequently over or against the prevailing cultural and ethical theories, philosophies, and ideologies of the day. Stellar examples of such authors are Georges Bernanos, Paul Claudel, Shusaku Endo, Graham Greene, Flannery O'Connor, and Evelyn Waugh.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in international catholic literature in the twentieth century and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Eastern Christianity and Islam
courseDescription: Examines the intertwined religious lives of Muslims and Christians in Muslim-majority lands. Students study fundamental aspects of Islamic thought and practice, from Islamic law (Shari'a) to Islamic mysticism (Sufism), and explore the heritage of Syriac and Arabic Christians and their encounters with Muslims down to the present day. Along the way, vibrant forms of artistic and musical expression that have shape the religious lives of Christians and Muslims alike are studied.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in eastern christianity and islam and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Intentional Communities and Sustainability
courseDescription: Includes study of intentional communities, monastic and non-monastic, and the role community plays in shaping sustainable practices in rural and urban settings. Involves travel to, and week-long participation in the work of Bethlehem Farm, Alderson, West Virginia, as well as several field trips in Baltimore.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in intentional communities and sustainability and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: What is Patience?
courseDescription: This course doubts if patience is only waiting, watching, and worrying about time going by. In the same light, patience is not merely suffering in silence. Rather, as the early church Fathers proposed, patience has many connotations, uses, and requirements.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in what is patience? and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Class and Poverty in Bible, Theology, and the Real World
courseDescription: Assists students in understanding poverty from biblical, theological, and political perspectives. What did Jesus mean when he said “The poor will always be with you”? What causes poverty?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in class and poverty in bible, theology, and the real world and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Doing Lived Theology
courseDescription: Using theological method and contextual theology, Baltimore is used as a text. Students in this course learn to read “the signs of the times” (Gaudium et spes, 4), and how these signs present themselves within the historical context of the Baltimore area, in light of the gospel. In so doing, students reflect on how the life of Christian faith might be lived out concretely within the Baltimorean context.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in doing lived theology and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Theological Foundations of Social Justice
courseDescription: Explores theological, philosophical, and ethical foundations for social justice with particular attention to Catholic social teachings and Catholic social ethics. Students learn the ethical and theological imperatives for justice, such as those found in the Gospels, and apply them toward the development of their personal, faith-based theo-ethic of justice.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in theological foundations of social justice and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Deaf and Disability Theologies
courseDescription: Provides an introduction to Deaf and disability theologies, a growing field that provides transformative ways for thinking about God, church, and society. Students engage topics such as the historical treatment of Deaf and disabled people, biblical interpretations of disabilities, the theological underpinnings of the eugenics movement, contemporary models of disability, disabilities in relation to worship and the sacrament, and the current status of people with disabilities in the life of the church.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in deaf and disability theologies and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Justice, Peace, and the Integrity of Creation: A Christian Theological Inquiry
courseDescription: Explores the ways in which justice, peace, and the integrity of creation are interrelated, and examines the challenges that this poses for ethical action. Students examine the political ecology of the contemporary global context; explore sources of Christian revelation that can help to judge this context; and begin to consider how they might more fully commit their lives to social and environmental justice.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in justice, peace, and the integrity of creation: a christian theological inquiry and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Contemporary Catholic Intellectual Life
courseDescription: A team-taught course exploring the wide spectrum of contemporary Catholic intellectual life, focusing on the areas of theology, philosophy, politics, and literature. Students seek to understand not only debates within those areas but also attempt to explore lines of continuity stretching across the different genres of thought. For instance, how are the debates in philosophy related to different approaches to literature?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in contemporary catholic intellectual life and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Senior Capstone
courseDescription: Students work with a faculty director to develop a capstone project. The project may involve independent research, service or practical experience, or a combination of both. Students produce a minimum of 15 pages of well-crafted written work.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior capstone and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Theology Immersion Experience
courseDescription: Students may earn one credit through department-sponsored immersion experiences. Students are expected to participate in 30 hours of preparation and reflection during or after the immersion experience. May be repeated three times for degree credit.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in theology immersion experience and strengthens skills used in theology work.

title: Introduction to Poetry and Fiction
courseDescription: A foundational course designed for students who wish to pursue study in creative writing or those who simply wish to "try it out." Students read various examples of contemporary fiction and poetry to acquire a sense of context. They draft and revise original stories and poems in order to develop an appreciation of what it means to create literature in the modern world. A prerequisite for WR 300-level offerings in fiction, poetry, or playwriting.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in introduction to poetry and fiction and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Fundamentals of Film Studies
courseDescription: Introduces film technology and techniques, coupled with a survey of film history from the silent era through contemporary cinema. Students learn to identify the specific roles of the artists who collaborate to create a film. They also learn film history through an introduction to major directors (e.g., Griffith, Eisenstein, Renoir, Welles, Hitchcock, Kurosawa) and movements (e.g., German Expressionism, Italian neorealism, film noir, the French New Wave).
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in fundamentals of film studies and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: History of Genre
courseDescription: Students learn about the history of a selected genre, such as the essay, short story, novel, or poem. Writing assignments may include textual analyses and academic essays, as well as multimedia projects like presentations, videos, websites, and blogs. Topic announced each time course is offered.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in history of genre and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Writing for the Web and Social Media
courseDescription: Students learn about the conventions, theories, and ethics of online discourse and write for the Web using industry-standard technology. Assignments include research and writing in the Web's major genres: reviews, how-to articles, website design, and blogs. Students also build a website and compose an online portfolio to showcase their work.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in writing for the web and social media and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Style
courseDescription: Students learn how to recognize, discuss, and manipulate forms of discourse at the level of the word, the phrase, the clause, the sentence, the paragraph, and the whole text. In mastering a substantial vocabulary of classical stylistic devices, including figures of speech and tropes, students come to appreciate the link between linguistic form and audience effects. The stylistic skills that students acquire in this course can be adapted for a variety of public, creative, and professional situations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in style and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Writing Center Practice and Theory
courseDescription: Prepares students to tutor in the Writing Center by addressing both practical and theoretical issues of one-to-one peer tutoring, such as consulting strategies, the role of grammar instruction, the role of computers, and record keeping. Students read current literature in the field, develop a sense of themselves as writers, role-play tutoring scenarios, observe tutors in the Writing Center, and tutor students (under supervision). By invitation only.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in writing center practice and theory and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Technical Writing
courseDescription: Prepares students from any field, including business and STEM, for jobs that require technical writing with an emphasis on audience and purpose. Students learn about project management, workplace ethics, document design, and basic research methods working individually and in teams to create documents such as grant proposals, websites, presentations, and multimedia applications.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in technical writing and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Civic Literacy
courseDescription: Students investigate the theoretical and experiential nature of literacy/literacies as a central form of civic action and social justice. Students collaborate with a local adult literacy program in Baltimore in a project-based service-learning model. By integrating theory (readings) and practice (service) through a variety of assignments such as essays, journals, advocacy pieces, and exams, this course challenges students to see literacy as multifaceted and to think critically about the links between literacy and choice, power, democracy, and freedom.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in civic literacy and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Writing Fiction
courseDescription: Training in the art of the short story. Students write several short stories for the course, revising the best of them for their grades. Workshop discussions evaluate work in progress and completed stories.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in writing fiction and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Forms of Fiction
courseDescription: A study in short fiction in its various forms, including ancient tales to nineteenth-century sketches and twenty-first-century microstories. Students gain the historical and critical context necessary for understanding such movements as realism, fabulism, and minimalism, examining the stories themselves to see how each genre is distinct. Writing activities afford students the opportunity to explore various stylistic elements of the short story.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in forms of fiction and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Advanced Fiction
courseDescription: Explores advanced study in fiction writing for students who are already familiar with the foundational skills of storytelling. Students read a variety of contemporary fiction to refine their understanding of plot, character development, style, and point of view and use these stories to inspire their own work. The course is designed to provide students the opportunity to develop a portfolio of polished writing.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced fiction and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Writing Poetry
courseDescription: A workshop course in writing poetry, emphasizing a range of subjects and types. Contemporary readings.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in writing poetry and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Poetic Forms
courseDescription: Studies poetic forms and techniques borrowed from poetry's rich traditions. Students explore these forms in their own writing, utilizing contemporary readings and workshop discussions.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in poetic forms and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Advanced Poetry
courseDescription: A workshop in advanced writing of poetry. Readings from current writers.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in advanced poetry and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Screenwriting for Film and Television
courseDescription: Means and methods of narrative screenplay writing for motion pictures and television are explored. Included are analysis of the structure and dialogue of selected screenplays, exercises in writing and evaluating screenplays, and an investigation of how screenplays are marketed in today's media. Final project: a completed screenplay.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in screenwriting for film and television and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Writing with Images
courseDescription: Inspired by comics, graphic novels, advertisements, info-graphics, and more, students write a variety of image-enriched texts—from blog posts to posters—to learn how texts with images create powerful arguments.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in writing with images and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Biography and Autobiography
courseDescription: Studies the ways writers create a "self" and an "other" in language. Covers the range from private writing such as journals to more public forms of biography and autobiography and the imaginative use of those forms. Students read a broad sample of authors and types of writing and write three essays in which they experiment with those types.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in biography and autobiography and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Writing about the Environment
courseDescription: Explores various representations of the American environment from European contact to the present in this discussion based, reading intensive course. The following questions are explored: What is nature? What is culture?
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in writing about the environment and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Travel Writing
courseDescription: Students explore the prose genre of travel writing while living and studying abroad. They read in the canon of contemporary and traditional travel literature-newspaper and magazine articles, short pieces, literary essays, and nonfiction books. Inspired and informed by their adventures in the here and now of travel abroad, they write a weekly travel blog and two major essays.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in travel writing and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Writing about Film
courseDescription: Students produce a series of critical essays about film after viewing and analyzing works representing various periods and styles, including films by such influential figures as Hitchcock, Fellini, and Truffaut. Familiarizes students with film concepts, terms, and recent trends in film criticism and theory. They will explore in their writing questions relating to such matters as genre, audience, theme, and censorship.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in writing about film and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Literary Reviewing
courseDescription: Writing reviews is often a good way to "break into" publishing. Students learn reviewing styles of a wide range of publications and write reviews of contemporary poetry and fiction appropriate to several of those journals.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in literary reviewing and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Memoirs of Crisis
courseDescription: A nonfiction workshop with contemporary readings centered on memoirs of survival and witness. An emphasis is placed on the literary memoir as a vital form to explore the political, social, and ethical crises of the current era. Classwork includes discussions, informal writing, and student presentations.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in memoirs of crisis and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Thinking about Crime Fiction
courseDescription: A team-taught, interdisciplinary course reflecting on a major cultural theme - the detective - closely tied to justice. Not only does the course help develop students’ conceptual, writing, and rhetorical skills, but rather uniquely does so by focusing on a cultural object oftentimes exemplifying these very skills. Most fundamentally, the tight link between conceptual rigor and justice offered in the ideal of the detective is pondered.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in thinking about crime fiction and strengthens skills used in writing work.
prerequisites: WR 100 and one additional WR 200-level course

title: Senior Seminar
courseDescription: A reading survey of contemporary writers and trends in contemporary writing. Texts are novels, books of poems, and nonfiction prose written within the last 10 years and chosen to provoke discussion of what it means to be a writer today. Requirements may include reading journals, oral reports, issue papers that arise out of class discussion, and a culminating nonfiction prose project that takes advantage of the seminar itself and years of deepening study in core and majors courses.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior seminar and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Senior Portfolio
courseDescription: An independent study designed for students who have taken introductory and advanced courses in a sequence in a specific genre. Students select and revise their best work to date and add new work to create a portfolio appropriate for admission to graduate school. Extensive reading is also required.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior portfolio and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Senior Seminar: Creative Writing
courseDescription: A capstone writing course for writing majors and minors with a focus on creative writing. Students read innovative contemporary creative writing from a variety of aesthetics and genres and analyze the technical choices made by the authors. Students also develop their own creative writing throughout the course and significantly revise at least one longer piece of writing.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior seminar: creative writing and strengthens skills used in writing work.

title: Senior Seminar: Rhetoric
courseDescription: In this culminating course for writing majors and minors, students read primary and secondary source texts in rhetorical theory, historical and contemporary, to survey a range of perspectives on, questions about, and debates over persuasion. The rhetorical theory explored in the course comes from a diversity of rhetoricians in the Western rhetorical tradition, but theories from non-Western traditions are also sampled. The course provides students an opportunity to substantively revise work that could help them gain employment, apply to graduate school, or even become published, in light of one or more theories they encounter in the course.
whyRecommended: Builds clear, practical knowledge in senior seminar: rhetoric and strengthens skills used in writing work.
